questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman with a history of ovarian cancer presents with difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a seated position, and combing her hair. On examination, characteristic clinical findings are noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms of "difficulty climbing stairs" and "combing hair" indicate proximal muscle weakness. When this weakness is associated with an underlying malignancy (like ovarian cancer), it is a classic paraneoplastic presentation of dermatomyositis. This idiopathic inflammatory myopathy often presents with skin findings such as a heliotrope rash or Gottron papules. Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A) and systemic sclerosis (Option C) are autoimmune conditions that can involve muscles, but they are not as specifically linked to this pattern of paraneoplastic proximal weakness as dermatomyositis. Cushing syndrome (Option D) can cause proximal muscle wasting due to steroid excess, but the direct clinical link to ovarian cancer makes an inflammatory myositis much more probable. Dermatomyositis requires evaluation of muscle enzymes (CK) and electromyography for diagnosis. In an older patient, its diagnosis necessitates a thorough screening for internal malignancies, as seen in this patient's history
questions.learning: The patient's symptoms of "difficulty climbing stairs" and "combing hair" indicate proximal muscle weakness. When this weakness is associated with an underlying malignancy (like ovarian cancer), it is a classic paraneoplastic presentation of dermatomyositis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a patient presenting with a blister on the hand and axillary lymphadenopathy, which specific history-related questions should be asked based on the findings of the clinical examination?
options: History of similar complaint in family members
questions.explanation: The combination of a primary inoculating lesion (hand blister) and regional lymphadenopathy (axillary) is highly suggestive of Cat Scratch Disease (CSD). CSD is caused by the bacterium Bartonella henselae, which is typically transmitted to humans through the scratch or bite of an infected cat, particularly kittens. Asking about "exposure to cats" is the most specific and relevant history to confirm this clinical suspicion. Exposure to rats (Option A) would suggest conditions like rat-bite fever or leptospirosis, which present differently. Family history (Option C) is less relevant for this acute infectious process. A tick bite (Option D) could suggest Lyme disease or Rickettsial infections, but the classic presentation of CSD focuses on the regional nodes draining a feline-induced skin lesion. Therefore, identifying contact with a cat provides the crucial epidemiological link for the diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of a primary inoculating lesion (hand blister) and regional lymphadenopathy (axillary) is highly suggestive of Cat Scratch Disease (CSD).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Crigler-Najjar syndrome Type-I is inherited as an:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autosomal recessive disorder

Crigler–Najjar syndrome Type I is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by complete absence of the enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1), resulting in failure of bilirubin conjugation and severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Key features:

• Inheritance: Autosomal recessive
• Enzyme defect: Complete deficiency of UGT1A1
• Type of bilirubin elevated: Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin
• Clinical presentation: Severe neonatal jaundice with a high risk of kernicterus
• Response to phenobarbital: No response (enzyme is completely absent)
• Treatment: Intensive phototherapy, exchange transfusion, and liver transplantation (definitive treatment)

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The following instrument is used to measure which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proptosis

The image shows Hertel's exophthalmometer used to measure proptosis.
An abnormal protrusion of the globe because of a space-occupying lesion in the orbit is called proptosis. Exophthalmometry measures protrusion of the apex of the cornea from the outer orbital margin (with the eyes looking straight ahead). An absolute protrusion of >20 mm or a difference of >2 mm between the two eyes is labelled as proptosis.

Instruments used to measure proptosis:

• Hertel’s exophthalmometer: the most common instrument used. Its advantage is that it measures both eyes simultaneously.
• Luedde exophthalmometer : The simplest instrument to measure proptosis

• Naugle Exophthalmometer : This is a superior and inferior orbital rim-based instrument.

Pseudoproptosis occurs when the eye has a proptotic anatomic appearance that is not caused by a mass effect from a lesion displacing the globe. Pseudoproptosis is seen in high myopia (due to increase in size of the eyeball), ipsilateral lid retraction (resultant sclera creates the impression of the globe protruding forward) and contralateral enophthalmos (the normal orbit, which is situated more anteriorly, may simulate proptosis when there is none).
questions.learning: Proptosis — The image shows Hertel's exophthalmometer used to measure proptosis. An abnormal protrusion of the globe because of a space-occupying lesion in the orbit is called proptosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What test is not used for testing olfaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arnold stick test

Arnold stick test is not a test used for olfaction.

Tests used for olfaction are as follows:

1. Smell diskettes are used as a screening test for olfaction. Reusable diskettes are used with the application of 8 different odorants. A questionnaire with illustrations is used to score the patient.
2. The University of Pennsylvania smell identification test (UPSIT) is a commercially available, self-administered test used to assess the function of an individual's olfactory system via smell identification. It uses microencapsulated odorants, which are released on scratching standardized odor-impregnated test booklets.
3. The 12-item version of UPSIT, also known as the cross-cultural smell identification test (CC-SIT), is useful for quantifying smell loss when less time is available. This test serves as a means to reliably assess olfactory function in less than 5 minutes.
4. The Sniffin' sticks test is a new test of nasal chemosensory performance based on pen-like odor-dispensing devices.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with a blood pressure of 220/120 mmHg in an altered sensorium. He also had an episode of vomiting and a history of weakness on the left side of his body. Which of the following is incorrect regarding hypertensive management in this case?
options: In hemorrhagic stroke, reduce the BP to less than 160/100 mmHg with antihypertensives to prevent rebleed
In hemorrhagic stroke, aggressive use of IV antihypertensive if SBP > 220
In ER multiple blood pressure readings should be taken before starting anti-hypertensive therapy
In ischemic stroke, BP should be reduced to <140/90 mmHg immediately
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. In ischemic stroke, BP should be reduced to <140/90 mmHg immediately

Option D is incorrect regarding hypertensive management in this case.  In ischemic stroke, BP should be reduced to <185/110 mmHg immediately before doing thrombolysis.

In ischemic stroke, blood pressure is generally not aggressively lowered immediately unless it is extremely high (usually >220/120 mmHg), because maintaining higher blood pressure can help ensure adequate perfusion of the brain tissue and reduce the risk of worsening ischemia. Before performing thrombolysis in ischemic stroke, BP must be reduced to <185/110mm Hg immediately, and not less than <140/90 mmHg.  If the BP is reduced to <140/90 mmHg, it would further compromise the cerebral perfusion and can increase the infarct size. The goal is typically to avoid lowering BP too quickly, and a more gradual reduction is preferred.

Other options

Option A: In hemorrhagic stroke, BP should be reduced to less than 160/100 mmHg with antihypertensives to prevent rebleed.

Option B: In the case of hemorrhagic stroke, if the systolic blood pressure (SBP) is greater than 220 mmHg, aggressive lowering of blood pressure with IV antihypertensives is recommended to reduce the risk of further bleeding.

Option C: In the emergency room, multiple blood pressure readings should be taken to accurately assess the patient's blood pressure before initiating any antihypertensive therapy, especially in a setting like hypertensive emergencies.
questions.learning: In ischemic stroke, BP should be reduced to 220/120 mmHg), because maintaining higher blood pressure can help ensure adequate perfusion of the brain tissue and reduce the risk of worsening ischemia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient chronically on corticosteroids was diagnosed with a complicated cataract and his slit lamp examination finding is shown below. What is this type of cataract called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior subcapsular cataract

The clinical scenario of chronic use of steroids along with slit lamp examination showing a granular appearance in the lens is suggestive of posterior subcapsular cataract.

Posterior subcapsular opacity lies in front of the posterior capsule and has a granular or plaque-like appearance on oblique slit lamp examination .On retro- illumination , black vacuoles are seen which are swollen migratory lens epithelial cells called as Wedl cells (or bladder cells). As it is in the centre of the eye it has a significant impact on vision. Symptoms like glare are often perceived and aggravated by miosis , near visual activity and in bright light.

The following conditions mainly present with a posterior subcapsular cataract and therefore have a similar clinical picture:

* Complicated cataract

* Steroid-induced cataract

* Radiation

These cataracts present with central opacities and has difficulty in seeing objects in bright light because:

* When a person is exposed to bright light, the pupil undergoes miosis (constriction).

* These central opacities come to lie directly in the path of axial rays, allowing no transmission of rays.

* Therefore, there is an inability to see objects in bright light.

* However, in dim light, when there is mydriasis (dilatation of pupil), some rays may pass around the opacity, leading to an improvement in dim-light vision.

Cortical cataract is further divided into the cuneiform and cupuliform types.

Cuneiform (70%)
Posterior subcapsular/Cupuliform (5%)

Radial spoke-like opacity starting in the periphery and extending centrally

Central saucer-shaped opacity in the posterior cortex just below the capsule

* Cuneiform and cupuliform patterns can be made out at this stage.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A lady from West Rajasthan presented with an ulcer surrounded by erythema on the right leg. Microscopy of the biopsy from the edge of the ulcer showed organisms with dark staining nuclei and kinetoplast. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leishmania tropica

The above clinical vignette is suggestive of cutaneous leishmaniasis.

Leishmaniasis is a slowly progressing indigenous disease caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Leishmania. It is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Phlebotomus sandfly which inoculates the flagellated promastigotes into the skin of the host in developing countries. In India, it is endemic to Bihar, West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Uttar Pradesh.

Causative organisms include:

• Old world leishmaniasis: Leishmania donovani, Leishmania major, and Leishmania tropica
• New world leishmaniasis: Leishmania mexicana complex and Leishmania braziliensis complex

The image given below shows a phlebotomus sandfly.

The image given below shows Chiclero ulcer/New World cutaneous leishmaniasis.

The image below shows Lutzomyia sandfly responsible for the New World cutaneous leishmanisis.

In human beings, the disease presents in four different forms with a broad range of clinical manifestations:

• Visceral leishmaniasis, or kala-azar,
• Cutaneous leishmaniasis,
• Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, and
• Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.

The life cycle of Leishmania involves two forms:

• The promastigote which develops and lives extracellularly in the sandfly vector and
• The amastigote multiplies intracellularly in the reticuloendothelial cells of the host.

When the infected sandfly bites a person, infectious promastigotes are released into the host dermis along with the sandfly saliva, which potentiates parasite infectivity. Amastigote form (as shown in the image below) is also known as Leishman-Donovan (LD) body. It is an intracellular form found inside macrophages, monocytes, and reticuloendothelial cells. It contains a kinetoplast, which consists of a parabasal body and a blepharoplast. Flagellum is absent.

Promastigote form (as shown in the below image) is present in the midgut of the female sandfly. The kinetoplast lies transversely near the anterior end. A single flagellum is seen. It is the infective form of L. donovani for humans.

Given below is the lifecycle of L. donovanii.

This condition causes fever with rigor and chills associated with splenomegaly and hepatomegaly. It lowers immunity, causes persistent fever, anemia, and liver and spleen enlargement, and if left untreated, death may occur due to opportunistic infection.

Diagnosis of kala-azar is mainly by demonstration of amastigotes within macrophages in tissue aspirates such as blood smears, bone marrow, splenic, or lymph node aspirate. It is the gold standard for diagnosis.

The image below shows amastigotes located intracellularly within macrophages.

Tests to detect leishmaniasis include:

• Rapid diagnostic test: rK39 Rapid diagnostic test and Kala-azar dipstick test strip. This is recommended by National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP) in India.
• Parasitological diagnosis: Demonstration of LD bodies in buffy coat smear - confirmatory.
• Aldehyde test of Napier: Widely used for surveillance.
• Serological tests for diagnosis: Rapid dipstick test, Direct agglutination test, ELISA, indirect fluorescent antibody test
• Leishmanin (Montenegro) test: Induration of 5mm or more is considered positive, usually positive 4-6 weeks (delayed-hypersensitivity) after onset in cutaneous leishmaniasis, valuable for distinguishing immune from nonimmune subjects and endemicity.

Drugs used in the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis are

• Sodium stibogluconate
• Miltefosine
• Amphotericin B

In Bihar, there is resistance to antimony so amphotericin-B-deoxycholate or miltefosine is preferred.

Other options:

Option B: Babesia is a protozoan parasite that causes babesiosis, a tick-borne disease. Babesiosis manifests as a malaria-like illness with fever, chills, and hemolytic anemia.

Option C: Trypanosoma is a genus of protozoan parasites responsible for diseases like African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) and American trypanosomiasis (Chagas disease). These diseases present with different clinical features, such as fever, swollen lymph nodes, and neurological symptoms in African trypanosomiasis, and fever, swelling at the infection site, and cardiomyopathy in Chagas disease.

Option D: Histoplasma is a dimorphic fungus that causes histoplasmosis, a systemic mycosis. It primarily affects the lungs and can disseminate to other organs in immunocompromised individuals. The clinical presentation of histoplasmosis is variable, but it does not typically present as a skin ulcer with erythema as described in the clinical scenario.
questions.learning: Leishmania tropica — The above clinical vignette is suggestive of cutaneous leishmaniasis. Leishmaniasis is a slowly progressing indigenous disease caused by a protozoan parasite of the genus Leishmania.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 40-year-old man reports excessive, uncontrollable worry about everyday activities, financial matters, and his health for the past two years, accompanied by restlessness, fatigue, and disturbed sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) (Option D): excessive and uncontrollable worry about a variety of topics (finances, health, daily life) occurring more days than not for at least six months. He also exhibits the required physical symptoms, including restlessness, fatigue, and disturbed sleep. Depression (Option A) primarily involves a low mood and loss of interest rather than pervasive worry. Illness anxiety disorder (Option B) is limited to worries about having a serious illness. Somatoform disorder (Option C) involves multiple unexplained physical complaints. GAD is a chronic condition that significantly impairs daily functioning. It is often treated with a combination of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and medications like SSRIs or SNRIs . Because the man's anxiety is broad, persistent, and accompanied by physiological tension, GAD is the definitive clinical diagnosis for his presentation
questions.learning: The patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) (Option D): excessive and uncontrollable worry about a variety of topics (finances, health, daily life) occurring more days than not for at least six months.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is not true regarding naive T-cell interaction with CD4 effector T-cells?
options: PD-1 on T cell interacts with PD ligand 1 on APC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PD-1 on T cell interacts with PD ligand 1 on APC

PD-1 on T cell interacts with PD ligand 1 on APC is not true regarding naive T cell interaction with CD4 effector T-cells.

T-cell activation requires two signals that are delivered by APCs (Option A). They include:

• Antigens displayed by APCs in the form of peptides bound to MHC molecules, that are recognised by T-cell receptors
• Costimulatory signal (as it stimulates T cells in conjunction with antigen) provided by molecules on APCs that engage particular costimulatory receptors on T cells

CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2) are the costimulatory molecules present on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). They bind to the CD28 protein present on T cells (Option B). This promotes the expansion of antigen-stimulated T cells and their differentiation into effector and memory cells. (Option D).
questions.learning: PD-1 on T cell interacts with PD ligand 1 on APC PD-1 on T cell interacts with PD ligand 1 on APC is not true regarding naive T cell interaction with CD4 effector T-cells.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a follow-up case of prostate cancer, what do we need to check?
questions.explanation: Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) is the most critical and sensitive marker for monitoring the progression and recurrence of prostate cancer. Serial PSA checks allow for the early detection of biochemical recurrence after surgery or radiotherapy and help evaluate the effectiveness of hormonal therapy. Alkaline phosphatase (Option A) is a marker for bone turnover and may be elevated in the presence of bone metastases, but it is not specific for prostate cancer follow-up. Testosterone (Option C) is monitored specifically in patients undergoing androgen deprivation therapy to ensure "castrate" levels are maintained. Acid phosphatase (Option D), once common, is an outdated marker that has been superseded by the superior sensitivity of PSA. A rising PSA level is often the first indicator of treatment failure, necessitating a change in management. Thus, PSA remains the definitive follow-up tool

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An autopsy was performed to find the cause of death of a person brought dead to the casualty and it showed a fracture of the thyroid cartilage and bruising around the neck. The cause of death is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Throttling

Both bruising around the neck and the fracture of the thyroid cartilage are findings seen in throttling. Throttling/manual strangulation is when bare hands are used to compress the neck and strangulate.

Mechanism of death:

• Occlusion of blood vessels supplying blood to the brain (carotid arteries).
• Occlusion to airway probably plays a minor role if any, in causing death
• Carotid sinus pressure may result in vagus nerve stimulation, resulting in cardiac arrest (vagal inhibition)

Autopsy findings:

• Bruising of neck: due to the grasping of the neck by the assailant.
• Abrasions on the neck: fingernail marks from assailant or victim
• Fracture of thyroid cartilage
• Inward fracture of greater cornu of the hyoid bone.
questions.learning: Throttling Both bruising around the neck and the fracture of the thyroid cartilage are findings seen in throttling. Throttling/manual strangulation is when bare hands are used to compress the neck and strangulate.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is helpful in predicting the virulence of a disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Case fatality rate

The case fatality rate represents the killing power (or virulence) of the disease.

Case fatality rate = Total number of deaths due to a particular disease X 100 / Total number of cases due to the same disease

The case-fatality rate is thus the proportion of people with a particular disease who die from that disease. It is a measure of the severity of the disease, the deadliness of an outbreak, and may be used to evaluate any public health measures implemented.

Due to changes in the agent, host, and environmental factors in different epidemics, the case fatality rate for the same disease may vary in different epidemics. It is typically used in acute infectious diseases. Eg: Food poisoning, measles, cholera, etc.

The case-fatality rate is not a true rate, but actually a proportion. Hence, the term case-fatality ratio is often preferred.

Pearl PF0955: Case Fatality Rate

* Case fatality rate =  (Total number of deaths due to a particular disease)/(Total number of cases due to the same disease)x 100

* It is a good indicator of severity or killing power of a disease.

* It is used mostly in acute and infectious diseases.

* No time interval is used.

* Case fatality rate is closely related to virulence.

* Limitation of CFR is that its usefulness for chronic diseases is limited because the period from onset to death is variable.

* It is expressed in percentage.

* CFR is an incidence proportion and not a true rate.

* CFR may vary for the same disease in different epidemics.

*

Case fatality of a few diseases:

* Rabies - 100% especially after symptoms manifest

* Ebola - 25 to 90%, average - 50%

* Yellow fever - 15 to 50%

* Chicken pox - 0.001%

* Diseases with a high case fatality rate: Tetanus, Rabies, Botulism, Ebola.

* Diseases with a low case fatality rate: Leprosy, Trachoma, Lymphatic filariasis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient department with pain, redness, and swelling around his great toe. His serum uric acid is elevated. His mother also reports that he frequently bites his lips and has spasticity and dystonia. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The combination of juvenile gout (painful, swollen great toe with hyperuricemia) and the behavioral hallmark of self-mutilation (lip biting), along with spasticity, is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. This disorder results from a deficiency of Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). HGPRT normally recycles purines; without it, purines are shunted into the degradation pathway, producing excessive uric acid. Serum uric acid levels are typically very high (e.g., ). Homocysteine oxidase (Option A) and Dihydrothymidine oxidase (Option B) are not involved in purine metabolism or the Lesch-Nyhan phenotype. Xanthine oxidase (Option D) is actually the enzyme that produces uric acid; its deficiency would cause hypouricemia, not hyperuricemia. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is a rare X-linked condition, explaining why the patient is a male. Management focuses on lowering uric acid with allopurinol and managing neurological and behavioral symptoms with supportive therapy and physical restraints
questions.learning: The combination of juvenile gout (painful, swollen great toe with hyperuricemia) and the behavioral hallmark of self-mutilation (lip biting), along with spasticity, is diagnostic of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following conditions are contraindications for non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation in patients with respiratory failure? I. Craniofacial abnormalities II. Significant burns III. Respiratory failure with PaCO₂ of 60 mmHg IV. Cardiovascular instability Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Non-invasive positive-pressure ventilation (NIPPV) (e.g., CPAP or BiPAP) provides ventilatory support without endotracheal intubation. It is most beneficial in acute exacerbation of COPD with hypercapnic respiratory failure, acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and selected immunocompromised patients.

However, NIPPV requires a well-fitting mask, an intact airway, hemodynamic stability, and patient cooperation. Certain conditions make its use unsafe or ineffective.

The following are contraindications to NIPPV:

• I. Craniofacial abnormalities: Prevent proper mask seal and may make mask application impossible.
• II. Significant facial burns: Prevent mask fitting and increase the risk of tissue injury.
• IV. Cardiovascular instability (e.g., shock, life-threatening arrhythmias): Requires immediate invasive airway management and hemodynamic support.

III. Respiratory failure with PaCO₂ of 60 mmHg is not a contraindication. In fact, hypercapnic respiratory failure due to COPD is one of the strongest indications for BiPAP, provided there are no contraindications.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the current ideal total fertility rate (TFR) in India?
questions.explanation: In demography, a Total Fertility Rate (TFR) of "2.1" is known as the "replacement level fertility". This is the ideal rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, without migration. Achieving a TFR of 2.1 has been the primary goal of India’s National Population Policy since 2000. A TFR higher than 2.1 (like Options A and B) leads to population growth. A TFR lower than 2.1 (like Option D) eventually leads to a shrinking population. According to recent data (NFHS-5), India has actually achieved a national TFR of 2.0, which is below the replacement level. However, the "ideal" or "target" replacement level remains globally recognized as 2.1. Reaching this target is essential for long-term socio-economic stability and ensuring that the dependency ratio of the country remains balanced as the population ages
questions.learning: In demography, a Total Fertility Rate (TFR) of "2.1" is known as the "replacement level fertility". This is the ideal rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, without migration.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 65-year-old diabetic woman presents with painless loss of vision. The ocular findings are shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis and management for this patient?
options: Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL

The given clinical scenario and the above image are suggestive of an immature senile cataract and the appropriate treatment is phacoemulsification with posterior intraocular lens implantation.

An immature senile cataract is characterized by partial opacification of the lens. The cuneiform and cupuliform patterns of opacification are seen and the lens appears greyish-white. Iris shadow is visible. Slit-lamp examination shows areas of the normal and cataractous cortex.

The treatment of choice for immature senile cataracts is treated by extracapsular cataract extraction by phacoemulsification and foldable posterior chamber intraocular lens implantation.

Other options:

Option A: Zonular cataract is a developmental type of cataract in which opacification occupies a discrete zone in the lens. It is the most common type of congenital cataract presenting with visual impairment. Lensectomy is the treatment of choice for congenital cataracts.

Option B: Rosette cataract presents after close globe injuries (blunt trauma) resulting in damage to the lens fibers and capsule resulting in hydration of lens fibers by aqueous humor. This results in opacification of the posterior subcapsular cortex along the posterior sutures. It presents as a flower-shaped opacification. Iridodialysis occurs due to dehiscence of the iris from the ciliary body at its root. The pupil becomes D-shaped. Surgery is recommended in case of visual impairment.

Option C: Sunflower cataract is seen in Wilson disease due to the deposition of cuprous oxide in the anterior lens capsule and subcapsular cortex in a stellate pattern. D-penicillamine is an effective treatment modality.
questions.learning: Immature senile cataract and phacoemulsification with IOL The given clinical scenario and the above image are suggestive of an immature senile cataract and the appropriate treatment is phacoemulsification with posterior intraocular lens implantation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hormone is responsible for the development of the structure labeled as 1 in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estrogen

The structure labeled as 1 in the given image is the lactiferous duct, which develops under the influence of estrogen.

Estrogen stimulates the hypertrophy and proliferation of the ductal system and the stroma. It also causes hypertrophy of the uterus during pregnancy and relaxes the pelvic ligaments and pubic symphysis to aid in parturition.

Progesterone (Option D) leads to lobular growth and alveolar budding and causes the alveolar cells to become secretory. It also inhibits uterine contractions and is thus responsible for maintaining pregnancy. It stimulates fallopian tube secretions, which provide nutrition to the developing morula and blastocyst.

Prolactin (Option C) a hormone from the anterior pituitary, stimulates the secretion of milk from the alveolar cells. Suckling stimulates this secretion. Prolactin levels are high in pregnancy. However, there is limited milk production prior to delivery because estrogen and progesterone inhibit this process. Thus, after delivery, as their levels fall, the lactogenic action of prolactin takes over.

Milk is secreted continuously into the alveoli but is only ejected into the ducts during suckling. When the baby suckles, oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary. It leads to milk ejection due to the contraction of the myoepithelial cells that surround the alveoli. This process is known as the milk letdown reflex.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The following light reflex is seen in a patient. How much is the deviation?
questions.explanation: The image demonstrates the Hirschberg test, used to estimate the degree of ocular deviation. According to this test, each 1 mm of displacement of the corneal light reflex from the center corresponds to approximately 15 prism diopters (PD) of deviation. When the reflex is located at the corneal periphery (limbus), it indicates a deviation of roughly 45 PD. A 30 PD deviation (Option A) would be seen if the reflex was midway between the center and the limbus. 90 PD (Option C) represents a massive deviation where the reflex falls on the sclera. Degree (Option D) is not the standard clinical unit for this test, which uses prism diopters. Thus, the limbal position of the reflex confirms a 45 PD deviation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 34-year-old female presents with a lump in her left breast for 2 years. On examination, a 6 x 4 cm mass is palpated. Dimpling of the skin and bloody discharge from the nipple is present. The lesion is invading the pectoralis major muscle. Ipsilateral Level I and Level II matted axillary lymph nodes present. There was no distant metastasis. What is the TNM staging (AJCC 8th)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T3N2M0

TNM staging of the tumour is T3 N2 M0.

In the given scenario:

• 6 x 4 cm mass - T3
• Ipsilateral Level I and Level II matted axillary lymph nodes- N2
• No distant metastasis - M0.

In tumour size assessment, the greatest dimension is taken into consideration. For example, in a 6 x 4 cm lump, 6 cm is taken into account, and the tumour is classified as T3 (>5 cm). If 2 lumps are present in the same breast, staging is according to the bigger lump. If lumps are present in bilateral breasts, separate staging is done for both lumps.

Any contralateral lymph node involvement is considered as distant metastasis.
questions.learning: T3N2M0 TNM staging of the tumour is T3 N2 M0. In the given scenario: • 6 x 4 cm mass - T3 • Ipsilateral Level I and Level II matted axillary lymph nodes- N2 • No distant metastasis - M0.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A family consumes only polished rice. Which of the following combination of vitamin deficiency and enzymatic defect will be present in this family?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine-transketolase

The consumption of polished rice leads to thiamine deficiency which leads to defective transketolase activity.

Polished rice is rice that has had its husk, bran, and germ removed, leaving only the endosperm. This processing method results in a loss of nutrients, including thiamine.

Thiamine pyrophosphate (Vit B1) is the cofactor of transketolase. This reaction requires two cofactors:

• Mg2+
• Thiamine diphosphate (vitamin B1)

Transketolase and transaldolase are involved in the non-oxidative phase of the HMP pathway.

Thiamine deficiency can lead to beriberi, a condition characterized by peripheral neuropathy, weakness, and cardiovascular symptoms. In severe cases, it can also lead to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is characterized by confusion, ataxia, and vision disturbances. Thiamine deficiency can be prevented by consuming a balanced diet that includes unprocessed grains, legumes, and other sources of thiamine. Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.
questions.learning: Thiamine-transketolase — The consumption of polished rice leads to thiamine deficiency which leads to defective transketolase activity. Polished rice is rice that has had its husk, bran, and germ removed, leaving only the endosperm.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A neonate was brought with complaints of poor feeding, vomiting, acidosis, and cataract. Urine Benedict’s test was positive, while urine glucose was negative. The enzyme defective in this case is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

A neonate with poor feeding, vomiting, acidosis, cataracts, and positive Benedict’s test (reducing sugar present) but negative glucose is classic for galactosemia.

Deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT)

• Inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate → UDP-galactose
• Accumulation of:

o    Galactose-1-phosphate (toxic to liver)

o    Galactitol (via aldose reductase → causes cataracts)

Clinical features explained:

• Vomiting, poor feeding: After milk intake (lactose → glucose + galactose)
• Hepatic dysfunction → acidosis
• Cataracts: Due to galactitol accumulation
• Benedict’s positive, glucose negative: Indicates non-glucose reducing sugar (galactose)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Fructokinase: Essential fructosuria (benign)
• Sucrase: Causes sucrose intolerance (no cataracts)
• Lactase: Causes lactose intolerance (diarrhea, no systemic toxicity)
questions.learning: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase — A neonate with poor feeding, vomiting, acidosis, cataracts, and positive Benedict’s test (reducing sugar present) but negative glucose is classic for galactosemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient underwent a left submandibular gland excision during which the hypoglossal nerve was injured. Which of the following deficits would be seen in this case?
options: Deviated tongue to the contralateral side
Deviated tongue to the same side
Loss of taste in posterior 1/3rd of the tongue
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Deviated tongue to the same side

A hypoglossal nerve injury would damage all muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus resulting in deviation of the tongue to the same side. Since, the left hypoglossal nerve is injured in the above scenario, the tongue will deviate to the left side.

Hypoglossal nerve injury:

* Ipsilateral tongue atrophy

* Paralysis of all muscles except palatoglossus resulting in ipsilateral deviation of the tongue on protrusion

* Paralysis of geniohyoid and thyrohyoid resulting in deviation of larynx to the contralateral side.
questions.learning: Deviated tongue to the same side — A hypoglossal nerve injury would damage all muscles of the tongue except the palatoglossus resulting in deviation of the tongue to the same side.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: At what level does the spinal cord end in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. L1-L2

The distal termination of the spinal cord is the lower border of L1 in adults.

Because the spinal cord ends at L1, lower nerve roots course some distance before exiting the intervertebral foramina. These lower spinal nerves form the cauda equina.

Note:

In children, the spinal cord ends at L3 and moves up with age.
questions.learning: L1-L2 — The distal termination of the spinal cord is the lower border of L1 in adults. Because the spinal cord ends at L1, lower nerve roots course some distance before exiting the intervertebral foramina.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 40-year-old smoker presents with soreness of tongue since last 2 months. On examination, it is found that the oral hygiene is poor and there is a white plaque over the lateral border of the tongue. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Edge biopsy of the lesion

A persistent white patch (leukoplakia) on the lateral border of the tongue in a middle-aged smoker is considered premalignant until proven otherwise. The lateral border of the tongue is a high-risk site for oral squamous cell carcinoma, and any lesion persisting for more than 2 weeks requires histopathological evaluation by biopsy.

An edge (incisional) biopsy should be performed to confirm the diagnosis and detect epithelial dysplasia or squamous cell carcinoma.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Oral vitamin C supplementation: Has no role in the evaluation or treatment of suspected leukoplakia.
• B. Oral antifungal treatment: Oral candidiasis typically presents as white plaques that can be scraped off. A non-scrapable lesion in a smoker requires biopsy, not empirical antifungal therapy.
• D. Local topical cauterization: Definitive treatment should only be planned after histological diagnosis.
questions.learning: Edge biopsy of the lesion — A persistent white patch (leukoplakia) on the lateral border of the tongue in a middle-aged smoker is considered premalignant until proven otherwise.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) includes which of the following? 1. Asymptomatic neurocognitive disorder 2. Minor neurocognitive disorder 3. HIV-associated dementia Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND) is a spectrum of cognitive impairment caused by HIV infection of the CNS. According to the Frascati criteria, HAND includes:

• Asymptomatic Neurocognitive Impairment (ANI)
• Mild Neurocognitive Disorder (MND) (previously called minor neurocognitive disorder)
• HIV-Associated Dementia (HAD)

Why are the other statements correct?

• 1. Asymptomatic neurocognitive disorder ✔️: Included in HAND.
• 2. Minor (Mild) neurocognitive disorder ✔️: Included in HAND.
• 3. HIV-associated dementia ✔️: Most severe form of HAND.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient on Anti PD1 immunotherapy(Nivolumab) comes with pruritus, eczema, and urticarial rashes. Histopathological examination reveals a subepidermal blister. The direct Immunofluorescence of the lesions showed Linear C3 and IgG on the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bullous pemphigoid

In the given clinical scenario history of use of Anti-programmed cell death 1 (PD1) targeted immune checkpoint inhibitors with HPE showing subepidermal split and direct Immunofluorescence of the lesions showed Linear C3 and IgG on basement membrane is suggestive of bullous pemphigoid.

Anti-programmed cell death 1 (PD1) targeted immune checkpoint inhibitors such as nivolumab and pembrolizumab are associated with an increased risk of development of bullous pemphigoid. Histopathology will show the presence of subepidermal bullae with eosinophils. Immunofluorescent microscopy will show the presence of subepidermal split and deposition of IgG antibodies and C3 at the dermo-epidermal junction.

Bullous pemphigoid is one of the most common subepidermal immunobullous disorders. It is mostly a disease of the elderly. It is characterised by a subepidermal split, with tissue-bound and serum IgG antibodies against BP180, more than BP 230 antigens on hemidesmosomes, necessary to maintain the structure of.

Bullous pemphigoid is associated with psoriasis and treatments of psoriasis, like phototherapy and psoralen. There was an association seen with debilitating neurological conditions like stroke, Parkinsonism, cognitive impairment and multiple sclerosis, and haematological malignancies like lymphomas and myeloid leukaemia. It is also precipitated by drugs like diuretics, penicillamine and psycholeptics.

Clinical features include:

• Prodromal phase with excoriated papules, eczematous or urticarial skin lesions and haemorrhagic crusts may be seen.
• Bullous phase is characterised by:

• Intense pruritus is almost constantly present.
• Symmetrically distributed tense bullae and vesicles over the flexural aspects and abdomen of the body.
• Partly haemorrhagic crusts, erythematous plaques with an annular pattern are seen.
• Lesions heal without scarring, provided there are no superinfections.
• The bullae contain clear, sometimes haemorrhagic exudates.
• Nikolsky's sign is negative.
• Oral or mucosal lesions and milia formation are rare.

The image given below shows the lesions seen in bullous pemphigoid.

Histopathology will show the presence of subepidermal bullae with eosinophils. Immunofluorescent microscopy will show the presence of subepidermal split and deposition of IgG antibodies and C3 at the dermo-epidermal junction.

The below image shows linear IgG deposits at dermo-epidermal junction seen in bullous pemphigoid.

Untreated bullous pemphigoid has a chronic, self-limiting course, with remissions and relapses. Complete remissions are possible with treatment.

Bullous pemphigoid is mainly treated with topical and systemic corticosteroids. Other drugs used like azathioprine, dapsone, doxycycline and immunomodulatory are also used.

Other options:

Option A-Pemphigus vulagaris is an intraepidermal immunobullous disease. It occurs commonly between the 4th to 6th decade. They present with flaccid blisters. Firm pressure over the lesion separates the epidermis from the dermis. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Mucosal involvement will be seen in the form of buccal and palatal erosions

Option C-Dermatitis herpetiformis typically appears in the 4th decade, and the patients present with itching and rash, most typically over the extensor surfaces of the elbows, knees, buttocks, and scalp. The majority of the patient have symptoms related to gluten-sensitive enteropathies, like bloating, diarrhea, and other gastrointestinal complaints. Immunofluorescence microscopy will show the deposition of IgA antibodies in the papillary dermis in a granular or fibrillar pattern. Complement 3 may also be found along with the IgA deposits.

Option D-Pemphigus foliaceous shows antidesmoglein-3 antibodies, anti-desmocollin antibodies and a predominance of anti-desmoglein-1 antibodies. Lack of mucosal involvement in pemphigus foliaceous, where anti-desmoglein-1 antibodies are prominent, is due to the low expression of desmoglein 1 in the mucosa. In pemphigus vulgaris, where anti-desmoglein-3 antibodies are prominent, mucosal involvement is extensive in early stages as desmoglein 3 is abundantly present in the mucosa.
