questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Bell's palsy is characterized by:
options: Ipsilateral upper and lower halves of the face.
Contralateral upper and lower halves of the face.
Ipsilateral lower half of the face.
Contralateral lower half of the face.
questions.explanation: Bell's palsy is an idiopathic, lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII). Because the lesion occurs after the nerve has exited the brainstem, it affects all the muscles of facial expression on the "ipsilateral" (same) side. This includes both the upper half of the face (inability to wrinkle the forehead or close the eye tightly) and the lower half (drooping of the corner of the mouth, loss of nasolabial fold). In contrast, an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion, such as a stroke, typically causes "contralateral" weakness of only the "lower" half of the face, sparing the forehead because the upper facial muscles receive bilateral innervation from the motor cortex. Thus, the clinical hallmark of Bell's palsy is the complete paralysis of the entire same side of the face. Other symptoms can include loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and hyperacusis. Therefore, the "ipsilateral upper and lower" involvement is the key diagnostic feature
questions.learning: Bell's palsy is an idiopathic, lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII). Because the lesion occurs after the nerve has exited the brainstem, it affects all the muscles of facial expression on the "ipsilateral" (same) side.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient develops shortness of breath specifically during physical exertion in cold weather, which is relieved after using salbutamol. What is the most likely explanation for this condition?
options: Vagal stimulation due to cold air exposure
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction triggered by cold air
Airway hyperreactivity due to cold-induced asthma exacerbation
questions.explanation: Transient airway narrowing during or after physical activity is known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB). In winter, cold and dry air causes heat and moisture loss from the airways, triggering hyperreactivity and subsequent bronchospasm. This condition is classically relieved by short-acting beta-agonists like salbutamol. Vagal stimulation (Option A) usually causes bradycardia or nasal symptoms rather than exercise-specific breathlessness. Decreased cardiac output (Option B) is not the mechanism for respiratory symptoms that respond to bronchodilators. Cold-induced asthma exacerbation (Option D) is a general term, but EIB is the more precise diagnosis when exercise is the specific trigger described. Spirometry or an exercise challenge test is used for diagnosis, while pre-exercise salbutamol inhalation is the standard management to prevent attacks during intense activity in cold environments
questions.learning: Transient airway narrowing during or after physical activity is known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB). In winter, cold and dry air causes heat and moisture loss from the airways, triggering hyperreactivity and subsequent bronchospasm.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with corneal scar has a visual acuity of 6/36, which improves to 6/18 with a pinhole. The most likely reason for this is ____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Irregular astigmatism

The given findings suggest that the most likely reason is irregular astigmatism.

In refractive errors up to 3D, there is an improvement with pinhole to 6/6, if the macula is normal. Pinhole prevents the peripheral rays and also reduces the spherical aberration.

However, in this patient, it improved to only 6/18. A thing to note is that the corneal scar mentioned in the case would make the surface highly uneven, indicating irregular astigmatism. So, the best answer is irregular astigmatism.
questions.learning: Irregular astigmatism — The given findings suggest that the most likely reason is irregular astigmatism. In refractive errors up to 3D, there is an improvement with pinhole to 6/6, if the macula is normal.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding the effect of Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase deficiency?

1. Decrease in reduced glutathione
2. Decreased NADPH
3. Decreased lipid peroxidation
4. Decreased RBC membrane damage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 & 2 are correct.

Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes decrease in reduced glutathione and decreased NADPH.

G6PD is an important enzyme involved in the hexose monophosphate shunt. Defective enzyme function reduced the ability of red cells to protect themselves against oxidative injuries, thereby increasing lipid peroxidation and lead to hemolysis.

• G6PD reduces NADP to NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate.
• This NADPH then provides reducing equivalents needed for conversion of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione.
• This reduced glutathione acts as a cofactor in reactions that neutralize compounds such as H2O2, thereby protecting against oxidant injury.
• Exposure of G6PD deficient red cells to oxidative stress leads to crosslinking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains, which then becomes denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates called ‘Heinz bodies’, thereby producing membrane damage.
• When these inclusion bearing RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these Heinz bodies.
• The resultant cells are called ‘Bite cells’.

Clinical features:

• Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular
• Hemolytic anaemia
• Hemoglobinemia
• Hemoglobinuria

The episode of hemolysis is self-limiting, since only the older RBCs are at risk for lysis, leaving the G6PD-replete younger RBCs in circulation. The recovery phase is heralded by reticulocytosis.
questions.learning: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes decrease in reduced glutathione and decreased NADPH. G6PD is an important enzyme involved in the hexose monophosphate shunt.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following molecular analysis methods is used to detect monkeypox virus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Real time PCR

Real-time PCR is used to detect monkeypox virus which contains enveloped double-stranded DNA.

Real-time PCR helps quantify the PCR and gives an estimate of the pathogen DNA load in the specimen. It uses fluorescent dyes or specific DNA probes. It is also known as qPCR (Quantitative PCR)

Other types of PCR:

* Reverse transcriptase PCR: The enzyme reverse transcriptase (RT) is used to synthesize a complementary copy of DNA (cDNA) from RNA and this cDNA is then used as a template for PCR.

* Multiplex PCR: Primers to more than one pathogen are used simultaneously and hence multiple products are obtained.

* Nested PCR: It involves the sequential use of two primer sets. The first primer set is used for amplification and the amplicon obtained is then used as a target sequence for second amplification. This ensures specificity.

Other options

Option A: Sanger's technique was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins. The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin. Sanger’s reagent is 1- Flouro 2,4 Dinitro benzene. Only dipeptides and tripeptides can be sequenced by this method.

Option B:  Western blot, also called immunoblots, is a technique used to study protein molecules. The proteins undergo electrophoresis and then are transferred to a membrane. These proteins are then tagged with the specific antibodies and visualized.

Option C: ELISA (Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) involves the use of an immunosorbent, which is an absorbing material that is specific for one of the components of the reaction, either the antigen or antibody.
questions.learning: Real time PCR Real-time PCR is used to detect monkeypox virus which contains enveloped double-stranded DNA. Real-time PCR helps quantify the PCR and gives an estimate of the pathogen DNA load in the specimen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment option for an 8 cm endometrial cyst?
questions.explanation: An 8 cm endometrial cyst (endometrioma or "chocolate cyst") is a large lesion that warrants active surgical intervention. The most appropriate and standard treatment is surgical cystectomy (Option B), usually performed laparoscopically. Cystectomy involves excising the cyst wall, which provides higher relief of symptoms and a lower rate of recurrence compared to other methods. Needle aspiration (Option A) carries an extremely high risk of recurrence and potential spillage of irritant contents, making it less preferred. Medical management with GnRH agonists (Option C) can shrink the cyst temporarily and improve pelvic pain but will not resolve a large 8 cm collection. Conservative management (Option D) is generally only for very small ( cm) cysts; a large 8 cm cyst is at high risk for ovarian torsion or rupture. Therefore, laparoscopic excision is the definitive clinical standard
questions.learning: An 8 cm endometrial cyst (endometrioma or "chocolate cyst") is a large lesion that warrants active surgical intervention. The most appropriate and standard treatment is surgical cystectomy (Option B), usually performed laparoscopically.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the contraceptive device given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lippe

The contraceptive device shown in the image above is a Lippe's loop.

Lippes Loop is a 1st generation IUD that comes in four sizes – A, B, C and D. It is an S-shaped device, usually made of polyethene. The tail, which is usually made of fine nylon, projects into the vagina after insertion. The larger loops, used in multiparous women, have higher rates of removal due to side effects but have greater anti-fertility effects.

The Lippes Loop has a minimal amount of barium sulphate in it to allow for X-ray observation.

IUD - Intrauterine devices are contraceptive devices inserted into the uterine cavity. The different generations of IUDs include:

* First-generation IUDs : Inert or non-medicated devices like Lippes loop.

* Second-generation IUDs : Medicated with metallic elements like copper eg: Cu-T-220 C, Nova T, Multi-load Cu-250, Multi-load Cu-375.

* Third-generation IUDs: Hormone-containing IUDs like Progestasert, Mirena (LNG-20).

The various IUDs are shown in the image below:
questions.learning: Lippe — The contraceptive device shown in the image above is a Lippe's loop. Lippes Loop is a 1st generation IUD that comes in four sizes – A, B, C and D.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old child shows hyperflexible fingers and can touch the dorsum of the hand with an extended wrist. The child also demonstrates the sign shown in the image. On cardiac auscultation, a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is heard after the first heart sound. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This clinical vignette is a classic "pattern recognition" question for medical exams, combining dermatological, musculoskeletal, and cardiac findings. Key Clinical Features from the Prompt: 1. Gorlin Sign (Image): The child touching the tip of the nose with the tongue is known as the Gorlin sign. It is present in approximately 50% of EDS patients due to a hypermobile tongue/frenulum (but only 10% of the normal population). 2. Joint Hypermobility: Touching the dorsum of the hand with an extended wrist is a clear indicator of systemic joint hyperlaxity (a key component of the Beighton Score). 3. Cardiac Auscultation: A mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is the classic description of Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP), which is frequently associated with connective tissue disorders like EDS. Why the other options are wrong: (B) Marfan's syndrome: While Marfan's also features hypermobility and MVP, the Gorlin sign is highly characteristic of EDS. Marfan's typically presents with tall stature, arachnodactyly (long fingers), and ectopia lentis (upward lens dislocation), which are not mentioned here. (C) Loeys-Dietz syndrome: This involves aggressive arterial aneurysms and a bifid uvula or hypertelorism. While it is a connective tissue disorder, it doesn't classically present with the Gorlin sign. (D) Osteogenesis imperfecta: This is characterized by blue sclera, multiple bone fractures, and hearing loss. While there is some joint laxity, the core skeletal and ocular features are missing from this case
questions.learning: This clinical vignette is a classic "pattern recognition" question for medical exams, combining dermatological, musculoskeletal, and cardiac findings.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following lobes of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median

The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae.

Uvula vesicae is an elevation in the mucous membrane of the urinary bladder, behind the internal urethral orifice. It is often enlarged in benign prostatic hypertrophy.
questions.learning: Median — The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae. Uvula vesicae is an elevation in the mucous membrane of the urinary bladder, behind the internal urethral orifice.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A child is brought to the emergency department after consuming an unknown fruit and shows signs of poisoning. Based on the description of the fruit and the clinical features observed, what type of poisoning is most likely in this case?
questions.explanation: Datura poisoning (also known as thorn apple poisoning) is common in children who ingest the seeds or fruit. The plant contains tropane alkaloids like atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine, which cause a classic anticholinergic toxidrome. Symptoms are often remembered by the mnemonic: "Dry as a bone (no sweat/dry mouth), red as a beet (flushing), blind as a bat (dilated pupils), hot as a hare (fever), and mad as a hatter (delirium/hallucinations)". Poppy seeds (Option A) would cause an opioid toxidrome with pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression. Mushroom poisoning (Option C) usually presents with severe gastrointestinal distress or liver failure depending on the species. Cannabis poisoning (Option D) results in ataxia, lethargy, and a characteristic "stoned" appearance with conjunctival congestion. Datura is a common roadside plant in India, making it a frequent topic in pediatric emergency medicine and forensic toxicology exams
questions.learning: Datura poisoning (also known as thorn apple poisoning) is common in children who ingest the seeds or fruit. The plant contains tropane alkaloids like atropine, hyoscyamine, and scopolamine, which cause a classic anticholinergic toxidrome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 31-year-old woman who develops pain and sensory loss over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh following vaginal delivery is most likely experiencing injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
options: The lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh
questions.explanation: Pain and numbness confined to the anterolateral aspect of the thigh are classic for meralgia paresthetica, which results from compression or injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (also called the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve). This nerve is a pure sensory nerve that passes beneath the inguinal ligament, making it vulnerable to compression. Such injury commonly occurs after prolonged vaginal delivery, especially when the patient is maintained in a forced lithotomy position for an extended period. Compression may result from leg supports, prolonged hip flexion, or pressure from the fetal head. The sciatic nerve (Option A) causes sensory loss over the posterior leg with associated motor weakness. The obturator nerve (Option B) supplies the medial thigh and affects thigh adduction. The ilioinguinal nerve (Option C) provides sensation to the groin and labia majora. Most cases of meralgia paresthetica are self-limiting and resolve with conservative management, but correct identification of the sensory distribution is essential to exclude more serious motor nerve injuries
questions.learning: Pain and numbness confined to the anterolateral aspect of the thigh are classic for meralgia paresthetica, which results from compression or injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (also called the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In the context of contraceptive effectiveness, the Pearl Index is utilized to evaluate:
questions.explanation: The Pearl Index is the standard statistical measure used to describe the clinical effectiveness of a contraceptive method. It specifically calculates the number of accidental pregnancies (Option A) that occur per 100 woman-years of exposure to the method. A lower Pearl Index indicates a more effective and reliable contraceptive. It does not measure population size (Option B), the general fertility rate (Option C) of a region, or the number of abortions (Option D) . The formula for the index is: . This index is essential for clinicians to counsel patients on the "failure rate" of various methods, such as comparing the high effectiveness of IUCDs to the lower effectiveness of barrier methods. Therefore, the Pearl Index is uniquely and strictly associated with evaluating accidental pregnancies in family planning studies
questions.learning: The Pearl Index is the standard statistical measure used to describe the clinical effectiveness of a contraceptive method. It specifically calculates the number of accidental pregnancies (Option A) that occur per 100 woman-years of exposure to the method.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 21-year-old woman presents with multiple painless, beefy-red ulcers on the vulva. Based on the characteristic appearance of these lesions, which pathogen is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of multiple painless ulcers with a characteristic "beefy-red" granulation tissue base is pathognomonic for Granuloma Inguinale (Donovanosis). This condition is caused by the bacterium Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium). The ulcers are often highly vascular and bleed easily on contact. Chlamydia trachomatis (Option A) causes lymphogranuloma venereum, which typically presents with a small, transient, painless ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes). Haemophilus ducreyi (Option C) causes Chancroid, which features painful ulcers. Herpes simplex virus (Option D) causes clusters of painful vesicles that evolve into ulcers. The definitive diagnosis of Donovanosis is made by identifying "Donovan bodies" (intracellular bacteria) in tissue smears. Therefore, the specific "beefy-red" painless presentation identifies Klebsiella granulomatis as the responsible pathogen
questions.learning: The clinical description of multiple painless ulcers with a characteristic "beefy-red" granulation tissue base is pathognomonic for Granuloma Inguinale (Donovanosis).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with easy fatigability, back pain, and radiological evidence of multiple lytic lesions in the skull. Bone marrow biopsy findings point toward a hematological malignancy. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of bone pain, "multiple lytic lesions" in the skull (punched-out lesions), and anemia (fatigability) in an older adult is classic for Multiple Myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell dyscrasia characterized by the malignant proliferation of a single clone of plasma cells. The provided bone marrow histology confirms this by showing a "sheet-like proliferation of plasma cells" with eccentric nuclei and a perinuclear halo (Hoff). CML (Option A) and CLL (Option B) are leukemias involving mature myeloid and lymphoid cells, respectively, and do not typically cause lytic bone lesions. Hairy cell leukemia (Option D) is characterized by splenomegaly and B-cells with hair-like projections, not bone destruction. Common laboratory findings in myeloma include the "M-spike" on serum protein electrophoresis, hypercalcemia, and renal insufficiency (the CRAB criteria). Treatment involves proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulators, and potentially autologous stem cell transplantation
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation of bone pain, "multiple lytic lesions" in the skull (punched-out lesions), and anemia (fatigability) in an older adult is classic for Multiple Myeloma.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Identify the fracture shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The lateral elbow X-ray shows a fracture at the proximal end of the radius, specifically involving the radial head, which lies just below the capitulum of the humerus. The fracture appears as an irregularity and disruption in the contour of the radial head, a classic finding in radial head fractures, commonly caused by a fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH injury). Why other options are incorrect: (B) Elbow fracture: This is a non-specific term and does not identify the exact anatomical site of injury. (C) Medial epicondyle fracture: This would involve the medial side of the distal humerus, not the proximal radius as seen here. (D) Lateral epicondyle fracture: This affects the lateral distal humerus, whereas the fracture in the image is clearly located in the radial head region
questions.learning: The lateral elbow X-ray shows a fracture at the proximal end of the radius, specifically involving the radial head, which lies just below the capitulum of the humerus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: TB test done only on whole blood sample is ___________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Interferon gamma release assay

TB test done on a whole blood sample is the interferon-gamma release assay. It has been used for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis in patients with HIV(who frequently have a negative Mantoux test).

Interferon-gamma release assays include:

• QuantiFERON-TB Gold
• T-SPOT.TB

QuantiFERON-TB Gold quantitates the amount of IFN-γ produced by CD4+ T cells in response to the antigens from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT- Plus) is an improved version of the QuantiFERON-TB Gold test. QuantiFERON-TB Gold detects only TB-specific CD4+ responses. However, QuantiFeron-TB Gold Plus detects both CD8+ and CD4+ T-cell responses to TB-specific antigens.

T-SPOT.TB determines the total number of individual effector T cells expressing IFN-γ.

The TrueNat TB test is a new molecular test that can diagnose TB in one hour as well as test for rifampicin resistance. This test uses a sputum sample taken from the patient. Only about 0.5 ml of the sample is required. Gene Xpert is also a molecular method of testing that cannot use blood as a sample. (Option A and B)
questions.learning: Interferon gamma release assay TB test done on a whole blood sample is the interferon-gamma release assay. It has been used for the diagnosis of latent tuberculosis in patients with HIV(who frequently have a negative Mantoux test).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A man was brought to the emergency after he suddenly became unconscious while working in the field. On examination, his temperature was 105 degrees Fahrenheit and his skin turgor was decreased. Which of the following would not be seen in the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sweating

The given clinical vignette in a patient with signs of dehydration and a body temperature of 105°F is highly suggestive of heatstroke. Sweating would not be seen in a patient with heatstroke.

The body has various mechanisms to maintain body temperature within a range of 36–37°C. When the body temperature is elevated by exposure to high environmental temperatures or physical exertion, the central control area in the medial preoptic and anterior hypothalamic nuclei is activated. This engages the autonomic pathways that promote sweating and cutaneous vasodilation, causing the heat to dissipate and bring the body to normal temperature.

Heatstroke occurs due to the failure of the heat regulation center of the hypothalamus. The person fails to lose heat by cutaneous circulation and sweating. It is likely to develop when the body temperature rises to a range of 105°F to 108°F. The predisposing factors include high temperature, increased humidity, minor infections, old age, and physical activity.

It is a medical emergency that leads to homeostatic imbalance. The symptoms include dizziness, abdominal distress, vomiting, delirium, and eventually leading to loss of consciousness. On examination, the skin is dry, hot, and flushed, with a complete absence of sweating (anhidrosis). Other signs seen in heat stroke are tachycardia, Kussmaul-type rapid deep breathing (tachypnea), hypotension, cardiac failure, dizziness, muscle cramping, confusion, and seizures.

Heatstroke can cause damage to multiple organ systems, including the brain, kidneys, and liver, which can lead to life-threatening complications. It is essential to initiate rapid cooling and supportive care measures to prevent permanent injury or death. The cooling methods used to treat heatstroke include:

• Cold water immersion: The patient is immersed in a tub of cold water, which is the most effective way to lower body temperature.
• Evaporative cooling: The patient's body is sprayed with water while fans blow air over the body to help facilitate evaporation and cooling.
• Applying cold packs: Applying ice packs to the neck, armpits, and groin can help cool the body by targeting areas where large blood vessels are located close to the skin surface.
• Misting and fanning: Spraying the patient with cool water and using a fan to circulate air can help promote evaporative cooling.

Preventive measures for heatstroke include staying hydrated, taking regular breaks in shaded areas, and avoiding strenuous activities during the hottest part of the day.

Other Options

• Option A: Tachypnea - Rapid, deep breathing (Kussmaul breathing) can be seen in heatstroke as the body tries to eliminate excess heat through increased respiratory rate.
• Option B: Hypotension - Dehydration and vasodilation in an attempt to dissipate heat can result in hypotension in heatstroke patients.
• Option D: Red hot skin - Heatstroke patients often present with hot, flushed skin as a result of increased blood flow to the skin surface and the body's inability to dissipate heat effectively.
questions.learning: Sweating — The given clinical vignette in a patient with signs of dehydration and a body temperature of 105°F is highly suggestive of heatstroke. Sweating would not be seen in a patient with heatstroke.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient was brought to the ER after a road traffic accident. On examination, left-sided hydropneumothorax was noted. Thoracostomy was done and around 1800 ml of blood was drained in 1 hour. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
options: Continue resuscitation for the next 6 Hours
Administer a hemostatic agent through the chest tube
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Emergency thoracotomy

Given the significant blood loss (1800 ml) and the patient's critical condition, the most appropriate management in this scenario would be an emergency thoracotomy.

A thoracotomy is a surgical procedure in which an incision is made into the chest to access the thoracic cavity. It is performed in critical situations to control bleeding and repair injuries to the chest structures, including the lung and blood vessels.

In this case, the patient's condition is serious due to the combination of pneumothorax, hydrothorax, and a rapid blood loss of 1800 ml in just 1 hour. This level of bleeding suggests a severe injury to blood vessels or vital structures within the chest. Emergency thoracotomy would provide direct access to the bleeding source, allowing for immediate control of bleeding, repair of injuries, and restoration of stable conditions.

Indications for thoracotomy:

* Initial tube thoracostomy drainage of >1000 ml (penetrating injury) or >1500 ml (blunt injury) of frank blood

* Ongoing tube thoracostomy drainage of >200 ml/ hr for 3 consecutive hours in non-coagulopathic patients with hemothorax

* Caked hemothorax despite the placement of two chest tubes

* Massive air leak from chest tube with inadequate ventilation

* Open pneumothorax

* Great vessel injury

* Pericardial tamponade

* Cardiac herniation

* Tracheobronchial injury

* Esophageal perforation

Other Options:

Option A: Thoracentesis involves the removal of fluid or air from the pleural space using a needle or catheter. However, given the severity of the situation with rapid blood loss, this procedure alone would not adequately address the underlying issues or stop the significant bleeding.

Option B: Continued resuscitation for the next 6 hours is not appropriate in this scenario due to the patient's critical condition and substantial blood loss. Immediate intervention is required to stabilize the patient's condition and address the underlying causes of the blood loss.

Option C: While hemostatic agents can be useful in certain bleeding situations, the rapid blood loss and critical nature of the presented case call for a more immediate and direct approach, such as an emergency thoracotomy, to achieve rapid control of bleeding and prevent further complications.
questions.learning: Emergency thoracotomy Given the significant blood loss (1800 ml) and the patient's critical condition, the most appropriate management in this scenario would be an emergency thoracotomy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following provides valuable information about the reproductive behavior of couples within a population?
questions.explanation: The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is defined as the average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her childbearing years (15–49) experiencing the age-specific fertility rates of a given year. It is considered the most comprehensive indicator of the reproductive behavior of couples and the ultimate completed family size in a population. The General Fertility Rate (GFR, Option C) is a simpler measure of the number of births per 1,000 women of reproductive age. The Gross Reproduction Rate (GRR, Option D) measures only the average number of daughters born, while the Net Reproduction Rate (NRR, Option B) also accounts for the mother's survival to reproductive age. TFR is a critical metric for demographic planning; a TFR of 2.1 is known as "replacement-level fertility," the rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next without migration. Most developed nations have a TFR below this level, while many developing nations are working toward this target to stabilize population growth
questions.learning: The Total Fertility Rate (TFR) is defined as the average number of children a woman would have if she were to pass through her childbearing years (15–49) experiencing the age-specific fertility rates of a given year.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman who underwent a forceps-assisted delivery 24 hours ago presents with severe perineal pain. Her blood pressure is 80/60 mmHg, and examination reveals a perineal swelling with bluish discoloration. Which of the following management steps should not be performed in this situation??
options: Repair the wound in the ward
questions.explanation: This patient is presenting with a postpartum vulvar hematoma, a serious complication of instrumental delivery. The hypotension (BP 80/60) indicates significant internal blood loss and impending shock. Attempting to repair or explore the wound in the ward (Option A) is dangerous and strictly discouraged, as it does not allow for proper anesthesia, sterile conditions, or the adequate lighting needed to achieve complete hemostasis. Shifting the patient to the Operating Theater (Option C) for surgical exploration and ligation of the bleeding vessel is the correct management. Giving a blood transfusion (Option B) is essential to stabilize her hemodynamics. Informing a senior obstetrician (Option D) is also mandatory for expert management of a life-threatening hemorrhage. Therefore, the only inappropriate action is attempting a bedside repair in an unstable patient
questions.learning: This patient is presenting with a postpartum vulvar hematoma, a serious complication of instrumental delivery. The hypotension (BP 80/60) indicates significant internal blood loss and impending shock.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: McCall culdoplasty is done in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Enterocele repair

McCall's culdoplasty is used in enterocele repair.

An enterocele is herniation of the pouch of Douglas and small bowel loops into the rectovaginal septum. Enteroceles are most commonly associated with uterine prolapse. Patients present with the following clinical features:

* Fecal incontinence

* Sexual dysfunction

* Constipation/diarrhea

* Mass descending PV

* Pelvic pain or pelvic discomfort

* A bulge in the posterior vaginal wall:

* Upper 1/3rd - enterocele

* Lower 2/3rd - rectocele

* Peristalsis may be observed in the bulge

Enterocele repair is done via the following methods:

* Vaginal approach - it is usually preferred over an abdominal approach. In McCall's culdoplasty, the uterosacral ligaments are used to suspend the vaginal vault. The posterior peritoneum and uterosacral ligaments are approximated.

* Abdominal approach - it is preferred in cases where there is associated fecal incontinence. It includes:

* Moschcowitz repair - the pouch of Douglas is obliterated by several purse-string sutures.

* Halban's procedure - the peritoneal sac is obliterated using vertical sutures. This can also be done transvaginally.
questions.learning: Enterocele repair McCall's culdoplasty is used in enterocele repair. An enterocele is herniation of the pouch of Douglas and small bowel loops into the rectovaginal septum.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a unilateral throbbing headache associated with nausea and vomiting. She has had similar episodes in the past where the headache usually lasts for 1-2 days, and she prefers sitting in a dark room during the attacks. She also gives a history of a myocardial infarction 2 years ago. Which of the following drugs cannot be prescribed to this patient to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sumatriptan

The clinical vignette is suggestive of an acute attack of migraine. Sumatriptan is contraindicated in a patient with a history of myocardial infarction.

Triptans are selective 5HT 1B/1D agonists. They are indicated in the management of acute attacks of migraine. They act by arresting the nociceptive nerve signalling in the trigeminovascular system. They also act by vasoconstricting, not only the intracranial vessels but other vessels too. Hence it is contraindicated in patients with a history of ischemic or vasospastic coronary artery disease (history of stroke or transient ischemic attacks), cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic or basilar migraines, or ischemic bowel diseases. Triptans are also contraindicated in patients with uncontrolled hypertension.

Migraine is the second most common cause of headaches and is seen more commonly in women. It presents as an episodic headache associated with nausea, vomiting, photosensitivity, and sensitivity to sound (phonophobia). Common triggers include bright lights, sounds, and hunger. The release of vasoactive peptides such as calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) by the trigeminal nucleus cells is the theory used to explain the pathogenesis of the condition. The neurotransmitters serotonin and dopamine also play a part.

A migraine attack has four phases: premonitory (prodrome), aura, headache, and postdrome; each has distinct and sometimes disabling symptoms, which may overlap.

Migraine can broadly be classified into:

* Migraine without aura (70-80%): Common migraine.

* Migraine with aura (20-30%): Classic migraine.

The migraine disability assessment score (MIDAS) can be used to assess the severity of the condition. Avoidance of recognized triggers is helpful to avoid symptoms. The various drugs used to treat an acute attack of migraine are:

* Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen (Option C)

* Triptans

* CGRP Receptor Antagonists (rimegepant)

* 5-HT1/F receptor agonists (lasmiditan- Option D)

* Dopamine receptor antagonists (domperidone)

The various FDA-approved drugs used in prophylaxis include propranolol (Option A), valproate, topiramate, and flunarizine.

Pearl PF1050: Simplified diagnostic criteria for migraine

Repeated attacks of headache lasting 4-72 h in patients with a normal physical examination, no other reasonable cause for the headache, and

At Least 2 of the following features

* Unilateral pain

* Throbbing pain

* Aggravation by movement

* Moderate or severe intensity

Plus at Least 1 of the following features

* Nausea/vomiting

* Photophobia and phonophobia
questions.learning: Sumatriptan — The clinical vignette is suggestive of an acute attack of migraine. Sumatriptan is contraindicated in a patient with a history of myocardial infarction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What defect is seen in Bernard Soulier syndrome?
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive bleeding disorder characterized by a primary defect in platelet adhesion. The underlying pathology is a deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet membrane glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) complex. This complex acts as the essential receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF); without it, platelets cannot adhere to the exposed subendothelial matrix during vascular injury. Patients typically present with mucocutaneous bleeding and thrombocytopenia with characteristic "giant platelets" on a peripheral smear. Deficiency of the GpIIb/IIIa receptor (Option A) is seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia, which affects platelet aggregation. Deficiency of von Willebrand factor (Option C) defines von Willebrand disease. Deficiency of ADP receptors (Option D) occurs in rare disorders like P2Y12 defects, impacting the aggregation pathway. Therefore, the GpIb receptor defect is the specific hallmark of Bernard-Soulier syndrome
questions.learning: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive bleeding disorder characterized by a primary defect in platelet adhesion. The underlying pathology is a deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet membrane glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) complex.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The world's only licensed malaria vaccine, MOSQUIRIX (RTS,S), is prepared from which component of Plasmodium falciparum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Circumsporozoite protein

RTS,S (brand name MOSQUIRIX) is a recombinant protein-based vaccine that targets the circumsporozoite protein (CSP) of Plasmodium falciparum, the protein found on the surface of the sporozoite — the pre-erythrocytic stage injected by the Anopheles mosquito during a bite.

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Vaccine name | RTS,S / MOSQUIRIX

| Target antigen | Circumsporozoite protein (CSP) of P. falciparum

| Carrier/adjuvant | Fused with Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) + AS01 adjuvant

| Status | First licensed malaria vaccine

| Efficacy | \~26–50% (partial protection, wanes over time)

| Stage targeted | Pre-erythrocytic (sporozoite stage) — prevents hepatocyte invasion

Why each distractor is wrong:

• A. Gametocytic protein — Gametocyte-stage antigens are the target of transmission-blocking vaccine candidates (e.g., Pfs25), not RTS,S.
• B. Polysaccharide sheath — Plasmodium has no polysaccharide capsule/sheath; this is a feature of certain bacteria (e.g., pneumococcus), not protozoa.
• D. Lipoprotein envelope — Malaria parasites don't have a lipoprotein envelope in the way enveloped viruses do; this is a distractor with no real basis in Plasmodium biology.

Exam Pearl: Remember "CSP for Circumsporozoite" — RTS,S works by inducing antibodies + CD4+ T-cell response against CSP, blocking sporozoites from invading hepatocytes. A newer vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, also targets CSP but with higher efficacy (\~70-80%) and was WHO-recommended after RTS,S — good to remember for newer-pattern questions, since INICET/NEET PG increasingly tests recent WHO vaccine recommendations.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with hemoptysis, blood-coloured nasal discharge. On examination, there is septal perforation. Biopsy from the nose shows necrosis and non-caseating granuloma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wegener's granulomatosis

The given clinical scenario showing septal perforation, bloody nasal discharge with non caseating granuloma is suggestive of Wegener's granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

Wegener's granulomatosis is a systemic disorder which primarily involve the upper airways, lungs, kidneys, and the skin

Involvement of the upper respiratory tract in granulomatosis with polyangiitis manifests as:

* Paranasal sinusitis, serous otitis media

* Nasal ulcers, purulent or bloody nasal discharge

* Nasal perforation leading to the destruction of septum and saddle nose deformity

* Subglottic tracheal stenosis

General symptoms like fatigue night sweats, and arthralgia is also seen. Once lung involvement happens, cough and hemoptysis begins. Renal involvement is late and is detected as RBC and casts in urine.

Diagnosis is primarily by nasal biopsy which will show necrosis and non-caseating granuloma. X-ray chest will show cavitations in case of lung involvement.

Management consists of systemic steroids, cyclophosphamide and azathioprine

Other options:

Option A: Tuberculosis presents with generalised symptoms but is accompanies by a caseating granuloma

Option B: Leprosy can present as a deformity on the nose and nasal perforation but is often accompanied by crusting. It is also accompanied by skin symptoms like anaesthesia and nerve involvement

Option C: Sarcoidosis presents as nodules on the septum and epistaxis but presents without caseation
questions.learning: Wegener's granulomatosis — The given clinical scenario showing septal perforation, bloody nasal discharge with non caseating granuloma is suggestive of Wegener's granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A group of experts each delivers an individual speech on a common topic without any discussion among them, and one person provides a summary at the end. What is this type of academic session called?
options: Workshop (B) Symposium A Symposium is an academic session where multiple experts present prepared individual speeches or papers on different aspects of a single common topic. A defining characteristic of a symposium is the lack of interaction or discussion between the experts themselves during the presentations; instead, a chairperson or moderator provides a summary of the key points at the conclusion. In a Panel Discussion (Option A), the experts interact with each other and often engage in a Q&A session with the audience. A Seminar (Option C) is usually a more interactive study session for a smaller group led by an expert. A Workshop (Option D) emphasizes hands-on, practical training and active participation by all attendees to learn a specific skill. Therefore, the "serial speech" format without inter-panel discussion is specific to a symposium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman whose last delivery was 5 years back presents with secondary amenorrhea of 2 years. She does not bleed on giving estrogen and progesterone. A laparoscopy shows the following. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Genital TB

Absence of withdrawal bleeding after estrogen–progesterone challenge indicates endometrial damage. Laparoscopic caseous nodules and tubercles are classic for genital tuberculosis, which destroys the endometrium and causes amenorrhea.
questions.learning: Genital TB Absence of withdrawal bleeding after estrogen–progesterone challenge indicates endometrial damage. Laparoscopic caseous nodules and tubercles are classic for genital tuberculosis, which destroys the endometrium and causes amenorrhea.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Frozen section was done during the surgery of carcinoma breast. This procedure will be useful for all except
options: To confirm definitive diagnosis immediately in all cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. To confirm definitive diagnosis immediately in all cases

Frozen section analysis performed during breast carcinoma surgery is not suitable for definitive diagnosis due to technical challenges, potential quality issues in processing and staining, and the difficulty of obtaining accurate results.

Frozen section analysis is performed when a prompt biopsy report is required, allowing the surgeon to make immediate decisions regarding the further steps of management.

• Frozen section analysis plays a valuable role in assessing involvement of sentinel lymph nodes during surgery (option A). When a positive node is identified intraoperatively, the surgeon can proceed with immediate axillary lymph node clearance. On the other hand, if the sentinel node does not show tumor involvement, further axillary dissection can be avoided.
• It also helps in diagnosing nodal metastasis in clinically identified lymph nodes (option C). However, it may not detect subcapsular micrometastases.
• While performing breast-conserving surgeries, assessment of tumor margins (option B) using frozen sections is helpful in ensuring complete tumor excision.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of the primary survey?
options: Removing clothes to inspect for wounds
Taking CT scan of the patient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Taking CT scan of the patient

Taking a CT scan of the patient is a part of secondary survey.

Primary survey identifies and manages the most immediately life-threatening pathologies first.

The secondary survey includes investigations that help identify all other injuries, excluding the apparent ones. This includes X-rays of the spine and extremities and a CT of the abdomen, head, chest, and spine.
questions.learning: Taking CT scan of the patient Taking a CT scan of the patient is a part of secondary survey. Primary survey identifies and manages the most immediately life-threatening pathologies first.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which type of hernia is characterized as a funicular hernia?
questions.explanation: A funicular hernia is a specific clinical subtype of an indirect inguinal hernia. It occurs when the processus vaginalis remains partially open (the funicular part), while the lower portion surrounding the testis is normally obliterated. This allows the hernial sac to descend into the inguinal canal, often stopping just short of the scrotum or within the upper scrotum, without communicating with the tunica vaginalis. A direct inguinal hernia (Option A) results from a weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach's triangle) and is not related to the processus vaginalis. Femoral hernias (Option C) pass through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. Umbilical hernias (Option D) occur through a defect in the umbilical ring. Understanding these anatomical variations is critical for surgical planning, as the funicular type of indirect hernia specifically involves the contents traveling within the spermatic cord but being separate from the testis
questions.learning: A funicular hernia is a specific clinical subtype of an indirect inguinal hernia. It occurs when the processus vaginalis remains partially open (the funicular part), while the lower portion surrounding the testis is normally obliterated.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man has the following lesion over the face. He complains of bleeding while itching. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BCC

The given history with the image showing an ulcer over the face with pearly, rolled-out borders points to a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is an epithelial tumor arising from basal cells. It is the most common type of skin cancer most commonly seen over the face, above the line joining corner of the mouth, and lobule of the ear. Risk factors for BCC include ultraviolet radiation (strongest risk factor), age 40-80 years with excessive sun exposure, light-skinned people, and exposure to arsenic compounds, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, and infrared light. It is more common in males than females. It is also associated with syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum and Gorlin's syndrome.

Features of BCC include:

• Pearly nodule with rolled border
• Tortuous telangiectatic vessels
• Surface which can get ulcerated with raised and beaded edge, often with a central depression or umbilication
• Bleeding on minor trauma

BCC has various subtypes such as nodular (most common type), pigmented, nodulocystic, morphoeic, infiltrative, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus.

It is locally aggressive and can erode the bone or facial sinuses. It rarely metastasizes via lymph nodes.

The occasional presence of melanin in the nodular variant of BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

Depending upon the type of the lesion, a shave, punch or excisional biopsy may be employed for diagnosis. X-ray or CT may be needed if there is a local invasion. Histology shows peripheral palisading of cells.

Treatment:

• Surgical: Wide excision (4-6 mm clearance) with a skin graft or flap or primary suturing
• Mohs' surgery for BCC close to the eyes, nose, or ear to preserve more tissue.
• Non-surgical: Radiotherapy, vismodegib and sonedegib.

Other options:

Option A: Dermatofibrosarcoma, also known as dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) is a rare, slow-growing, well-differentiated primary fibrosarcoma of the skin, associated with increased production of platelet-derived growth factor-beta. It presents as a protuberant nodule within a firm, indurated plaque that can ulcerate. They are locally aggressive tumors with high recurrence rates. Treatment is wide excision and Mohs microscopic surgery. Imatinib is used for unresectable, metastatic, and recurrent tumors. The given image below shows a DFSP near the umbilicus.

Option B: Marjolin's ulcer is a painless, slow-growing, locally malignant, well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma that occurs in a chronic scar (burns scar, scar of venous ulcer). It presents as an indurated, non-tender ulcer with raised and everted edges with scarring in the surrounding area with marked fibrosis. The ulcer can spread to the lymph nodes when it reaches the normal skin. A wedge biopsy and MRI of the region involved confirm the diagnosis. Management is by wide excision, for larger ulcers, amputation is done. The given image below shows a marjolin's ulcer of the leg.

Option D: Naevus is a common benign neoplasm caused due to mutations in the components of the RAS signaling pathway. It has various types, such as congenital naevus, blue naevus, Spitz naevus, halo naevus, and dysplastic naevus. The given image below shows a patient with multiple dysplastic nevi.
questions.learning: BCC — The given history with the image showing an ulcer over the face with pearly, rolled-out borders points to a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is an epithelial tumor arising from basal cells.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant woman in her third trimester experiences dizziness while climbing stairs and is found to have low blood pressure. Which physiological change in pregnancy most likely explains this finding?
options: Increased plasma volume and increased peripheral vascular resistance
Decreased plasma volume and peripheral vascular resistance
Increased plasma volume and decreased peripheral vascular resistance
Decreased plasma volume and increased peripheral vascular resistance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased plasma volume and decreased peripheral vascular resistance

Pregnancy is associated with an increase in plasma volume and a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance (PVR). Progesterone and other vasodilators (e.g., nitric oxide, relaxin) cause systemic vasodilation, leading to a fall in blood pressure despite an increase in cardiac output. This explains symptoms such as dizziness or lightheadedness, especially on exertion or with postural changes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Increased plasma volume and increased peripheral vascular resistance: PVR normally decreases, not increases, during pregnancy.
• B. Decreased plasma volume and peripheral vascular resistance: Plasma volume increases by 40–50% during pregnancy.
• D. Decreased plasma volume and increased peripheral vascular resistance: Opposite of the normal physiological adaptation of pregnancy.
questions.learning: Increased plasma volume and decreased peripheral vascular resistance Pregnancy is associated with an increase in plasma volume and a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance (PVR).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 40-year-old man presents with complaints of facial puffiness and frothy urine. Given below is the histological image of the condition. What do you think is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Membranous nephropathy

The image is characteristic of membranous nephropathy. The given hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained image shows uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall. (intense pink color)

Membranous nephropathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in older adults, with a peak incidence in 30–50 years and a male:female ratio of 2:1.

It is a form of chronic immune-complex-mediated disease.

It can be primary (75% of cases) or secondary (associated with systemic diseases/identifiable etiologic agents).

Microscopy:

• Light microscopy: diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall without cellular proliferation. Irregular spikes projecting from the basement membrane are best seen with silver stains.
• Immunofluorescence microscopy: granular deposits containing Ig and complement along the glomerular basement membrane
• Electron micrograph: electron-dense subepithelial deposits (epimembranous spikes) and effacement of foot processes of podocytes

Image: The silver stain of the glomerulus highlights the proteinaceous basement membranes in black. There are characteristic "spikes" of basement membrane between the immune deposits of membranous nephropathy. The black basement membrane material shown here appears as projections in the capillary loops.
questions.learning: Membranous nephropathy — The image is characteristic of membranous nephropathy. The given hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained image shows uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A factory worker sustains burns involving 25% of his body during the course of employment and subsequently develops infections and related complications. Under the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act, which benefit is he entitled to receive?
questions.explanation: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act, the Extended Sickness Benefit is provided to insured workers who suffer from any of 34 specified long-term diseases or severe complications from work injuries that require prolonged treatment. Since the worker's 25% burns led to chronic infections and complications, he is eligible for this benefit, which can provide paid leave for up to 2 years at a higher daily rate (140% of the standard rate). Dependants' Benefit (Option A) is only applicable if the worker dies as a result of an employment injury. Standard Sickness Benefit (Option B) is limited to 91 days in a year and is for short-term illnesses. Enhanced Sickness Benefit (Option D) is specifically for insured persons undergoing sterilization procedures (vasectomy/tubectomy). Therefore, the extended benefit is the only one designed for prolonged medical complications
questions.learning: Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act, the Extended Sickness Benefit is provided to insured workers who suffer from any of 34 specified long-term diseases or severe complications from work injuries that require prolonged treatment.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A psychiatrist prescribes lithium for a patient who is diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding lithium?
options: Lithium is teratogenic if given to pregnant females
Lithium toxicity is exacerbated with thiazide
Lithium can decrease thyroid hormone levels
Hemodialysis is not useful in lithium overdose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hemodialysis is not useful in lithium overdose

Option D is the incorrect statement regarding lithium. Haemodialysis is used in lithium overdose.

Lithium is a small monovalent cation. It is used in the treatment of acute mania and the prevention of recurrences of bipolar disorder in adults or adolescents. Lithium is a mood stabiliser with suicide reduction in bipolar patients and is also efficacious in unipolar depressive patients who respond inadequately to antidepressant therapy.

Lithium toxicity occurs with the concomitant use of

* Thiazide diuretics (chlorthalidone)—Diuretics cause Na⁺ loss, which promotes proximal tubular reabsorption of Na⁺ as well as Li⁺. Hence, plasma levels of lithium rise. (Option B)

* Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors

* Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

* Tetracyclines

* Loop diuretics (furosemide)

These act by increasing the tubular reabsorption of lithium, resulting in decreased excretion of lithium and thereby increasing the serum lithium levels, causing toxicity.

Adverse effects—Serum lithium levels greater than 1.5 mEq/L are considered toxic.

* Acute intoxication is characterised by vomiting, profuse diarrhea, coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, and convulsions.

* Central nervous system: Lithium at therapeutic levels causes fine tremors, and at toxic levels causes coarse tremors. Incoordination, ataxia, and slurred speech can occur at peak serum concentrations.

* With long-term use, some patients develop renal diabetes insipidus. Patients present with polyuria and polydipsia.

* Lithium therapy causes significant weight gain.

* Lithium therapy is associated with hypothyroidism. This is due to interference with the release of thyroid hormone, which leads to a fall in circulating T3 and T4 levels and a subsequent increase in TSH secretion from pituitary enlargement and stimulation of the thyroid. (Option C)

* Lithium is contraindicated in pregnancy. Early pregnancy causes Ebstein anomaly in the foetus. Foetal lithium exposure is associated with neonatal goitre, CNS depression, hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), and cardiac murmur. (Option A)

Treatment of lithium overdose—There is no specific antidote. Osmotic diuretics and sodium bicarbonate infusion promote lithium excretion. Haemodialysis is indicated if serum levels are > 4 mEq/L.

Pearl PF0735: Lithium in bipolar disorder

Guidelines for Lithium therapy

Mania, hypomania, bipolar disorder, etc.

Blood levels of lithium:

For therapeutic purpose (treatment of acute mania) : 0.8-1.2 mEq/L

For prophylaxis (to prevent relapse of bipolar disorder): 0.5-0.8 mEq/L

Toxic levels of lithium: >/= 1.5 mEq/L

Contraindications:

• CKD
• Heart disease
• Hyponatremia or diuretic use

Baseline studies:

• BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen), Creatinine, Calcium, Urine analysis
• Thyroid function test
• ECG in patients with coronary risk factors

Acute adverse effects:

• Tremor, ataxia, weakness
• Polyuria, polydipsia
• Vomiting, diarrhea
• Cognitive impairment

Chronic adverse effects:

• Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
• Thyroid dysfunction
• Hyperparathyroidism

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to the clinic with fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, followed by the appearance of a rash that begins behind the ears and subsequently spreads to the chest, back, and abdomen. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical constellation of the "3 Cs" (Cough, runny nose/Coryza, and Conjunctivitis) followed by a high fever and a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears is the classic diagnostic pattern for Measles. This specific cephalocaudal (head-to-toe) progression of the rash is a hallmark of the disease. Rubella (Option C, German measles) presents with a similar but milder rash and significant lymphadenopathy (posterior auricular and suboccipital), and usually lacks the severe "3 Cs" prodrome. Dengue (Option B) and Chikungunya (Option D) are vector-borne diseases that present with high fever and severe "bone-breaking" joint or muscle pain, but they do not typically show this specific head-to-trunk rash progression and respiratory prodrome. Measles remains a significant public health threat and is associated with serious complications like pneumonia and encephalitis. Prevention via two doses of the MR (Measles-Rubella) vaccine is a high priority in global pediatric immunization programs
questions.learning: The clinical constellation of the "3 Cs" (Cough, runny nose/Coryza, and Conjunctivitis) followed by a high fever and a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears is the classic diagnostic pattern for Measles.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old bedridden patient presents with sudden-onset breathlessness and chest pain, and a CTPA has been performed. Which non- invasive investigation would be useful to help confirm the underlying etiology?
questions.explanation: A bedridden patient presenting with sudden dyspnea and chest pain is highly likely to have a Pulmonary Embolism (PE), often originating from a Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT). While CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the gold standard for diagnosing PE, a Doppler ultrasound of the legs is an essential non-invasive tool to confirm the etiology by identifying the source thrombus in the deep veins. D-dimer (Option A) is a sensitive screening tool but is often elevated in hospitalized or bedridden patients regardless of PE, making it non-specific. MRI (Option B) and a Coagulogram (Option C) are not the primary diagnostic steps for confirming acute PE or its venous source. Finding a clot on Doppler in this symptomatic patient strongly supports the diagnosis of venous thromboembolism. Immediate treatment involves anticoagulation with heparin or LMWH. Preventing DVT in bedridden patients through mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis is a fundamental aspect of inpatient clinical care
questions.learning: A bedridden patient presenting with sudden dyspnea and chest pain is highly likely to have a Pulmonary Embolism (PE), often originating from a Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about carcinoid tumours of appendix?
options: Size appears to be the best predictor of malignant behavior and metastatic potential
Arise from Kulchitsky cells of the crypts of Lieberkühn
Most common location is the base of the appendix
Most common tumour of the appendix
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Most common location is the base of the appendix

The most common location of the carcinoid tumor of the appendix is the tip of the appendix (i.e., the distal third of the appendix).

Carcinoid tumor:

* Synonym – Argentaffinoma

* It arises in argentaffin tissue (Kulchitsky cells of the crypts of Lieberkühn).

* It is the most common tumor of the appendix

* It is 10 times more common than any other neoplasm of the appendix.

* Most often, it presents with symptoms of subacute or recurrent appendicitis.

* It is frequently found in the distal third (mostly tip) of the appendix.

* Moderately hard, yellow tumor between the intact mucosa and the peritoneum.

* Microscopically:

* Tumor cells are small, arranged in small nests within the muscle, and have a characteristic pattern using immunohistochemical stain chromogranin A

* Carcinoid tumor of the appendix rarely give rise to metastasis.

Treatment :

* Appendicectomy has been shown to be a sufficient treatment.

* Indications for right hemicolectomy:

* Cecal wall involvement

* Tumour ≥ 2 cm in size

* Lymph nodal involvement
questions.learning: Most common location is the base of the appendix — The most common location of the carcinoid tumor of the appendix is the tip of the appendix (i.e., the distal third of the appendix).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following muscles primarily functions as an abductor of the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA) is the only muscle that functions as a true abductor of the vocal cords. By rotating the arytenoid cartilages laterally, it opens the rima glottidis, which is essential for breathing. Damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which supplies this muscle, can lead to vocal cord paralysis in an adducted position, potentially causing airway obstruction. Option A (Lateral cricoarytenoid) is a primary adductor, closing the vocal cords for speech and swallowing. Option C (Thyroarytenoid) and Option D (Vocalis) are involved in shortening and relaxing the vocal cords to change the pitch and quality of the voice. Because the PCA is the "safety muscle" of the larynx, its function is paramount during surgery on the thyroid or neck. Bilateral PCA paralysis is a medical emergency requiring tracheostomy or surgical lateralization of the cords to restore an adequate airway for the patient
questions.learning: The posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA) is the only muscle that functions as a true abductor of the vocal cords. By rotating the arytenoid cartilages laterally, it opens the rima glottidis, which is essential for breathing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A young girl presented to the OPD for examination. She is tall and thin with slender fingers, and dislocated lenses. Workup revealed cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. Which amino acid supplement is required in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cysteine

The clinical picture of a tall and thin young girl with slender fingers, dislocated lenses, and cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is suggestive of classic homocystinuria. The amino acid supplement required in this scenario is cysteine.

Classic homocystinuria is a metabolic disorder of methionine metabolism, due to cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency. It is an autosomal recessive condition.

Cystathionine beta-synthase is a pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme that condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine. The absence of this enzyme will cause cysteine deficiency, hence cysteine needs to be supplemented in the diet.

Clinical features:

• Affected children are initially asymptomatic.
• Ectopia lentis (subluxation of the lens) is seen first, after 3 years of age.
• Intellectual disability and psychiatric and behavioral disorders.
• Thromboembolic episodes.
• Skeletal abnormalities resembling those of Marfan syndrome: They are tall and thin with elongated limbs and arachnodactyly (slender fingers).

Elevations of both methionine and homocysteine in body fluids are the diagnostic laboratory findings. The diagnosis is established by molecular analysis of cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) or by assay of the enzyme in cultured fibroblasts, phytohemagglutinin-stimulated lymphocytes, or liver biopsy specimens. Treatment includes restriction of methionine intake and supplementation with cysteine, betaine, vitamins B6, B12, and folate.

The image below shows arachnodactyly.

Methionine supplementation is required in non-classical homocystinuria. It is due to impaired re-methylation of homocysteine to methionine. This can be caused by defective methionine synthase or reduced availability of two essential cofactors, 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, and methylcobalamin.

Elevated homocysteine levels with low levels of methionine will be seen. Treatment includes methionine supplementation and administration of methyl folate, hydroxocobalamin, and betaine.
questions.learning: Cysteine — The clinical picture of a tall and thin young girl with slender fingers, dislocated lenses, and cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is suggestive of classic homocystinuria.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which disorder is characterized by the presence of a cherry-red spot on the retina?
questions.explanation: A cherry-red spot on the retina is a classic clinical finding observed in several metabolic storage disorders and vascular conditions. It occurs because the fovea remains transparent and reveals the underlying red choroid, while the surrounding ganglion cells are swollen and opaque due to the accumulation of storage material. Tay-Sachs disease is the most well-known lysosomal storage disorder associated with this sign, caused by a deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase A. Fabry's disease (Option B) is more commonly associated with cornea verticillata rather than a cherry-red spot. Gaucher's disease (Option C) typically presents with hepatosplenomegaly and bone pain; while ocular findings exist, they rarely include a classic cherry-red spot. Von Gierke's disease (Option D) is a glycogen storage disease that primarily affects the liver and kidneys, not the retina. Besides storage diseases, a cherry-red spot is also a pathognomonic finding in Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO), which is an ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate intervention to restore blood flow

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery is used for AV shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis and is present behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendon calcaneus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus, approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the tendon calcaneus, making it easily accessible.

It is commonly used for arteriovenous shunting with the great saphenous vein in haemodialysis.

Peroneal artery lies deep, anterior tibial continues as dorsalis pedis on the dorsum of foot, and dorsalis pedis is not located behind the medial malleolus.
questions.learning: Posterior tibial artery — The posterior tibial artery runs behind the medial malleolus, approximately 2.5 cm anterior to the tendon calcaneus, making it easily accessible.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are options for management of a pancreatic pseudocyst? 1. Pancreaticoduodenectomy 2. Cystogastrostomy 3. Percutaneous drainage 4. Endoscopic drainage Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

A pancreatic pseudocyst is managed based on its size, symptoms, and complications. Treatment options include internal drainage (cystogastrostomy), endoscopic drainage, or percutaneous drainage in selected cases.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Pancreaticoduodenectomy ❌: Not indicated for a pancreatic pseudocyst; reserved for malignancy or selected pancreatic head lesions.
• 2. Cystogastrostomy ✔️: Standard surgical internal drainage for pseudocysts adjacent to the stomach.
• 3. Percutaneous drainage ✔️: Option in selected patients, especially infected pseudocysts or poor surgical candidates.
• 4. Endoscopic drainage ✔️: Preferred minimally invasive approach (transmural or transpapillary) for suitable pseudocysts.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 A pancreatic pseudocyst is managed based on its size, symptoms, and complications. Treatment options include internal drainage (cystogastrostomy), endoscopic drainage, or percutaneous drainage in selected cases.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which among the following helps in the maturation of collagen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ascorbic acid

Ascorbic acid/Vitamin C helps in the maturation of collagen.

Collagen is synthesized intracellularly in fibroblasts. Each polypeptide chain of collagen has about 1000 amino acid residues composed of Glycine-X-Y repeats, where X and Y are proline and hydroxyproline predominantly.

Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues takes place intracellularly as a part of post-translational modification with the help of prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase. These enzymes require iron in a reduced state in its active site. Vitamin C/ascorbic acid keeps iron in a reduced state in these enzymes and thus helps in the maturation of collagen. Deficiency of vitamin C leads to scurvy which is characterized by bleeding tendencies, anemia, and skeletal abnormalities due to defective collagen in the connective tissue.

Steps of post-translational modification of collagen includes

* Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues

* Glycosylation of hydroxylysine residues

* Formation of intrachain and interchain disulfide bonds

* Triple helix formation

* Cleavage of 25–35 kDa portions at both carboxy and amino terminal end

* Quartered staggered arrangement

* Oxidative deamination of lysine and hydroxylysine residues

* Formation of intrachain and interchain crosslinks

Other options:

Option B: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-containing enzyme that helps in covalent crosslinking collagen fibers. Deficiency of copper results in defective function of lysyl oxidase, and reduced cross-linkage of collagen leading to a condition called Menke's disease. Zinc has no role in collagen maturation.

Pearl PF0669: Synthesis of collagen and its disorders

1. Collagen backbone
Preprocollagen - Glycin-proline-lysine

2. Hydroxylation

Of proline and lysine in the presence of Vit C.

Deficiency of Vit C causes Scurvy.

3. Glycosylation
Formation of procollagen and resulting triple helix

4. Cleavage of terminals of procollagen
Resulting in the formation of tropocollagen

5. Cross-linking by lysyl oxidase (copper-containing enzyme)

Formation of mature collagen.

Defect causes Menkes disease and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was admitted to the hospital with a history of prolapsing rectal mass and painless rectal bleeding. The histopathological image of the mass is as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Juvenile polyp

The clinical features and the histopathological image showing characteristic cystically dilated crypts and glands are suggestive of a juvenile polyp.

Juvenile polyps are malformations of epithelium and lamina propria commonly located in the rectum. It is seen in children <5 years of age. The typical presentation is painless rectal bleeding. Sometimes there may be a proliferating rectal mass.

The disease may be sporadic or syndromic.

• Sporadic juvenile polyp occurs as a single mass and is called retention polyp.
• Juvenile polyposis syndrome is characterized by multiple hamartomatous polyps, which may be premalignant.

Morphologically, both of these types are indistinguishable.

• Gross appearance: They appear as pedunculated, smooth reddish lesions, and with cystic spaces.
• Microscopic appearance: The cysts appear as dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory debris.

Note: Complex glandular architecture and the presence of smooth muscle cutting through the lamina propria are seen in Peutz-Jeghers polyps.
questions.learning: Juvenile polyp — The clinical features and the histopathological image showing characteristic cystically dilated crypts and glands are suggestive of a juvenile polyp.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Supravital stains are used in the identification of all except ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Copper in tissue

In the following options all except copper can be visualised by supravital stains like methylene blue and brilliant cresyl blue.

Reticulocytes have blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm due to the presence of a reticular (mesh-like) network of ribosomal RNA which can be stained by supravital stains.Reticulocytosis indicates effective erythropoiesis, which refers to a good bone marrow response to anemia which is seen hemolytic anemias and acute blood loss.

Heinz bodies are seen in G6PD deficiency where the RBCs are exposed to high levels of oxidants causing the cross-linking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains. The globin chains become denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates known as Heinz bodies which can cause intravascular hemolysis. These can be detected by supravital staining.

Histology of non-hodgkin lymphoma in an elderly male, showing reticulocytosis and spherocytosis:

Note:

To visualize the copper in tissues e.g in Wilson's disease, liver biopsy samples are stained using rubeanic acid/rhodanine stain to visualize the cytoplasmic copper.
