questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sebaceous cyst

The image shows a dark-colored summit over a swelling, usually seen in a sebaceous cyst.

Sebaceous cysts are the retention cysts of the sebaceous gland that are usually present on the face, scalp, or scrotum. They contain yellowish-white cheesy material with fat and epithelium.

Clinical features:

• The swelling is painless, soft, and freely mobile.
• Though non-transilluminating, they are Paget's test positive (fluctuant).
• Punctum is seen in 70% of the patients with sebaceous cysts. They are dark in color due to the accumulation of denuded epithelium.
• They also have an unpleasant sebum odor.
• The swelling can ulcerate and become painful (Cock’s peculiar tumor).
• Some cysts over the scalp may also harden over time (Sebaceous horn).
• Many may get infected and lead to abscess formation.

Treatment:

• Excision including skin adjacent to punctum using elliptical incision-dissection method.
• Incision and avulsion of cyst wall.
• In the presence of an abscess, an initial treatment with an incision later followed by excision of the cyst

Other options:

Option A: Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types:

1. Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development
2. Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube/duct
3. Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma
4. Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto, meso, and endoderm)

Option C: Meningiomas are benign tumors arising from the meningothelial cells of the dura. They present with headaches, seizures, or focal neurological deficits.

Option D: Postauricular cutaneous mastoid fistula is a rare complication of chronic otitis media that heals very slowly and needs surgical closure.
questions.learning: Sebaceous cyst — The image shows a dark-colored summit over a swelling, usually seen in a sebaceous cyst. Sebaceous cysts are the retention cysts of the sebaceous gland that are usually present on the face, scalp, or scrotum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following clinical factors has the worst prognosis in a case of acute limb ischemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Paralysis

Paralysis is seen in a nonviable limb and has the worst prognosis in a case of acute limb ischemia.

The classification of acute limb ischemia is:

a)Viable (I):

* Mild pain

* No sensory or motor deficits

* Capillary refill normal

* Doppler evaluation normal

* Urgent evaluation to be done

b)Marginally threatened(IIa):

* Moderate pain

* Minimal sensory deficit( in toes) with no motor deficit

* Delayed capillary refill is seen here

* Abnormal arterial doppler

* Urgent revascularization is needed

c)Immediately threatened(IIb):

* Severe pain

* Paraesthesia and mild to moderate muscle weakness

* Delayed capillary refill

* Abnormal arterial doppler

* Emergency revascularization is needed.

d)Nonviable(III):

* Irreversible muscle and tissue damage.

* Pain is variable here due to the death of the nerves

* Profound sensory loss, paralysis, and rigor of the limbs

* Abnormal arterial and venous dopplers

* Amputation is needed here

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 54-year-old woman presents with heartburn and shiny, tight, thickened skin over her hands associated with non-pitting edema. Serological testing is positive for anti–topoisomerase I antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient displays the core features of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), including skin thickening (sclerodactyly) and esophageal symptoms (heartburn). The definitive diagnostic marker is the Topoisomerase I (Anti-Scl-70) antibody, which is highly specific for the Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis subtype (Option B). This subtype is characterized by rapid skin involvement that extends proximal to the elbows and knees, and a high risk of internal organ disease like interstitial lung disease, as noted in this patient. Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (Option A) (CREST syndrome) is associated with Centromere antibodies and limited skin involvement. Raynaud's phenomenon (Option C) is a symptom (color change in fingers) that is often the first sign of scleroderma but is not the diagnosis for the full clinical picture. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (Option D) involves GI polyps and pigmentation . Thus, the specific antibody profile confirms the diffuse type
questions.learning: The patient displays the core features of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), including skin thickening (sclerodactyly) and esophageal symptoms (heartburn).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old is brought to the opd with complaints that she is able to hear the sound of speech but has difficulty understanding words. Her PTA and BERA were inconsistent with each other, with PTA being more or less normal. Her middle latency and cortical responses were absent. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Auditory neuropathy

In the clinical scenario, the history of a child presenting with complaints of inability to understand words with abnormal BERA and normal PTA(Pure Tone Audiometry) is suggestive of auditory neuropathy.

Auditory neuropathy/auditory dyssynchrony is a condition that affects the neural processing of auditory stimuli.

Pathophysiology

• Injury to the synaptic junction between inner hair cells of the cochlea and dendrites of spiral ganglion neurons
• Direct damage to the dendrites of the spiral ganglion neurons
• Direct injury to the spiral ganglion neurons
• Direct axonal damage to the auditory nerve

Auditory neuropathy should be suspected in any child with severe speech and language delay out of proportion with the presumed hearing loss.

All of the following must be present in newborns to diagnose auditory neuropathy:

• Absent or severely abnormal ABR test results at maximal stimulus (100 dBnHL)
• Normal outer hair cell function as determined by OAEs(Otoacoustic emission)
• Absent or elevated stapedial reflex thresholds

In addition, adults with mildly to moderately abnormal pure tone thresholds and speech discrimination scores out of proportion with suspected hearing loss should undergo additional evaluation. Some patients may have normal or slightly elevated audiogram pure tone thresholds

Management includes conventional hearing aids. If a child does not progress with hearing aid devices and shows limited speech discrimination abilities, cochlear implantation is the next viable option.

Other options

Option A:

Michel aplasia: There is a complete absence of bone and a membranous labyrinth. Even the petrous apex is absent but external and middle ears may be completely unaffected. The child presents with congenital sensorineural hearing loss. No hearing aids or cochlear implantation can be used.

Option B:

Malingering(Nonorganic hearing loss)

In this type of hearing loss, there is no organic lesion. Usually, there is a motive to claim some compensation for being exposed to industrial noises, head injury, or ototoxic medication. The patient may present with any of the three clinical situations: Total hearing loss in both ears, total loss in only one ear, or exaggerated loss in one or both ears.

Investigations

Inconsistent results on Repeat Pure Tone and Speech Audiometry Tests: Normally, the results of repeat tests are within +5 dB. A variation greater than 15 dB is diagnostic of nonorganic hearing loss (NOHL).

Absence of Shadow Curve: Normally, a shadow curve can be obtained while testing bone conduction, if the healthy ear is not masked. This is due to the transcranial transmission of sound to the healthy ear. The absence of this curve in a patient complaining of unilateral deafness is diagnostic of NOHL.

Inconsistency in PTA and SRT: Normally, the pure tone average (PTA) of three speech frequencies (500, 1000, and 2000 Hz) is within 10 dB of the speech reception threshold (SRT). An SRT is better than PTA by more than 10 dB points to NOHL.

Stenger Test: It helps in identifying malingering

Acoustic Reflex: Threshold Normally, the stapedial reflex is elicited at 70-100 dB sensation level. If the patient claims total deafness but the reflex can be elicited, it indicates nonorganic hearing loss (NOHL).

Option C:

Otosclerosis is the disease of the bony labyrinth in which a normal dense endochondral layer of the bony otic capsule is replaced by irregularly laid spongy bone. It has a positive family history with an autosomal dominant trait. It is more commonly seen in females between 20-30 years of age and the hearing loss is aggravated during pregnancy and menopause. It may be associated with osteogenesis imperfecta and a viral infection like measles.

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fissula ante fenestram.

Patients present with a bilateral conductive type of hearing loss, tinnitus (commonly in cochlear type and active stage), paracusis Willisii (better hearing in noisy surroundings than in a quiet place), vertigo, and a monotonous, well-modulated soft speech.

The tympanic membrane is quite normal and mobile. Eustachian tube function is also normal. Pure tone audiometry shows a dip at 2000 Hz in the bone conduction curve known as the Carhart's notch. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

On examination, Schwartz sign/flamingo flush showing a red blush of the tympanic membrane due to vascularity can be seen.

Treatment includes medical, surgical management, and hearing aids. Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage to speed up the maturity of the active focus and halt further cochlear loss. The treatment of choice is surgical management which includes stapedotomy/stapedectomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Hearing aids are used in patients who refuse or are unfit for the surgery.
questions.learning: Auditory neuropathy — In the clinical scenario, the history of a child presenting with complaints of inability to understand words with abnormal BERA and normal PTA(Pure Tone Audiometry) is suggestive of auditory neuropathy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A child with a history of night-blindness presented to you with the following findings. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phrynoderma

A child having night-blindness, and multiple keratotic papules on elbows as shown in the image suggests a diagnosis of phrynoderma or toad-skin. This can occur due to the deficiency of vitamin A.

Phrynoderma is not specific to vitamin A deficiency. It may also be associated with deficiencies of B complex, riboflavin, vitamin C, vitamin E, and essential fatty acids. It manifests as groups of papules with a central keratotic plug. The commonest sites are elbows and knees. They are present around the follicles and give the skin a rough texture. Treatment involves the correction of poor diet and administration of a multivitamin preparation containing vitamin A.

Option B: Keratosis pilaris is an inherited abnormality of keratinization. It affects the follicular orifices leading to keratotic follicular plugging, perifollicular erythema, and follicular atrophy. It usually presents during puberty. They present as small, keratotic papules on the extensor aspects of the limbs, particularly the arms which can lead to ingrowing of the hair. Treatment is purely reserved for cosmetic purposes.

Option C: Darier disease is an autosomal dominant genodermatosis characterized by keratotic papules that show acantholysis and dyskeratosis. ATP2A2 gene mutations are present in Darier disease. Histologically, acantholysis (separation of keratinocytes) and blistering are seen in the suprabasal epidermis.

It presents with discrete or confluent rough, greasy, skin-colored papules in seborrheic areas (trunk, face scalp margins) and flexures (perineum, axillae, groin). There may also be isolated nipple hyperkeratosis. Nail findings include fragility, painful longitudinal splits, or distinctive red and white longitudinal bands terminating in V-shaped nicks.

Option D: Follicular eczema is a form of atopic dermatitis that presents with a discoid patch formed due to the coalescence of the follicular lesions with peripheral excoriation marks. The biopsy shows spongiotic dermatitis.
questions.learning: Phrynoderma — A child having night-blindness, and multiple keratotic papules on elbows as shown in the image suggests a diagnosis of phrynoderma or toad-skin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 34-year-old male, who had been consuming maize as a primary staple food for an extended period, presented with glossitis and a pigmented rash in areas exposed to the sun. Additionally, a lesion was observed on his neck, as depicted in the image provided. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pellagra

The given clinical secnario and image finding showing casal's necklace is suggestive of pellagra. It is caused due to niacin deficiency.

Niacin is a nutrient that is synthesized in the body from tryptophan. The term niacin represents two compounds nicotinic acid and nicotinamide. It acts as a precursor for the coenzymes NAD and NADP, which are important in various oxidation and reduction reactions.

Niacin deficiency causes pellagra. It is usually seen in individuals with a corn/ maize-based staple diet, a history of alcohol consumption, hartnup disease, and carcinoid syndrome.

The primary manifestations of pellagra are often referred to as the 4D's as follows, diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, leading to death. Other manifestations include, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, bright red glossitis, generalized weakness, irritability, casal’s necklace(pigmented scaly skin rash around the neck).

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone. Treatment is oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Other options :

Option B : Scurvy is caused due to vitamin c deficiency. It is associated with symptoms like bleeding gums, bruising, joint pain, and fatigue. Scurvy is not associated with a rash like the one described, nor does it typically cause cognitive dysfunction or diarrhea. Hence, high-dose vitamin C would not improve this patient’s symptoms.

Option C : Megaloblastic anemia is an RBC disorder caused by a deficiency of Vitamin B12 or folic acid. This deficiency results in impaired DNA synthesis, leading to ineffective hematopoiesis and distinctive morphologic changes, including abnormally large erythroid precursors and red cells.

Option D : Beri beri is caused due to thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency. It is characterized by symptoms such as muscle weakness, peripheral neuropathy, cardiovascular issues, and confusion.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child is evaluated for short stature. The child’s height matches parental stature, and bone age is appropriate for chronological age. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Familial (genetic) short stature is the most likely diagnosis when a child is healthy but short, their growth velocity is normal, and their height is consistent with their "mid-parental height". A defining laboratory feature is that the bone age is equal to the chronological age, indicating that the child is growing at their genetically predetermined rate and will likely reach a short final adult height. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (Option B) is characterized by a "delayed bone age," meaning the child has more room to grow and will eventually reach a normal height later than peers. Undernutrition (Option C) and Growth Hormone Deficiency (Option D) typically present with a significant reduction in growth velocity (crossing centiles on a growth chart) and often a delayed bone age. Since this child’s height and bone age are both consistent with their genetics and age, no treatment is necessary other than reassurance
questions.learning: Familial (genetic) short stature is the most likely diagnosis when a child is healthy but short, their growth velocity is normal, and their height is consistent with their "mid-parental height".

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary objective for usage of health index by NITI Aayog?
options: Raise funding to the private hospitals
Rank the state according to health status
Assess the efficiency of the government hospital
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rank the state according to health status

The Health Index developed by NITI Aayog, in collaboration with MoHFW and World Bank, is primarily used to rank States and Union Territories based on their health performance.

It assesses indicators related to health outcomes, governance, and key inputs/processes, enabling inter-state comparison and competitive federalism.

The index is not meant for hospital-level efficiency assessment or district identification, but for tracking and incentivizing overall state-level health improvements.
questions.learning: Rank the state according to health status — The Health Index developed by NITI Aayog, in collaboration with MoHFW and World Bank, is primarily used to rank States and Union Territories based on their health performance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
You are working in a primary health center (PHC) situated in a high seismic zone. Which of the following will you do as part of preparedness for an emergency?

1. Disaster preparedness by making sure all financial and other resources are available
2. Increase public awareness through campaigns and loudspeakers
3. Conduct a simulation for the disaster and assess the response
4. Follow instructions given over the phone or radio by higher officials
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3

Steps 1, 2, and 3 are done as part of preparedness for an emergency by someone working in a PHC situated in a high seismic zone.

Emergency preparedness refers to long-term development activities that strengthen the capacity of a country to effectively manage all kinds of emergencies. It involves the following steps:

1. Disaster preparedness by making sure all financial and other resources are available
2. Increase public awareness through campaigns and loudspeakers
3. Conduct a simulation for the disaster and assess the response
4. Evaluate the risk of disaster
5. Information sessions coordination with news media
6. Adopt standards and regulations

Disaster risk management is a systematic process using administrative decisions, policies, and strategies to lessen the impacts of natural hazards and disasters. The steps are:

• Response - This includes activities such as:

• Search, rescue, and first aid: This step is important since the organized relief services will be able to address only a small fraction of demand after a major disaster.
• Field care: This includes making health care available regardless of facilities and operating status.
• Triage: Classifying the injured based on the severity of the injuries and chances of survival with medical intervention.
• Tagging: Tags with name, age, triage category, diagnosis and treatment are put for identification purposes.
• Identification of the dead: The dead bodies should be shifted from the disaster site to the mortuary.

• Rehabilitation - This includes measures that lead to the restoration of pre-disaster conditions. These measures include water supply restoration, food safety, basic sanitation, personal hygiene, and vector control.
• Mitigation - This includes measures to prevent disasters from causing emergencies or to lessen the likely effects of emergencies. Some of them are flood mitigation, land use planning, improved building codes, and the reduction and protection of vulnerable populations or structures.
• Preparedness - This is a program that aims at strengthening the capacity of a country to manage all types of emergencies efficiently. Its objective is to ensure that appropriate measurements are taken for the relief and rehabilitation of disaster victims.

Some measures that should be followed by all in case of an emergency include:

• Avoiding telephone use, unless it is to call for help
• Listen to and carry out the radio or loudspeaker broadcast messages
• Carry out the official instructions given over the radio or by loudspeaker
• Keep a family emergency kit ready

Note: Vaccination of the general population post-disaster against typhoid, cholera, and tetanus is not recommended.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man suffered from a stroke 2 days ago. He now presents with involuntary, violent, and flinging movements of the limbs on one side. What is the likely site of lesion in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Subthalamic nuclei

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of hemiballismus. A lesion in subthalamic nuclei is responsible for this condition.

A lesion in the subthalamic nucleus causes sudden, violent, involuntary, and flinging movements confined to one side of the body, commonly affecting the proximal muscles of the limbs, a condition called hemiballismus. The movements are seen contralateral to the side of the lesion, i.e., involuntary movements of the right arm and leg are seen in the lesion of the left subthalamic nucleus and vice versa.

Basal ganglia circuits have both direct and indirect pathways. The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibits it. The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in the indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors.

The subthalamic nucleus is a part of the indirect pathway. Hence, a lesion at subthalamic nuclei leads to loss of inhibitory effect of the indirect pathway resulting in dopaminergic overactivity. This is responsible for features of hemiballismus.

This movement disorder is usually self-limiting and tends to resolve spontaneously after weeks or months. Dopamine antagonistic agents can be given to manage it as well.

Other options:

Option B: A lesion in the globus pallidus can give rise to athetosis. This involves spontaneous and continuous writhing movements of the hand, arm, neck, or face.

Options C and D: A lesion in the putamen and caudate nucleus can give rise to chorea. Chorea is defined as rapid, semi-purposeful, graceful, dance-like nonpatterned involuntary movements involving distal or proximal muscle groups.
questions.learning: Subthalamic nuclei — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of hemiballismus. A lesion in subthalamic nuclei is responsible for this condition.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which nerve is responsible for causing ear pain following a tonsillectomy procedure?
questions.explanation: Post-tonsillectomy ear pain is a common phenomenon known as "referred otalgia". This occurs because the tonsillar fossa is primarily supplied by the tonsillar branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). This same nerve also provides sensory innervation to the middle ear via Jacobson’s nerve (the tympanic branch). When the nerve endings are irritated in the throat following surgery, the brain misinterprets the signals as originating from the ear. Option B (Facial nerve) and Option C (Trigeminal nerve) provide some sensory supply to the external ear, but they are not the primary mediators of post-tonsillectomy pain. Option D (Vagus nerve) can cause referred pain from the larynx or esophagus via Arnold's nerve, but not typically from the tonsils. Management of referred otalgia involves adequate systemic analgesia and counseling the patient that the ear itself is healthy. Persistent unilateral referred otalgia in an adult smoker can also be a red flag for an occult oropharyngeal malignancy
questions.learning: Post-tonsillectomy ear pain is a common phenomenon known as "referred otalgia". This occurs because the tonsillar fossa is primarily supplied by the tonsillar branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Heme is derived from which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation: The synthesis of heme is a complex multi-step process that begins in the mitochondria. The initial, rate-limiting step involves the condensation of succinyl-CoA (from the TCA cycle) with the amino acid Glycine. This reaction is catalyzed by the enzyme delta-aminolevulinate synthase (ALA synthase) and requires pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6) as a cofactor. Glutamine (Option A) is vital for purine and pyrimidine synthesis. Glutamate (Option C) serves as a neurotransmitter and a precursor for GABA and glutathione. Valine (Option D) is a branched-chain essential amino acid. Heme is the oxygen-binding prosthetic group found in hemoglobin, myoglobin, and cytochromes. Defects in the heme biosynthetic pathway lead to various types of porphyrias, which can present with neurological or cutaneous symptoms. Understanding that glycine is the fundamental amino acid precursor for heme is a core concept in biochemistry, linking protein metabolism directly to the production of essential iron-carrying molecules in the blood and tissues
questions.learning: The synthesis of heme is a complex multi-step process that begins in the mitochondria. The initial, rate-limiting step involves the condensation of succinyl-CoA (from the TCA cycle) with the amino acid Glycine.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl with pigmented hair was noted. Which of the following amino acids is more likely to bind with keratin leading to this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cysteine

Cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that is abundant in keratin, the principal structural protein of hair. During melanin synthesis, dopaquinone reacts with cysteine to form cysteinyldopa, which is the precursor of pheomelanin (yellow-red pigment). The incorporation of melanin into keratin gives hair its characteristic pigmentation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Methionine: A sulfur-containing essential amino acid involved in methylation reactions, but it is not the amino acid that directly combines with dopaquinone in melanin synthesis.
• B. Lysine: Important for collagen cross-linking and protein synthesis, but it has no specific role in hair pigmentation.
• D. Glycine: The most abundant amino acid in collagen, not keratin, and does not participate in melanin synthesis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant is brought to the OPD with a swelling which developed after around 15 hours after birth. The clinical image is given below. What could be the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cephalhematoma

In the given clinical picture, the swelling over the infant's head is likely to be a cephalhematoma.

Cephalohematoma is a collection of blood in between the pericranium and the flat bone (subperiosteal) of the skull, usually unilateral and over a parietal bone. It is never present at birth but gradually develops after 12–24 h. The swelling is limited by the suture lines of the skull as the pericranium is fixed to the margins of the bone.

The arrow mark in the radiographic image below represents cephalohematoma.

Other options:

Subgaleal hematoma occurs between the galea aponeurotica and the periosteum. It is commonly caused by birth trauma, particularly forceps or vacuum-assisted delivery. Subgaleal hematoma can cross suture lines and typically presents as a soft, fluctuant swelling on the scalp.

Caput succedaneum is an edema of the scalp that can cross suture lines. It is usually present at birth or develops shortly after due to pressure on the presenting part of the head during labor. It generally resolves within a few days.

Encephalocele is a neural tube defect that results in a sac-like protrusion of the brain and its meninges through an opening in the skull. It is a congenital condition and is typically diagnosed at birth or via prenatal ultrasound.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following information needs to be disclosed in order to establish valid consent for surgical treatment? I. Condition and reasons why it warrants surgery II. Type of surgery proposed III. Unexpected hazards of proposed surgery IV. The surgical experience and expertise of the operating surgeon Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Valid informed consent is a legal and ethical requirement before any surgical procedure. For consent to be valid, the patient must have the capacity to decide, give consent voluntarily, and receive adequate information regarding the proposed treatment, including its risks, benefits, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

The following information must be disclosed:

• I. Condition and reasons why it warrants surgery: The patient should understand the diagnosis and why surgery is being recommended.
• II. Type of surgery proposed: The nature and purpose of the planned operation must be explained.
• III. Unexpected hazards (material risks) of the proposed surgery: Significant risks, complications, benefits, alternatives, and the consequences of not undergoing surgery should be discussed.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. The surgical experience and expertise of the operating surgeon: Disclosure of the surgeon’s personal experience or expertise is not a routine legal requirement for valid informed consent. Consent focuses on the procedure and its risks, not the surgeon’s credentials, unless specifically asked by the patient or required in exceptional circumstances.

questions.text: The following instrument is used for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Myringotomy

The given instrument with an arrowed blade and angled shank is a myringotome. It is used for myringotomy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A researcher studying immune regulation in the liver observes that viable CD4⁺ T lymphocytes are selectively engulfed by hepatocytes without being immediately destroyed. This specialized cell-in-cell phenomenon is believed to contribute to peripheral immune tolerance. Which of the following terms best describes this process?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enclysis

Enclysis is a recently described cell-in-cell phenomenon in which hepatocytes selectively internalize live CD4⁺ T cells, particularly regulatory T cells (Tregs), playing a role in hepatic immune homeostasis and immune tolerance.

Unlike classical phagocytosis, the engulfed lymphocytes are viable at the time of uptake, and the process is unique to hepatocytes.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Efferocytosis: Refers to the phagocytic clearance of apoptotic (dead or dying) cells by macrophages and other phagocytes. It does not involve live CD4⁺ T cells.
• B. Entosis: A live cell actively invades another live cell, most commonly seen in epithelial tumors. It is associated with cell competition rather than immune regulation.
• D. Emperipolesis: Describes the passage of intact viable cells through the cytoplasm of another cell without being digested. It is classically seen with megakaryocytes containing neutrophils or lymphocytes (e.g., Rosai–Dorfman disease).

High-yield pearl:

| Cell-in-cell phenomenon | Characteristic feature | Classic example

| ----------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------

| Enclysis | Hepatocyte engulfs live CD4⁺ T cells | Hepatic immune tolerance

| Efferocytosis | Clearance of apoptotic cells | Macrophages removing dying neutrophils

| Entosis | One live epithelial cell enters another | Epithelial cancers

| Emperipolesis | Viable cell passes through another cell without digestion | Megakaryocytes; Rosai–Dorfman disease

Exam tip:

• Enclysis = Hepatocytes + live CD4⁺ T cells (especially Tregs), whereas efferocytosis = apoptotic cells, entosis = tumor cell-in-cell, and emperipolesis = intact cells within another cell without destruction.
questions.learning: Enclysis Enclysis is a recently described cell-in-cell phenomenon in which hepatocytes selectively internalize live CD4⁺ T cells, particularly regulatory T cells (Tregs), playing a role in hepatic immune homeostasis and immune tolerance.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A doctor receives two court summons—one to appear as a witness in a murder case and another to give expert medical testimony. Which summons should the doctor attend as a priority?
options: Appearance for providing medical expert opinion
questions.explanation: A criminal court summons in a murder case carries a legal imperative and higher priority over other civil or expert witness duties. Legal attendance is mandatory unless a legitimate legal excuse is provided. While providing an expert medical opinion is professionally significant, a direct court order in a criminal matter represents a primary legal obligation that the doctor must prioritize. Appearance for expert opinion (Option B) is considered important but is typically subordinate to a direct criminal court summons. The timing of receipt (Option C) is irrelevant, as the chronological order of summonses does not override the legal gravity and mandatory nature of a criminal case involving a serious offense like murder. Therefore, the doctor must attend the criminal court first to fulfill their judicial duty in the murder trial, ensuring compliance with the law's highest mandates
questions.learning: A criminal court summons in a murder case carries a legal imperative and higher priority over other civil or expert witness duties. Legal attendance is mandatory unless a legitimate legal excuse is provided.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Inspiratory stridor is found in what kind of lesions:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supraglottic

Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi such as bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea like laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

Stridor is an audible respiratory noise that gets produced by turbulent airflow through an obstructed upper airway. It is an inspiratory sound that may have an expiratory component. It is distinct from stertor which is a snoring-like noise produced from an obstructed nasopharynx or oropharynx.

The intensity and pitch of sounds originating from the respiratory system vary based on their site of origin within the respiratory tract and may be heard with or without a stethoscope. Usually, the pitch of the sound increases, and the intensity decreases as one goes lower into the respiratory tract.
questions.learning: Supraglottic Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman with a recent history of travel to Africa presents with fever, altered mental status, and focal neurological deficits. Laboratory investigations identify an infecting organism that possesses a unique ability to adhere to vascular endothelium, enabling sequestration within blood vessels and thereby evading splenic clearance. What is this phenomenon known as?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of travel to Africa, fever, and neurological deficits (Cerebral Malaria) combined with the blood smear point to Plasmodium falciparum infection. A unique and lethal property of P. falciparum is cytoadherence. This occurs when the parasite expresses proteins (like PfEMP-1) on the surface of infected red blood cells (iRBCs), forming "knobs." These knobs bind to endothelial receptors (like ICAM-1 or CD36) in capillary beds. This sequestration prevents the iRBCs from passing through the spleen, where they would be cleared by macrophages. Rosetting (Option A) is the adherence of iRBCs to uninfected RBCs, which also contributes to microvascular obstruction. Agglutination (Option B) is a general term for cell clumping. Schizogony (Option D) is the asexual reproductive phase within the host. Sequestration in the brain leads to the confusion and coma seen in cerebral malaria. Understanding these mechanical properties of the parasite is critical for managing severe malaria and predicting its multisystem complications
questions.learning: The clinical history of travel to Africa, fever, and neurological deficits (Cerebral Malaria) combined with the blood smear point to Plasmodium falciparum infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following areas of the brain are correctly matched with the neurotransmitters they release? 1. Substantia nigra - Dopamine 2. Locus ceruleus - Acetylcholine 3. Raphe nucleus - Serotonin

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with asthma on inhaled corticosteroids and LABA continues to have exacerbations. FEV1 is normal, and there is no improvement with salbutamol challenge. The symptoms worsen seasonally. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step? LABA – Long-Acting Beta Agonist LAMA – Long-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Add Omalizumab

The given clinical vignette points towards a probable diagnosis of allergic asthma, which is treated with omalizumab.

FEV1 is normal, which indicates that the obstructive lung disease (asthma) has not worsened. As the symptoms worsen seasonally, this strongly suggests allergic asthma.

Omalizumab is a recombinant humanised monoclonal antibody against IgE. It is used in severe allergic asthma (IgE-mediated) and is effective in treating chronic urticaria. When applied subcutaneously, it neutralises circulating free IgE without triggering the activation of mast cells and other inflammatory cells. When exposed to an antigen, the mast cell surface receptors (Fcε R1) release a limited amount of IgE, resulting in bronchoconstriction.

questions.text: A HIV patient with fever, chronic diarrhea presented to OPD. His stool was examined which showed the following oocysts. Identify the components used for staining the stool.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A study was conducted on a group of people to study the factors that increase and inhibit the secretion of insulin. Which of the following factors inhibit its secretion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epinephrine

Epinephrine inhibits insulin secretion by acting on α-adrenergic receptors of pancreatic β-cells, reducing insulin release during stress or hypoglycemia.

All others- acetylcholine, gastric inhibitory polypeptide, and glucagon stimulate insulin secretion.

Insulin is secreted by the pancreatic beta cells in response to increased blood glucose concentration. It promotes liver uptake, storage, and the utilization of glucose from the blood. If blood glucose levels are high, they cause glucose to be rapidly stored in the liver in the form of glycogen. It also promotes the conversion of this excess glucose to fatty acids. When glucose levels fall, insulin secretion is decreased and activation of enzyme phosphorylase split glycogen to release stored glucose into the circulating blood.

Mechanism of insulin secretion:

Glucose enters beta cells of the pancreas via GLUT-2 receptors. Once inside, it is phosphorylated by glucokinase (rate-limiting step) to glucose-6-phosphate which is oxidized to form adenosine triphosphate (ATP). This ATP causes the closure of ATP-sensitive potassium channels and hence depolarization. This leads to opening voltage-gated calcium channels and Ca2+ influx. This stimulates the fusion of the insulin-containing vesicles with the cell membrane and the secretion of insulin into the extracellular fluid by exocytosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presents with impotence and bilateral resting pain. The following finding is seen in the legs. At which level has the pathology occurred?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aortoiliac bifurcation

The given scenario of a male patient with impotence, bilateral resting pain, and the image showing a gangrenous foot with amputated toes is suggestive of Leriche's syndrome and it indicates that the level of occlusion is at the aortoiliac bifurcation.

Peripheral arterial diseases occur mainly due to atherosclerosis or thromboembolism. Lerich's syndrome is a rare condition in which aortoiliac obstruction causes impotence and claudication (crampy pain) in the thigh or buttocks. Other features of aortoiliac arterial occlusion include absent femoral and distal pulses and a bruit over the aortoiliac region.

In general, features of chronic lower limb arterial occlusion are intermittent claudication, rest pain, ulcers, gangrene, absence of arterial pulses, bruit, and delayed capillary refilling. Rest pain occurs when limb perfusion is so severely compromised that anaerobic respiration occurs even at rest. This causes pain that increases on lying down or elevation of the foot. It reduces when the foot hangs below.

Investigations that are useful include Doppler ultrasound, duplex scanning, ankle-brachial pressure index, and digital subtraction percutaneous angiography (DSA). Through a DSA, endovascular intervention can be performed along with obtaining information on the dynamic arterial flow.

Management is by exercise, smoking cessation, control of diabetes, and weight loss if obese. Drugs such as HMG CoA reductase inhibitors and 75 mg of clopidogrel or aspirin should be given. Transluminal angioplasty and stenting are useful.

Other options:

Options A and D: Femoropopliteal occlusion can lead to claudication in the calf with a palpable femoral pulse but absent distal pulses.

Option B: Iliac obstruction causes thigh and calf claudication with a bruit over the aortoiliac region. The femoral and distal pulses are absent.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 68-year-old female patient has had a diabetic cataract for the past 3 months. Accumulation of which of the following substances is responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sorbitol + fructose

A diabetic cataract occurs due to the accumulation of sorbitol and fructose within the lens.

In diabetic patients, increased levels of blood glucose lead to high levels of glucose in the aqueous humor. The excess glucose in the aqueous humor is metabolized into sorbitol through the polyol pathway by the enzyme aldose reductase. Sorbitol is then converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase but at a much slower rate. In addition, the polar nature of sorbitol prevents its intracellular removal through diffusion.

Sorbitol and fructose accumulate in the lens and the osmotic stress so produced results in overhydration, hydropic lens fibers, and apoptosis of the lens epithelial cells. Thus, the secondary osmotic overhydration is responsible for cortical opacities in a distinct pattern causing snowflake cataracts as shown below.

Diabetes mellitus:  Snowflake cataract

Blunt trauma: May present as rosette-shaped cataract

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Codman's triangle is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Codman's triangle is a pathognomonic radiological sign of an aggressive or malignant bone lesion. It appears when a rapidly growing tumor lifts the periosteum away from the bone cortex, leaving a triangular area of new subperiosteal bone at the margin of the lesion. This is most classically seen in Osteogenic sarcoma (Osteosarcoma), the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children. While it can occasionally be seen in aggressive osteomyelitis (Option A), the "sunburst" appearance and Codman's triangle are hallmarks of osteosarcoma. Aneurysmal bone cysts (Option B) typically show a "soap-bubble" appearance with an intact, though thinned, cortex. Chondrosarcomas (Option D) are cartilage-forming malignant tumors that may show "popcorn" calcifications rather than the specific periosteal reaction of Codman's triangle. Recognizing this sign is critical as it indicates a highly invasive process requiring urgent biopsy and staging to determine the appropriate oncological management

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Statement NOT true about β-oxidation of fatty acids:
options: CAT I and CAT II transport fatty acids
CoA released in cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CoA released in cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation

β-oxidation of fatty acids occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, and long-chain fatty acids require the carnitine shuttle for mitochondrial transport.

Carnitine Shuttle Steps:

1. CPT-I (CAT-I): Converts fatty acyl-CoA → acyl-carnitine in the cytosol/outer mitochondrial membrane.
2. Acyl-carnitine is transported into mitochondria.
3. CPT-II (CAT-II): Converts acyl-carnitine → fatty acyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing carnitine.

Key points:

• ATP is used earlier for fatty acid activation to fatty acyl-CoA.
• Carnitine is released inside mitochondria after reconversion.
• CoA remains within the mitochondrial matrix, not released in the cytosol during acyl-carnitine formation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: If a patient who is on metoprolol is started on verapamil, which of the following side effects would be seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bradycardia with AV block

The patient will be prone to developing bradycardia and AV block.

Both ß-blockers and non-dihydropyridine calcium blockers have a propensity to slow down SA Node function and AV conduction. A combination of these drugs increases the risk further and is contraindicated. In contrast, propranolol has safely been used with the dihydropyridine group (nifedipine) of calcium channel blockers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which kind of the following surgery will cause a profound decrease in vitamin B12?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. BPD-DS

Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD-DS) is the most malabsorptive bariatric procedure and is associated with the greatest risk of vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 absorption requires:

• Intrinsic factor (IF) produced by gastric parietal cells.
• An intact terminal ileum for absorption of the IF–B12 complex.

Following BPD-DS, reduced gastric acid and intrinsic factor production, along with bypass of a large segment of the small intestine, markedly impair vitamin B12 absorption. Lifelong vitamin B12 supplementation is therefore recommended.

• BPD-DS combines:

• Sleeve gastrectomy (reduced intrinsic factor production)
• Extensive intestinal bypass (marked malabsorption)

Why not the other options?

• B. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: Can cause vitamin B12 deficiency due to reduced intrinsic factor and bypass of the duodenum, but the deficiency is less severe than with BPD-DS.
• C. Billroth I: Partial gastrectomy with gastroduodenostomy; causes relatively less vitamin B12 malabsorption because intestinal continuity is largely preserved.
• D. Billroth II: Partial gastrectomy with gastrojejunostomy; may lead to vitamin B12 deficiency over time due to loss of parietal cells, but less profound than BPD-DS.
questions.learning: BPD-DS Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD-DS) is the most malabsorptive bariatric procedure and is associated with the greatest risk of vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. On examination, he has multiple injuries and is diagnosed with class III hemorrhagic shock. What is the approximate percentage range of blood loss in this condition?
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic shock is categorized into four classes based on the volume of blood lost. In Class III shock, the blood loss is estimated to be between 30% and 40% of total blood volume. This stage is characterized by marked hypotension, a heart rate between 120–140 bpm, tachypnea, and significantly decreased urine output (5–15 ml/hour). Class I shock (Option A) involves up to 15% loss with normal vital signs. Class II shock (Option D) involves 15–30% loss, often presenting with tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure. Class IV shock (Option C) involves more than 40% loss and is a life-threatening emergency with profound hypotension and lethargy. Identifying the class of shock is vital for determining the necessity of blood transfusions versus crystalloid resuscitation. Therefore, 30–40% loss is the definitive range for Class III
questions.learning: Hemorrhagic shock is categorized into four classes based on the volume of blood lost. In Class III shock, the blood loss is estimated to be between 30% and 40% of total blood volume.

questions.text: A pregnant woman presents with obstructed labor and is grossly dehydrated. Investigations reveal fetal demise. What will be the management? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cesarean section

In obstructed labor with fetal demise, the choice of delivery depends on the maternal condition and feasibility of vaginal delivery.

Key management principle:

• If the mother is severely compromised (e.g., gross dehydration, exhaustion, shock, or sepsis risk), immediate cesarean section is preferred to rapidly terminate labor and stabilize the mother.

Other options:

• Craniotomy or decapitation: destructive procedures used only when vaginal delivery is feasible and the mother is stable.
• Forceps extraction: requires fully dilated cervix and engaged fetal head.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspergillus

The given slide stained with GMS shows acute-angled (45o) uniform, branching septate hyphae which is suggestive of Aspergillus species.

Aspergillus species grow rapidly, producing aerial hyphae that bear characteristic conidial structures. Long aseptate conidiophores are seen with terminal vesicles on which phialides are arranged in basipetal chains.

The following image shows LPCB mount of Aspergillus fumigatus showing the long conidiophores with terminal vesicles.

Option A: Mucor produces nonseptate, broad hyphae with aerial sporangiophores which end in a sporangium.

Option B: Penicillium produces septate hyphae with branched, septate and brush-like conidiophores.

Option D: Rhizopus appears similar to Mucor but it has rhizoids with sporangiophores arising in groups directly above the rhizoids.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a stab injury to the lower chest, exhibiting bradycardia and hypotension that persist despite intravenous fluid resuscitation. Chest X-ray shows normal lung fields. What is the next appropriate step in managing this patient?
questions.explanation: In a patient with a penetrating lower chest injury presenting with persistent hypotension and bradycardia (suggestive of a shock state), the immediate priority is to identify the source of hemodynamic instability. Since the chest X-ray shows normal lung fields, a massive hemothorax or tension pneumothorax is unlikely, making tube thoracostomy (Option B) unnecessary at this stage. The clinical triad of hypotension, bradycardia, and persistent shock despite fluids in a thoracic trauma patient is highly concerning for cardiac tamponade. Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (eFAST) (Option A) is the most appropriate next step, as it can rapidly detect pericardial fluid at the bedside. CECT of the chest (Option C) or abdomen (Option D) would be inappropriate in a hemodynamically unstable patient due to the time required and the need for patient stability. Therefore, eFAST serves as the critical, immediate diagnostic tool to guide life-saving surgical intervention or pericardiocentesis
questions.learning: In a patient with a penetrating lower chest injury presenting with persistent hypotension and bradycardia (suggestive of a shock state), the immediate priority is to identify the source of hemodynamic instability.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 54-year-old female presented with shortness of breath. On examination, she had bibasal crackles and S3. Echocardiogram revealed poor cardiac contractility with an EF of 33%. Which of the following drugs can reduce mortality?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bisoprolol

This patient has HFrEF with reduced ejection fraction (33%).

Bisoprolol, a β₁-selective blocker, has proven mortality benefit in chronic systolic heart failure.

It reduces sympathetic overactivity and adverse ventricular remodeling.

Propranolol, pindolol, and labetalol do not show survival benefit in HFrEF.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the best step to establish a diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hepatic copper estimation

Wilson’s disease is a disorder of copper metabolism characterized by impaired biliary excretion of copper → accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea (Kayser–Fleischer ring).

Best diagnostic test: Hepatic copper estimation (liver biopsy) = gold standard

• Shows markedly increased hepatic copper (>250 µg/g dry weight)

Supporting findings:

• ↓ Serum ceruloplasmin
• ↑ 24-hour urinary copper excretion
• Kayser–Fleischer ring on slit-lamp (as shown)

Why not others:

• Serum ceruloplasmin: Low but not specific (can be low in other conditions)
• Urinary copper: Sensitive but not definitive
• Serum copper: Variable and unreliable

questions.text: A patient complains of decreased sensation in the lateral 3 ½ fingers of the palmar side of the right hand along with difficulty moving the upper phalanx of the thumb. Associated thenar atrophy is also present. What is the associated nerve injury in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. High median nerve

• Sensory loss over the lateral 3½ fingers (palmar side) with thenar muscle atrophy indicates a proximal median nerve lesion.
• Difficulty moving the upper phalanx of the thumb reflects weakness of thenar muscles (OP, APB, FPB) supplied by median nerve.
• Ulnar and radial nerves have different sensory distributions, while anterior interosseous nerve is purely motor and spares sensation and thenar eminence.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A woman presents to you at 36 weeks of gestation with complaints of feeling lightheadedness and dizziness when she lies on her back. She says she feels alright if she lies on her side or when walks. What is the most likely reason behind this?

IVC- inferior vena cava
options: Excessive venous pooling at the feet
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IVC compression

The most likely reason a woman at 36 weeks of gestation complains of feeling lightheadedness and dizziness when she lies on her back but feels alright if she lies on her side or walks is inferior vena cava (IVC) compression.

When the patient is supine during late pregnancy, the gravid uterus has a compressive effect on the IVC. This results in opening up collateral circulation through the means of paravertebral and azygos veins. However, in some cases, the collateral circulation is unable to open up, and the heart's venous return may get severely impaired. Syncope, tachycardia, and hypotension are produced as a result. The patient is rapidly turned to a lateral posture to return the blood pressure to normal. This phenomenon is called supine hypotension syndrome (postural hypotension).

Other options-

Option A- Individuals with elevated intracranial pressure may experience papilledema along with neck stiffness and visual problems. Several herniation syndromes can result from brain matter being forced through the fixed cranial apertures as the mass grows.

Option C- Pregnant women are advised to avoid heavy meals and not to go to bed immediately after the meal. They can cause heartburn, which is common in pregnancy due to the relaxation of the esophageal sphincter.

Option D- The pressure in the femoral vein is noticeably increased, especially in the later months. The gravid uterus puts pressure on the common iliac veins, particularly on the right side due to the dextrorotation of the uterus. In a lying down position during pregnancy, the femoral venous pressure increases from 8 to 10 cm of water to around 25 cm of water, and in a standing position, it increases to approximately 80 to 100 cm of water. This excessive pooling of blood in the lower limbs explains physiological edema during pregnancy. Edema, varicose veins, piles, and deep vein thrombosis are all caused by the extensibility of the veins and blood stasis in the venous system.
questions.learning: IVC compression — The most likely reason a woman at 36 weeks of gestation complains of feeling lightheadedness and dizziness when she lies on her back but feels alright if she lies on her side or walks is inferior vena cava (IVC) compression.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Attributable risk calculated to understand the relation between smoking and lung cancer is 90%. Which of the following is true?
options: 10% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated
90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in population if smoking is eliminated
90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated
10% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in population if smoking is eliminated
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated

Attributable risk (AR) describes the extent of outcome (lung cancer) that can be attributed to exposure (smoking). In the given scenario, an AR of 90% means that 90% of lung cancer cases among smokers are attributable to smoking. Therefore, 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated.

AR is the difference in incidence rates of disease between an exposed group and an unexposed group. AR is indicative of the extent of the disease attributed to the exposure. It also refers to the amount of disease that could be eliminated in the exposed persons if the exposure is controlled or eliminated. It also helps to determine the impact a successful preventive or public health program might have in case the exposure to cause is reduced or eliminated.

Population-attributable risk (PAR) is the difference in the incidence of disease in the total population and the incidence of disease among those not exposed to the supposed cause. PAR is useful in providing an estimate of the amount by which the disease could be reduced in that whole population if the suspected factor was eliminated or modified.

For example, a PAR of 90% in the context of smoking and lung cancer means that 90% cases of lung cancer in the population can be attributed to smoking.

Relative risk is defined as the ratio of incidence of the disease (outcome) among exposed and unexposed groups. It helps in establishing the association between a cause and a disease. However, it does not help in assessing the extent of the cause bringing about the disease (outcome).
questions.learning: 90% cases of lung cancer can be eliminated in smokers if smoking is eliminated Attributable risk (AR) describes the extent of outcome (lung cancer) that can be attributed to exposure (smoking).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not ligated for the control of epistaxis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Internal carotid artery

The internal carotid artery is not ligated in epistaxis control due to a high percentage of cerebral complications and high mortality.

The first step in treating epistaxis is to pinch the nose with the thumb and index finger for about 5 minutes. The patient should sit leaning slightly forward over a basin to spit out blood and breathe through the mouth (Hippocratic or Trotter’s method).

If the bleeding point is localized, cauterization can be done with electrocautery. In cases of uncontrolled bleeding or when the bleeding is posterior into the throat, anterior or posterior nasal packing may be required, respectively. If bleeding continues despite these measures, endoscopic procedures or vessel ligation can be considered.

The sphenopalatine artery is ligated first through a trans-nasal endoscope (Transnasal endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation). However, if the bleeding persists, maxillary artery ligation is done. If bleeding is still not controlled, external carotid artery ligation is done. It is important to note that if the bleeding site is located superior to the level of the middle turbinate, the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries should be ligated.
questions.learning: Internal carotid artery — The internal carotid artery is not ligated in epistaxis control due to a high percentage of cerebral complications and high mortality.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and acute diarrhea is started on ReSoMal for oral rehydration. Compared with standard WHO low-osmolarity ORS, ReSoMal contains:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lower sodium and higher potassium

• ReSoMal (Rehydration Solution for Malnutrition) is specially formulated for children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM).
• Children with SAM have excess total body sodium but marked intracellular potassium deficiency.
• Therefore, ReSoMal contains:

• Lower sodium (45 mmol/L vs 75 mmol/L in low-osmolar ORS)
• Higher potassium (40 mmol/L vs 20 mmol/L)

• It also contains more glucose and added magnesium, zinc, copper, and other micronutrients.
• ReSoMal helps prevent sodium overload while correcting potassium depletion.
• Exception: In SAM with profuse watery diarrhea or suspected cholera, standard low-osmolarity ORS is preferred because ReSoMal may not adequately replace sodium losses.
• Rehydration should be slow and carefully monitored to avoid heart failure.

| Component | ReSoMal | Low-osmolar ORS

| --------- | ------- | ---------------

| Sodium | 45 mmol/L | 75 mmol/L

| Potassium | 40 mmol/L | 20 mmol/L

questions.text: Identify the structure labeled in the cross- section image of the trachea displayed below.
questions.explanation: The cross-section of the trachea reveals a tube held open by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings. The posterior "gap" between the open ends of these cartilage rings is bridged by a band of smooth muscle known as the Trachealis muscle. In the provided image, the arrow specifically points to this posterior muscular band. The Tracheal cartilage (Option B) forms the rigid anterior and lateral framework shown as the outer gray ring. Submucosal glands (Option C) are located deep to the epithelium but would appear as small glandular structures rather than a distinct posterior muscle band. The perichondrium (Option D) is the thin layer of dense connective tissue that surrounds the cartilage itself. The trachealis muscle is functionally important as it allows the esophagus (located directly posterior) to expand during swallowing and can contract to narrow the tracheal lumen to increase airflow velocity during coughing. Therefore, based on its location and structure, it is definitively the trachealis muscle
questions.learning: The cross-section of the trachea reveals a tube held open by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings. The posterior "gap" between the open ends of these cartilage rings is bridged by a band of smooth muscle known as the Trachealis muscle.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the culture media used for tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium is the classic egg-based selective medium used for the cultivation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It contains glycerol, asparagine, and malachite green, the latter of which inhibits the growth of contaminating bacteria. Regarding the distractors, MacConkey medium (Option B) is used for the isolation of Gram-negative enteric bacilli, particularly differentiating lactose fermenters. Blood agar (Option C) is a general-purpose enriched medium used for fastidious organisms like Streptococci but does not support M. tuberculosis. Chocolate agar (Option D) is heated blood agar used for Haemophilus and Neisseria species. Because mycobacteria are extremely slow-growing and require specific nutrients provided by eggs and minerals, LJ medium is the gold standard for clinical TB culture
questions.learning: Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium is the classic egg-based selective medium used for the cultivation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It contains glycerol, asparagine, and malachite green, the latter of which inhibits the growth of contaminating bacteria.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with bronchial asthma is prescribed a salbutamol metered-dose inhaler (MDI) but has difficulty coordinating actuation with inspiration. His physician recommends using a spacer device with the MDI. Which of the following statements is true regarding the use of a spacer with an MDI?
options: It increases systemic absorption of the drug
It decreases drug wastage and oropharyngeal deposition
It makes the inhalation technique more complicated and less effective
It has no effect on drug delivery to the lungs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It decreases drug wastage and oropharyngeal deposition

A spacer (valved holding chamber) improves the effectiveness of a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) by reducing the need for precise coordination between actuation and inhalation. It slows the aerosol particles, allowing more drug to reach the lower airways while reducing drug deposition in the oropharynx and minimizing wastage, thereby improving both efficacy and safety.

• Particularly useful with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS): Reduces the risk of oral candidiasis and dysphonia.
• Technique: Actuate one puff at a time into the spacer, followed by slow deep inhalation (or tidal breathing in young children).

Why not the other options?

• A. It increases systemic absorption of the drug: Incorrect. Spacers reduce oropharyngeal deposition and systemic absorption of the swallowed drug, thereby decreasing systemic adverse effects.
• C. It makes the inhalation technique more complicated and less effective: Incorrect. Spacers simplify inhaler use, especially in children, elderly patients, and those with poor hand-breath coordination.
• D. It has no effect on drug delivery to the lungs: Incorrect. Spacers increase pulmonary drug deposition and improve drug delivery.
questions.learning: It decreases drug wastage and oropharyngeal deposition A spacer (valved holding chamber) improves the effectiveness of a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) by reducing the need for precise coordination between actuation and inhalation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate is brought to the pediatrician with complaints of bilious vomiting. The abdominal xray shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Duodenal atresia

The radiograph shows the presence of a double bubble sign which is a feature of the duodenal atresia.

Duodenal atresia is the blockade of the duodenum caused due to the failure of the vacuolization of the solid duodenum. It is associated with prematurity, Down’s syndrome, and polyhydramnios.

It is usually identified during the prenatal ultrasound, where it shows the presence of a double bubble sign. If the atresia goes unnoticed during the prenatal period, the babies usually present with bilious vomiting soon after birth. This is because the obstruction is distal to the ampulla of Vater in most cases. Abdominal radiographs also show the double-bubble sign if done before orogastric tube decompression. It is treated by duodenoduodenostomy.

Other options:

Option A: Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis will show the presence of an enlarged gastric gas bubble /single bubble. It is seen at 2-8 weeks of life, more commonly in boys. It presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting which can lead to hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Visible gastric peristalsis can also be observed.

Option B: Jejunal atresia on an abdominal radiograph shows the triple bubble sign. It is the most common type of gastrointestinal atresia. Presenting features include bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and failure to pass meconium.

Option D:  Colonic atresia is the least common type of intestinal atresia. A plain radiograph shows multiple dilated bowel loops, but differentiation between small and large bowel is not possible in neonates. A contrast enema study can confirm the diagnosis. The contrast does not pass proximally to the sigmoid colon as seen in the image.

Pearl PF2116: Radiological findings in various GI disorders

Duodenal atresia: Double bubble sign

Jejunal and ileal atresia: Multiple air-fluid levels (plain erect X-ray abdomen) presenting as triple bubble sign.

Congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: Single enlarged gastric gas bubble - single bubble sign

Sigmoid volvulus: Coffee bean sign

Achalasia cardia: Bird-beak sign

Small bowel obstruction: The obstructed bowel loops are central in location and show valvulae conniventes (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel) characteristic of jejunal involvement.

Large bowel obstruction: The presence of haustrations is a feature of large bowel obstruction. Haustral folds are irregular and do not cross the entire diameter of the bowel. These are absent in the caecum.

Caecal volvulus: Presence of caecal dilatation, single air-fluid level extending into the left upper quadrant, and absence of gas in the distal colon. The colonic haustrations are well maintained.

Midgut volvulus: Corkscrew appearance showing the duodenum and jejunum spiraling around the mesenteric vessels in upper GI contrast studies.

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC): Abdominal X-ray findings include pneumatosis intestinalis (air in the bowel wall).

Cystic fibrosis (CF): Abdominal x-ray with contrast enema reveals a microcolon with several meconium plugs.
questions.learning: Duodenal atresia — The radiograph shows the presence of a double bubble sign which is a feature of the duodenal atresia. Duodenal atresia is the blockade of the duodenum caused due to the failure of the vacuolization of the solid duodenum.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient wakes up unable to extend the wrist after sleeping with the arm hanging over the back of a chair. This condition is most likely caused by what underlying mechanism or injury?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes "Saturday night palsy," a compression injury of the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus. This results in "wrist drop" due to the inability to extend the wrist and fingers. According to Seddon's classification of nerve injuries, this type of temporary compression causes "neuropraxia"—a localized conduction block without any structural damage to the axon or its sheath. Recovery from neuropraxia is typically spontaneous and occurs within days to weeks. Axonotmesis (Option C) involves axonal damage with an intact sheath, requiring longer recovery. Neurotmesis (Option A) is a complete severance of the nerve and sheath, which does not recover without surgery. Neurolysis (Option B) is a surgical procedure to release a nerve from adhesions, not a type of injury. Conservative management including wrist splinting and physical therapy is usually sufficient for Saturday night palsy
questions.learning: The clinical scenario describes "Saturday night palsy," a compression injury of the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus. This results in "wrist drop" due to the inability to extend the wrist and fingers.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A dead body was found with a wound on the neck, with clean-cut edges, crushed tissues along disruption of the vertebral bones. Identify the type of wound.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chop wound

The given description of a wound with sharp edges accompanied by underlying tissue and bone injury is likely to be a chop wound.

CHOP WOUNDS (Slash wounds) are deep gaping wounds caused by a blow with the sharp cutting edge of a fairly heavy weapon, like a hatchet, an axe, sword, broad heavy knife, chopper, saber, or meat cleaver.

* The dimensions of the wound correspond to the crosssection of the penetrating portion of the blade.

* The margins are sharp and may show slight abrasion and bruising with marked destruction of underlying organs.

*

Mostly homicidal; maybe accidental due to power fans, bandsaws, or ship or airplane propellers; rarely suicidal.

*

They are usually seen on the exposed portions of the body like the head, face, neck, shoulders, and extremities.

Chop wounds are so-called because of the action in which they are produced. Depending on the type of instrument, they may resemble an incised or a lacerated wound. The shape of the wound may give clues to the type of weapon.

The below image shows a chop wound inflicted on the scalp.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following fertility indicator can change with changes in age-specific mortality rates?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Net reproduction rate

Net reproduction rate can change with changes in age-specific mortality rates. General fertility rate, total fertility rate, and gross reproduction rate are not dependent on age-specific mortality rate.

Net reproduction rate (NRR) is defined as the number of daughters a newborn girl will bear during her lifetime assuming fixed age-specific fertility and mortality rate.

India is aiming for an NRR of 1 as it is equivalent to the two-child norm. If the NRR is less than 1, then the population growth of a community is said to be inadequate.

Pearl PF1746: Fertility Indicators

Crude birth rate

* It is the simplest measure of fertility although its usage is unsatisfactory

* India, as per SRS bulletin 2018, had a birth rate of 20.0 per 1000 population

General Fertility Rate

* It is a better indicator of fertility than crude birth rate

* The demerit of this indicator is that not all women in the denominator are exposed to childbirth

Age-specific fertility rates is a more precise measure of fertility and is also a sensitive indicator of family planning achievement.

Total Fertility Rate

* It is the sum of all age-specific fertility rates multiplied by 5

* This measure gives the approximate magnitude of completed family size

Gross Reproductive Rate is the average number of girls that would be born to a woman if she experiences the current fertility pattern throughout her reproductive span, assuming no mortality.

Net Reproduction Rate

* It is a demographic indicator

* NRR of 1 is equivalent to approximately the 2 child norm

* If the NRR is less than 1, then the reproductive performance of the population is said to be inadequate
questions.learning: Net reproduction rate Net reproduction rate can change with changes in age-specific mortality rates. General fertility rate, total fertility rate, and gross reproduction rate are not dependent on age-specific mortality rate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy develops recurrent hypoglycemic episodes following moderate physical activity. Investigations show increased levels of ketone bodies, lactic acid, and triglycerides, along with hepatomegaly and renomegaly on examination. Which hepatic enzyme deficiency best explains these clinical and laboratory findings?
questions.explanation: The combination of fasting-induced hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), and renomegaly (enlarged kidneys) is pathognomonic for Von Gierke’s disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I) . This condition is caused by a deficiency in glucose-6-phosphatase, the enzyme responsible for converting glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose during glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Without this enzyme, the liver cannot release glucose into the blood, leading to severe hypoglycemia and the shunting of metabolites into pathways that produce lactic acid, triglycerides, and ketone bodies. Option B and C are metabolic intermediates, not enzymes whose deficiency causes this syndrome. Option D refers to complex carbohydrates involved in different storage disorders (mucopolysaccharidoses). Therefore, the inability to perform the final step of glucose release due to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency is the definitive enzymatic cause of this patient’s multi-system metabolic derangement
questions.learning: The combination of fasting-induced hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), and renomegaly (enlarged kidneys) is pathognomonic for Von Gierke’s disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I) .

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of behavioral changes over the past year, including hyperactivity, impulsivity, and poor academic performance. On examination, he has a diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid gland. Laboratory findings show: • TSH: elevated • T4: elevated • T3: elevated Which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Resistance to thyroid hormone

This patient has thyroid hormone resistance (Refetoff syndrome), characterized by:

• Elevated T3 and T4 with inappropriately normal or elevated TSH
• Due to mutation in thyroid hormone receptor (TRβ) → reduced tissue responsiveness

Pathophysiology:

• Peripheral tissues are resistant → reduced negative feedback
• Pituitary continues to secrete TSH → thyroid enlargement (goiter)
• Mixed clinical picture:

• Some tissues → hyperthyroid features (e.g., hyperactivity)
• Others → relatively hypothyroid

Why not other options?

• A. Hashimoto thyroiditis → ↑ TSH, ↓ T4
• B. TBG excess → ↑ total T4 but normal TSH
• C. Dyshormonogenesis → hypothyroidism pattern

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following form the marked structure except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2nd Palmar interossei

The structure marked in the image is the dorsal digital expansion of the middle finger. Palmar interossei do not attach to the middle finger and therefore it does not contribute to the dorsal digital expansion of the middle finger.

Palmar interossei are unipennate muscles originating from their own metacarpal bone. Their function is adduction. The middle finger does not need adduction and hence does not have palmar interossei.

Dorsal interossei are bipennate muscles originating from the adjacent metacarpal bone. They attach to the middle three fingers on both sides and do not attach on the thumb and little finger. Their function is abduction. The thumb and little finger have other muscles for abduction.

The lateral 2 lumbricals are unipennate and medial 2 lumbricals are bipennate. Their function is flexion at metacarpophalangeal joints.
