questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was done to assess nutritional status among young children in rural and urban areas. 30 children in rural and 20 children in urban areas were malnourished. Which of the following tests of significance is the most appropriate in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chi Square test

The most appropriate test of significance, in this case, is the chi-square test. It is used to compare qualitative data between 2 groups with independent measures.

Option B: Paired t-test compares paired data or pre-intervention and post-intervention data of the same group. This doesn't apply here as the groups are not paired.

Option C: The standard error of the mean is calculated for quantitative data, with a measure of central tendency as mean.

Option D: ANOVA is used to compare more than 2 groups.
questions.learning: Chi Square test — The most appropriate test of significance, in this case, is the chi-square test. It is used to compare qualitative data between 2 groups with independent measures.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: If the pH is reduced from 7.4 to 7.3 with the PO2 being constant at 100 mmHg, which line would PCO2 follow?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1

If the pH is reduced from 7.4 to 7.3 with the alveolar PO2 being constant at 100 mmHg, PCO2 would follow line 1.

This concept can be understood in three steps.

Step 1- Effect of CO2 on ventilation, when the alveolar PO2 is kept constant.

When the alveolar PO2 (PaO2) is kept constant, an increased amount of inspired CO2  leads to increase in the ventilation. The relation is a straight line.

The below graph shows the effect of CO2 on ventilation when alveolar PaO2 is kept constant at 100mm Hg.

Step 2. The shift of the above graph when PO2 changes.

When PO2 changes, the relation between the amount of CO2 inhaled and ventilation still remains in a straight line. However, the slopes of the lines change. The slope increases when alveolar PO2 decreases and vice versa. In other words, the lines move towards the left when PO2 decreases. However, the point of intersection of all these lines remains the same.

The below graph shows the relation between inspired CO2 and ventilation when alveolar PO2 is maintained at 40mm Hg, 55mm Hg, and 100 mm Hg. As the alveolar PO2 has decreased, the lines have shifted to the left. But they are all intersecting at the same point on the x-axis.

Step 3. The shift of the above graph when pH changes.

When pH decreases, as in acidosis, the CO2 response curve is similar to the above. The only difference is they are shifted to the left and have different points on the intersection on x- axis.

The below graphs show CO2 response curves when pH is 7.4, 7.3, and PO2 is 40mm Hg, 55mm Hg, and 100mm Hg. The lines have shifted to the left and have a different point of intersection.

In the question image, only line 1 has been shifted to the left and has a different point of intersection on x-axis compared to other lines. Therefore, line 1 is the answer.
questions.learning: 1 If the pH is reduced from 7.4 to 7.3 with the alveolar PO2 being constant at 100 mmHg, PCO2 would follow line 1. This concept can be understood in three steps.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray shows diffuse, bilateral alveolar opacities in a classic "bat-wing" or butterfly pattern, which is characteristic of pulmonary edema. The central distribution of these opacities, combined with cardiomegaly (an enlarged heart silhouette), strongly suggests a cardiogenic cause, such as left heart failure. Other common findings include Kerley B lines, which represent septal edema. Hydrothorax (Option B) and Pleural Effusion (Option C) appear as homogeneous opacities with a meniscus sign that blunts the costophrenic angles, rather than diffuse infiltrates throughout the lung parenchyma. Pulmonary Fibrosis (Option D) typically presents with reticular opacities, honeycombing, and reduced lung volumes, which differ from the fluffy alveolar pattern seen here. Treatment for cardiogenic pulmonary edema focuses on diuretics and oxygen to reduce volume overload

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: At a crime scene, blood stains are detected during forensic examination. Which of the following tests is not used for the identification of blood stains?
questions.explanation: In forensic science, the identification of blood involves presumptive and confirmatory tests. Takayama's test (Option B) and Teichman's test (Option C) are standard confirmatory tests that form characteristic hemochromogen and hemin crystals, respectively, when blood is present. Spectroscopy (Option D) is an advanced method used to identify the absorption bands of hemoglobin derivatives. Barberio's test (Option A), however, is not applicable for identifying blood stains; it is a specialized chemical test used specifically for the identification of semen by forming yellow needle-like crystals of spermine picrate. Accurately distinguishing between these biological fluid tests is a foundational skill in forensic medicine. Confirmatory tests for blood are essential to rule out other red substances (like rust or paint) and to provide definitive evidence for criminal investigations. Following these "presumptive-to-confirmatory" protocols ensures that the forensic evidence presented in a court of law is scientifically robust. Therefore, Barberio’s remains the correct outlier in the context of bloodstain identification

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Administration of which of the following vaccines is associated with the risk of intussussception?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rotavirus vaccine

Rotavirus vaccine is associated with a potential risk of intussusception, especially when the first dose of these vaccines is given to infants aged >12 weeks. Because of this risk, the rotavirus vaccine is not a part of catch-up immunization programs, as the age of the child is difficult to ascertain in such programs.

Rotavirus vaccines are oral, live attenuated vaccines and are of 3 types:

1. Rotarix (human monovalent) vaccine is administered in 2 oral doses:

• First dose: At 6 weeks, no later than 12 weeks (due to the risk of intussusception).
• Second dose: With a gap of 4 weeks from the first dose, to be given by 16 weeks and no later than 24 weeks.

2. RotaTeq (pentavalent bovine-human reassortant) vaccine is administered in 3 oral doses at 2, 4, and 6 months. The first dose is given between 6-12 weeks and subsequent doses within a 4-10 weeks gap. All the 3 doses should be given before 32 weeks.
3. Rotavac (monovalent liquid frozen) vaccine is administered in 3 oral doses, 4 weeks apart at 6,10 and 14 weeks. It should not be administered to children more than 8 months of age.
questions.learning: Rotavirus vaccine Rotavirus vaccine is associated with a potential risk of intussusception, especially when the first dose of these vaccines is given to infants aged >12 weeks.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: During a trip to a high-altitude mountainous region, a group of individuals experiences several physiological changes related to altitude exposure. Which of the following conditions is least likely to occur under high-altitude conditions?
questions.explanation: At high altitudes, the barometric pressure decreases, which directly reduces the partial pressure of inspired oxygen (O2). This leads to arterial hypoxia. Therefore, an increase in partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) in the blood is least likely to occur; in fact, blood levels characteristically drop. The other options represent standard compensatory mechanisms of high-altitude acclimatization. Hyperventilation (Option D) is the immediate response triggered by peripheral chemoreceptors to maximize oxygen intake. Over longer periods, the kidneys secrete erythropoietin, which stimulates an increase in Red Blood Cell (RBC) count and Hemoglobin (Hb) levels (Option B) to improve oxygen-carrying capacity. Additionally, muscle tissues adapt by increasing myoglobin content (Option C) to facilitate oxygen diffusion into the mitochondria. These physiological adjustments allow the body to function in an oxygen-deprived environment, but the primary challenge remains the inherently low atmospheric and arterial

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Many patients with unexplained rash and fever were reported from a village close to the Primary Health Centre (PHC). What is the first step in initiating the investigation of such an epidemic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Verification of diagnosis

The first step in investigating a suspected epidemic (outbreak) is to verify the diagnosis. This involves confirming that the reported cases are correctly diagnosed through clinical evaluation and appropriate laboratory investigations. Verification helps exclude diagnostic errors, laboratory mistakes, or misclassification before initiating a full-scale outbreak investigation. Verification includes:

• Reviewing clinical findings
• Examining laboratory reports
• Consulting clinicians and microbiologists
• Excluding laboratory or reporting errors

Why not the other options?

• A. Rapid search for all cases: This is done after the diagnosis has been verified and the outbreak has been confirmed.
• C. Confirm existence of epidemic: An epidemic can be confirmed only after ensuring that the diagnosis is correct.
• D. Defining the population at risk: This is a later step used to calculate attack rates and identify risk factors.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following regulate body temperature?
questions.explanation: The Hypothalamus serves as the body's master thermostat and primary center for thermoregulation. It contains specialized thermosensitive neurons that monitor both the core blood temperature and signals from peripheral skin receptors. The anterior (preoptic) hypothalamus primarily coordinates heat loss mechanisms, such as sweating and vasodilation, while the posterior hypothalamus coordinates heat conservation and production mechanisms, such as shivering and vasoconstriction. Basal ganglia (Option B) are involved in motor control and habit formation. The thalamus (Option C) acts as a major relay station for sensory information to the cortex. The limbic system (Option D) is primarily responsible for emotional processing and memory. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic set-point is the physiological basis of fever, where cytokines induce prostaglandin E2 production, leading the hypothalamus to perceive normal core temperatures as cold and initiating heat-generating responses. This regulatory function is critical for maintaining metabolic homeostasis within a narrow temperature range
questions.learning: The Hypothalamus serves as the body's master thermostat and primary center for thermoregulation. It contains specialized thermosensitive neurons that monitor both the core blood temperature and signals from peripheral skin receptors.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A woman, who is 4 days postpartum, presented with tearfulness, mood swings, and occasional insomnia. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Postpartum blues

Postpartum blues is the most likely diagnosis in a postpartum woman with tearfulness, mood swings, and insomnia from day 4.

Postpartum blues, also known as baby blues, is a transient mood disorder characterized by sadness, tearfulness, confusion, and dysphoria. There are no suicidal thoughts or thoughts of harming the baby. These symptoms typically develop 3-5 days after delivery. They are thought to be due to hormonal changes, the stress of giving birth, and the responsibilities of motherhood. They resolve spontaneously within 10-14 days.

Management involves reassurance, education, and support. The patient must be followed up and assessed if symptoms persist for >2 weeks to evaluate postpartum depression.

Other options:

Option A: When the symptoms of depressed mood, anxiety, insomnia, and weight changes start within 4 weeks as per DSM 5 or 6 weeks as per ICD 11, and the symptoms persist for ≥ 2 weeks, the diagnosis will be postpartum depression. The patient may have occasional thoughts of harming the baby and suicidal thoughts. It can persist for months to years when untreated.

Option C: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency that usually occurs within 4 weeks after delivery (DSM 5) or 6 weeks after delivery (ICD 11). The predominant symptoms are hallucinations, delusions, suicidal thoughts, and thoughts of harming the baby. Psychotic symptoms such as insomnia, restlessness, labile mood, and agitation are seen. Lithium, antipsychotics, and an antidepressant is the treatment of choice.

Option D: Postpartum anxiety is not defined by DSM-5. However, some platforms might describe postpartum anxiety as excessive or severe worry after childbirth.

Note:  Zuranolone is the first-ever oral drug to be approved specifically for the treatment of postpartum depression. It is a neuroactive steroid that enhances the action of GABA in the brain and regulates mood.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is being evaluated for pubertal development. She has onset of breast development, pubic hair has appeared, and she is at Tanner stage 2. Which of the following is the next likely event to occur according to Tanner staging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peak growth spurt

Sequence of pubertal development shows that after thelarche (onset of breast development, tanner stage 2) and pubarche (appearance of pubic hair, Tanner stage 2), the next most likely event is the peak height velocity (growth spurt). The growth spurt occurs early in female puberty, generally after Tanner stage 2 breast and pubic hair development.

In females at 10 to 11 years, the breast bud (thelarche) appears, which is the first sign of puberty, followed by the appearance of pubic hair (pubarche), growth spurt, and menarche. Thelarche > pubarche > growth spurt > menarche .

Tanner staging
Breast changes
Pubic hair changes

Stage 1

B1 - Denotes the prepubertal breast. At this infantile stage, only the papilla is elevated.

P1 - No pubic hair

Stage 2

B2 - Denotes thelarche. The breast buds are palpable, areola enlarges and the breast is elevated like a small mound.

P2 - The appearance of pigmented hair sparsely over the labia, either long or slightly curved.

Stage 3

B3 - There is further enlargement of the breast and its areola without separation of its contours.

P3 - Darker, coarser and curly hair

Stage 4

B4 - Preferential growth of the areola and nipple leads to formation of a secondary mound over the mound of the breast.

P4 - Preadult stage cover short inverted triangular distribution.

Stage 5

B5 - Formation of the mature adult breast.

P5 - Adult inverted triangular distributuion.

Other options:

Option B: Appearance of axillary hair – Axillary hair development occurs later, with stages A1 (no axillary hair), A2 (sparse axillary hair), and A3 (adult distribution). This follows pubic hair development and usually appears after the growth spurt.

Option C: Menarche is a late pubertal event, generally following thelarche by about 2 years.

Option D: Thelarche refers to the onset of breast development.
questions.learning: Peak growth spurt Sequence of pubertal development shows that after thelarche (onset of breast development, tanner stage 2) and pubarche (appearance of pubic hair, Tanner stage 2), the next most likely event is the peak height velocity (growth spurt).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 67-year-old patient with a history of thromboembolic stroke is currently taking aspirin and warfarin. He is complaining of a headache and appears confused after a fall in the toilet last night. NCCT of the head was done. What is the next best step in management? NCCT- Non contrast CT head
options: Vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma and neurosurgery consultation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma and neurosurgery consultation

The above clinical scenario and the plain computed tomography (CT) scan show a concave-convex-shaped hematoma on the left side suggestive of an acute subdural hematoma (SDH). Since, the patient is on anticoagulants, reversal with Vitamin K, FFP and immediate neurosurgical consultation would be the next best step.

Acute SDH results from the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid membrane and the dura. The tearing of a bridging vein running from the cerebral cortex to the dural sinuses is the most common cause of acute SDH.

Radiographic features of subdural haemorrhages-Crescent-like distribution around the periphery of the brain.
Crescent-shaped hypodense lesion on axial CT: Chronic subdural haemorrhage
Crescent-shaped hyperdense collections on CT: Acute subdural haemorrhage.

On head CT scan, acute SDH appears as a hyperdense, crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) lesion (as seen in this question)

Open craniotomy for the evacuation of acute SDH is indicated for the following:

* Thickness >1 cm

* Midline shift >5 mm

Emergent decompression is also recommended for a comatose patient with an acute subdural hematoma less than 1 cm in thickness causing a midline shift of less than 5 mm if any of the following criteria are met:

*  GCS drops by two or more points from the time of injury to the hospitalization

*  The patient presents with fixed and dilated pupils

* ICP is >20mm Hg

Other options:

Option A: Aspirin and Clopidogrel are given in patients with ischemic stroke. It is not required for this patient.

Option C: Mannitol is used to lower intracranial pressure. Raised features of intracranial pressure like vomiting, papilledema are not mentioned.

Option D: Only observation would be inappropriate in the case of Acute SDH.

Pearl PF1866: Intracranial haemorrhage

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which is not a branch of facial artery in the face?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mental

Mental is not a branch of the facial artery but the branch of the maxillary artery in the face.

The first part of the maxillary artery gives rise to the mental artery as a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar artery.

The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery which arises in the carotid triangle, above the origin of the lingual artery. It runs upwards in the neck and curves around the anteroinferior border of the masseter to enter the face.

Branches of facial artery in the neck
Branches of facial artery in the face

Ascending palatine artery
Premasseteric artery

Tonsillar branch
Superior and inferior labial arteries

Submental artery
Lateral nasal artery

Branches to submandibular gland
Angular artery

The premasseteric artery passes along the anterior border of the masseter and the surrounding tissues are supplied by it. The inferior labial artery mainly supplies the inferior labial glands. It then anastomoses with its controlateral fellow and with the mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery. The superior labial artery supplies the upper lip whereas the lateral nasal artery supplies the dorsum and alae of the nose. Both these arteries anastomose with its controlateral fellow.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following topical local anesthetics is commonly used in cataract surgery?
questions.explanation: In modern ophthalmic practice, particularly for small-incision cataract surgery, topical anesthesia is frequently used. Proparacaine 0.5% is the most common topical local anesthetic applied to the corneal surface. It provides rapid, effective surface anesthesia with a fast onset (within 30 seconds) and minimal corneal irritation. Bupivacaine 0.5% (Option B) is a long-acting anesthetic typically used for regional nerve blocks (like retrobulbar or peribulbar blocks) but is not the standard agent for purely topical application. Halothane (Option C) and Nitrous Oxide (Option D) are inhalation anesthetics used for general anesthesia, not for topical numbing. Topical anesthesia is preferred for its safety, immediate visual recovery, and avoidance of the risks associated with needle-based blocks, such as globe perforation or retrobulbar hemorrhage. It is often supplemented with intracameral lidocaine to ensure patient comfort during manipulation of the lens and iris
questions.learning: In modern ophthalmic practice, particularly for small-incision cataract surgery, topical anesthesia is frequently used. Proparacaine 0.5% is the most common topical local anesthetic applied to the corneal surface.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A mother brings her daughter with complaints that she eats excessively and then induces vomiting after meals. She is conscious about her weight, and her BMI is 25. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s behavior of binge eating followed by compensatory self-induced vomiting, coupled with an intense preoccupation with body weight and a normal BMI (25), is diagnostic for Bulimia Nervosa. Anorexia nervosa (Option A) is characterized by severe food restriction and an abnormally low body weight. Binge eating disorder (Option B) involves episodes of eating excessive amounts of food but lacks the subsequent compensatory purging behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, or excessive exercise). OCD (Option D) is characterized by obsessions and compulsions but is not primarily an eating disorder. Bulimia nervosa can lead to serious health issues, including electrolyte imbalances, dental erosion (from stomach acid), and parotid gland enlargement. Management typically involves a combination of nutritional counseling and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT). Fluoxetine is the only FDA-approved medication for the treatment of bulimia
questions.learning: The patient’s behavior of binge eating followed by compensatory self-induced vomiting, coupled with an intense preoccupation with body weight and a normal BMI (25), is diagnostic for Bulimia Nervosa.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is contraindicated in a pregnant woman diagnosed with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB)?
questions.explanation: Managing drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) in pregnancy is challenging due to the fetal toxicity of several second-line agents. Kanamycin (Option C), an aminoglycoside, is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy. Like other aminoglycosides (e.g., Streptomycin), it is known to cross the placenta and cause permanent ototoxicity (eighth cranial nerve damage) and potential nephrotoxicity in the developing fetus. Amoxicillin (Option A) is generally safe in pregnancy. Clofazimine (Option B) and Linezolid (Option D) are second-line agents that are often utilized in extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB cases; while they carry their own risks, they are considered "safer" alternatives or are used when the benefit outweighs the risk compared to the known teratogenicity of aminoglycosides. Therefore, because of its documented ability to cause fetal deafness, Kanamycin is the definitive "not safe" choice among the options provided
questions.learning: Managing drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) in pregnancy is challenging due to the fetal toxicity of several second-line agents. Kanamycin (Option C), an aminoglycoside, is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Arrange the sequence of lactation in the right order * Mammogenesis * Lactogenesis * Galactokinesis * Galactopoiesis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 - 2 - 3 - 4

The correct order of lactation is: Mammogenesis – lactogenesis – galactokinesis – galactopoiesis

Function
Definition
Hormone

Mammogenesis
Breast growth and development

Estrogen (ductal growth)

Progesterone (alveolar growth)

Lactogenesis
Initiation of milk secretion
Prolactin

Galactokinesis
Ejection of milk
Oxytocin

Galactopoiesis
Maintainence of lactation
Prolactin

Mammogenesis: This refers to the development and growth of the mammary glands. It occurs during puberty and pregnancy under the influence of hormones like estrogen and progesterone.

Lactogenesis: This is the process of milk production. There are two phases:

* a. Lactogenesis I: Also known as colostrum secretion, it begins during late pregnancy and continues after birth for a few days. The mammary glands produce colostrum, a thick, yellowish fluid rich in antibodies and nutrients.

* b. Lactogenesis II: Also known as transitional milk secretion, it begins around 2-5 days after birth. The mammary glands switch to producing mature milk.

Galactokinesis: This involves the movement of milk through the mammary ducts towards the nipple. It is facilitated by the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli in response to oxytocin release.

Galactopoiesis: This refers to the maintenance and regulation of milk production. It involves hormonal regulation, primarily prolactin, which stimulates milk synthesis and secretion. Additionally, factors like frequent breastfeeding or milk removal help maintain milk production.

So, the correct sequence is Mammogenesis (development of mammary glands) – Lactogenesis (milk production) – Galactokinesis (movement of milk) – Galactopoiesis (maintenance of milk production.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the histological slide shown below of the structure
questions.explanation: The given histological slide shows closely packed acinar cells with dark-stained nuclei and granular cytoplasm, characteristic of the exocrine pancreas. In addition, there are lighter-staining regions scattered within the tissue, one of which is indicated by the arrow. These pale areas represent the Islets of Langerhans, the endocrine component of the pancreas. This combination of dark exocrine acini and light endocrine islets is a hallmark feature of pancreatic tissue. The acini are responsible for secreting digestive enzymes, while the islets produce hormones such as insulin and glucagon. Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Lymph node: Shows lymphoid follicles and germinal centers, not acini or islets. (B) Glomerulus: Found in the kidney, characterized by a tuft of capillaries within Bowman’s capsule. (C) Spleen: Shows red pulp and white pulp, not glandular acinar arrangement

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In patients requiring warfarin therapy, what is the recommended target INR range for those with mechanical heart valves?
questions.explanation: Patients with mechanical prosthetic heart valves are at a high risk for thromboembolism and require lifelong anticoagulation with Warfarin. To ensure the valve does not clot while minimizing the risk of major bleeding, the international normalized ratio (INR) must be maintained within a specific therapeutic window. For most mechanical valves (especially mitral valves or older-generation aortic valves), the recommended target INR range is 2.5 to 3.5. A lower range of 2.0-3.0 (Option B) is the standard target for conditions like atrial fibrillation or deep vein thrombosis. Ranges below 2.0 (Option A) provide inadequate protection against valve thrombosis. Ranges above 3.5 (Option D) significantly increase the risk of intracranial and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Therefore, the 2.5-3.5 range represents the optimal balance of safety and efficacy for patients with mechanical heart valves

Glycine’s pI = (pK₁ 2.3 + pK₂ 9.6) ÷ 2 ≈ 6, where it exists mainly as a zwitterion with zero net charge.

questions.text: Varicella-zoster virus remains dormant in the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dorsal root ganglion

Varicella-zoster virus (VZV) is a human herpesvirus that causes varicella (chickenpox) as a primary infection and then remains in a latent form in the dorsal root ganglia for a variable period after which it can reactivate to cause herpes zoster (shingles).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A patient with pulmonary edema suddenly develops rapid shallow breathing and dyspnea due to stimulation of receptors located in alveolar walls near pulmonary capillaries. These receptors are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Juxtacapillary receptors

Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are sensory nerve endings located in the alveolar walls close to pulmonary capillaries. They are stimulated by conditions that increase pulmonary interstitial fluid, such as pulmonary edema, left ventricular failure, pneumonia, and pulmonary congestion. Activation of J receptors produces rapid, shallow breathing (tachypnea), dyspnea, and a sensation of air hunger.

Why not the other options?

• A. Irritant receptors – respond to inhaled irritants, smoke, dust, and noxious gases, causing cough and bronchoconstriction.
• B. Pulmonary stretch receptors – mediate the Hering–Breuer inflation reflex and are activated by lung inflation.
• D. Central chemoreceptors – respond to changes in CSF pH and PaCO₂, regulating ventilation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The clinical condition shown in the image is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Horseshoe kidney

The image shows fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys by an isthmus, producing the characteristic U-shaped configuration of a horseshoe kidney.

Key features:

• Usually fusion of the lower poles
• Kidneys are often malrotated
• The fused kidney typically lies lower than normal
• The inferior mesenteric artery commonly prevents normal ascent

Why not the other options?

• (a) Malrotated kidney: Abnormal orientation of the renal hilum without fusion.
• (b) Malascended kidney: Kidney remains abnormally low but is not necessarily fused.
• (c) Doughnut kidney: Usually refers to complete fusion of the kidneys, forming a ring-like configuration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with a history of ingestion of ten tablets of paracetamol. He has developed oliguria and liver function tests show deranged values. Which of the following can be used in the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. N-acetylcysteine

The clinical vignette suggests acetaminophen (Paracetamol) toxicity, which can be managed with N-acetylcysteine.

Early manifestations (within 4-12 hours) of acetaminophen toxicity include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Later, renal failure and myocardial injury may be seen. Low bilirubin levels along with raised aminotransferase levels are characteristic of the condition.

Acetaminophen toxicity is an important cause of acute liver failure. Ingestion of ≥25g can be fatal. Cytochrome P450 CYP2E1 metabolizes acetaminophen to N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine (NAPQI). Glutathione is responsible for its detoxification, after which it is excreted in the urine. When glutathione reserves are depleted or large amounts of NAPQI are formed, it binds to hepatocyte macromolecules. This can then lead to hepatocyte necrosis.

Initial management includes gastric lavage and oral charcoal or cholestyramine. It should be carried out within thirty minutes of ingestion. If they are used, gastric lavage must be done afterward before using another agent. Acetaminophen blood levels can be estimated from a nomogram plot. In patients with high acetaminophen levels, intravenous N-acetylcysteine administration within 8 hours of ingestion is recommended. It helps in the replenishment of glutathione. It is partially effective even up to 36 hours. Liver transplantation is necessary if signs of hepatic failure continue despite therapy.

Other options:

Option B: Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that is used in severe congestive cardiac failure. It acts on β-1 receptors at a dose of 2-10 mcg/kg/minute.

Option C: Ursodeoxycholic acid is a bile acid that is the first-line treatment for primary biliary cholangitis. It is useful in cholestatic drug hepatotoxicity, but is not recommended.

Option D: Furosemide is a loop diuretic commonly used in pulmonary edema and congestive heart failure. Side effects include hyponatremia, hypotension, and ototoxicity.
questions.learning: N-acetylcysteine — The clinical vignette suggests acetaminophen (Paracetamol) toxicity, which can be managed with N-acetylcysteine. Early manifestations (within 4-12 hours) of acetaminophen toxicity include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient developed difficulty in standing from a seated position, walking up steps, squatting and lifting arms overhead. Chronic therapy with which of the following drugs is likely to result in such presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glucocorticoids

Glucocorticoid-induced myopathy is a common complication of chronic corticosteroid therapy. It presents with painless, symmetric proximal muscle weakness, causing difficulty in rising from a chair, climbing stairs, squatting, and lifting the arms overhead. It results from muscle protein catabolism, predominantly affecting type II (fast-twitch) muscle fibers.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Acetaminophen❌: Does not cause myopathy; toxicity primarily affects the liver.
• B. Fexofenadine❌: A second-generation antihistamine that is not associated with proximal muscle weakness.
• D. Metformin ❌

• May rarely cause vitamin B12 deficiency or lactic acidosis, but does not cause steroid-like proximal myopathy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female, P2L2, presents with a mass per vaginum. On examination, infravaginal elongation of the cervix is noted. How will you treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fothergill surgery

The appropriate treatment for a 30-year-old female with infravaginal elongation of the cervix is Fothergill surgery.

Fothergill surgery, or the Manchester operation, involves performing an anterior colporrhaphy combined with the amputation of the cervix. During the procedure, the Mackenrodt ligaments are sutured in front of the cervix, and the operation concludes with a colpoperineorrhaphy. This surgical approach is particularly suitable for women under 40 years old who wish to maintain reproductive function, although it’s important to note that fertility may be reduced following the procedure.

Various other surgeries were performed for the management of uterovaginal prolapse:

1. Anterior colporrhaphy: This is done for cystocele or cystourethrocele.
2. Posterior colporrhaphy/ colpoperineorrhaphy: This is done for posterior defects like rectocele or rectal defects with perineal laxity.
3. Le Forte's repair(option B): This is preferred only in elderly women with advanced prolapse, or those unfit for surgery. Women wanting an active sexual life are poor candidates for this procedure as it creates an adhesive area in the midline.
4. Abdominal sling surgeries: Young women desirous of retaining menstrual and reproductive functions are ideal candidates. These surgeries use tapes as slings to prevent organ descent. These include:

1. Abdominal wall cervicopexy (modified by Purandare and Mathre) - sling attached to cervix posteriorly near uterosacral ligaments.
2. Shirodkar's sling surgery - the sling fixes the cervix to the lumbosacral fascia.
3. Khanna's sling surgery - sling fixed to the anterior superior iliac spine, strengthening the Mackenrodt's ligament.

5. Fothergill surgery (Manchester operation)
6. Ward-Mayo surgery: This is a combination of vaginal hysterectomy + pelvic floor repair. It is done in women >40 years, not desiring reproductive function.
7. Moschowitz surgery: This is performed for enterocele repair where the pouch of Douglas is obliterated.

Management of Vault prolapse:

• If the patient is fit for abdominal surgery: Transabdominal sacral colpopexy, i.e., suspending the vault to the sacral promontory extraperitoneally. It is best suited for younger women since coital difficulty following vaginal surgery is avoided
• If the patient is not fit for abdominal surgery: Right Transvaginal sacrospinous colpopexy. It is usually preferred in obese and elderly women, who are not fit for abdominal surgery.
• Colpocleisis is permissible if sexual activity is not desired.

Other options:

Option A: McCall culdoplasty is primarily used to prevent enterocele formation and provide support to the posterior vaginal apex, particularly following vaginal hysterectomy.

Option D: The Latzko procedure is a surgical technique used to treat vesicovaginal fistula. It involves removing the vaginal epithelium around the fistula and approximating the edges to promote healing.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the appropriate next step in management for a primigravida at 26 weeks of gestation who presents with a blood pressure of 150/90 mm Hg?
questions.explanation: The presentation of a blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg at 26 weeks of gestation in a primigravida suggests a potential diagnosis of pre-eclampsia. Pre-eclampsia is defined by new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks of pregnancy accompanied by proteinuria or organ dysfunction. The immediate and most essential next step to differentiate simple gestational hypertension from pre-eclampsia is a urine dipstick to screen for proteinuria. Uric acid levels (Option A), liver function tests (Option B), and a complete blood count (Option C) are important follow-up investigations to assess the severity of pre-eclampsia or the development of HELLP syndrome, but they are not the primary screening step. If the urine dipstick is positive (1+ or more), further quantification via a 24-hour urine protein or protein-creatinine ratio is warranted. Therefore, checking for proteinuria via dipstick is the critical initial management step in a pregnant woman with elevated blood pressure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician with abdominal pain and melena. She also complains of progressive fatigue and a 5 kg (11 Ib) weight loss over the last 2 months. She has a strong family history of colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. Colonoscopy shows a protuberant, friable mass in the ascending colon, and biopsy is diagnostic for colon adenocarcinoma. Genetic analysis confirms a mutation consistent with Lynch syndrome. Which of the following is most likely responsible for the development of colon cancer in this patient?
options: Insertion of abnormal bases into DNA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleotide mismatches that escape repair

Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer) is caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2. These genes normally correct base–base mismatches and insertion–deletion errors that occur during DNA replication.

Pathogenesis:

Defective mismatch repair leads to accumulation of unrepaired nucleotide mismatches, particularly in repetitive DNA sequences called microsatellites.

This results in microsatellite instability (MSI), which promotes mutations in genes controlling cell growth and apoptosis, leading to early-onset colorectal cancer and other malignancies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzyme activity decreases in fasting?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phosphofructokinase 1

During fasting, there is low insulin, and hence, the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 gets inhibited.

Phosphofructokinase 1 is an enzyme of glycolysis. It is induced by insulin and a well-fed state.

Other options:

Option A: Hormone-sensitive lipase mobilizes stored fats in a fasting state.

Option B: Glycogen phosphorylase is active in fasting state so as to produce glucose from glycogen.

Option C: Pyruvate carboxylase is an enzyme of gluconeogenesis. During the fasting state, the liver is flooded with fatty acids mobilized from adipose tissue. The resulting elevated hepatic acetyl CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase. Other enzymes of gluconeogenesis that are elevated in fasting include Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and Glucose-6-phosphatase.
questions.learning: Phosphofructokinase 1 During fasting, there is low insulin, and hence, the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 gets inhibited. Phosphofructokinase 1 is an enzyme of glycolysis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Anionic and weakly acidic drugs bind to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Albumin

Anionic and weakly acidic drugs bind to albumin.

After being distributed in the circulating blood, drugs bind to serum proteins to varying degrees. Among serum proteins, albumin and alpha-1 acid glycoprotein play important roles in protein binding for many drugs, which affects their distribution in the body.

Albumin is a major carrier of and binds to acidic drugs like phenytoin, NSAIDs. Whereas, α-1 acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs like lignocaine,disopyramide, quinidine and propranolol.

Importance of plasma protein binding:

Conditions resulting in acute phase reaction response leading to elevated levels of alpha-1 acid glycoprotein like Crohn’s disease, myocardial infarction, arthritis, cancer, etc. enhance binding of basic drugs. Conditions causing hypoalbuminemia result in decreased binding sites for acidic drugs.

When a drug is bound to the plasma proteins, it is kept in the blood, while the unbound (free) drug can produce a therapeutic effect, be metabolized, or excreted. In the majority of the drugs, this does not have a significant effect, but in drugs with a narrow therapeutic index like warfarin, it is clinically relevant as excessive free warfarin can produce toxicity.

Many drugs displace other drugs from their protein binding sites. This may cause an increase in the pharmacological effect of the displaced drug.

A drug bound to a plasma protein cannot cross membranes and this bound fraction of a drug is also not available for metabolism or glomerular filtration which can make the drug long-acting.

Other options:

Option B- Globulins are of three types - α,β, and γ-globulins. Globulins bind glucocorticoids and progesterone in the blood.

Option C- Lipoproteins like VLDL, LDL can bind anti-cancer drugs like 5-fluorouracil and doxorubicin.
questions.learning: Albumin Anionic and weakly acidic drugs bind to albumin. After being distributed in the circulating blood, drugs bind to serum proteins to varying degrees.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radioactive isotopes is used for teletherapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cobalt-60

Cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays and is commonly used in radiation therapy machines called cobalt units or teletherapy units. These units deliver radiation from outside the body, targeting the tumor.

Other options:

A) Iodine-125: This radioactive isotope is commonly used in brachytherapy for treating prostate cancer. It emits low-energy gamma rays that can effectively target and treat the cancerous tissue.

C) I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for systemic radiotherapy.

D) Iridium-192: This is a commonly used radioactive isotope in brachytherapy. It emits high-energy gamma rays and is used for treating various types of cancer, such as cervical, prostate, and breast cancer. Iridium-192 is often used in temporary brachytherapy, where the radioactive source is temporarily placed in the body and then removed after a specific period of treatment.

In summary, while Iodine-125 and Iridium-192 are commonly used in brachytherapy, Cobalt-60 is primarily used in external beam radiation therapy. Iodine-131 is used in other medical applications, such as thyroid cancer treatment and diagnostic imaging.
questions.learning: Cobalt-60 Cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays and is commonly used in radiation therapy machines called cobalt units or teletherapy units. These units deliver radiation from outside the body, targeting the tumor.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During a routine thyroid examination, a 45-year- old woman is found to have a palpable thyroid nodule, and fine-needle aspiration cytology confirms papillary thyroid carcinoma. Which of the following statements regarding papillary thyroid cancer is NOT true?
options: It often presents with cervical lymph node metastases
It is the most common type of thyroid cancer.
questions.explanation: Papillary thyroid cancer is derived from the follicular cells of the thyroid, not the parafollicular C-cells. Parafollicular C-cells give rise to medullary thyroid cancer, which secretes calcitonin. The other statements are correct: it is indeed the most common type of thyroid cancer (Option B), accounting for over 80% of cases. It is known for its slow growth and frequent spread to cervical lymph nodes (Option A), although this does not significantly worsen the generally excellent prognosis. Most well-differentiated thyroid cancers, including papillary, are TSH dependent (Option D), meaning that suppressing TSH levels with levothyroxine is a key part of post-operative management to prevent recurrence. Histologically, it is recognized by characteristic features such as "Orphan Annie eye" nuclei and psammoma bodies. Understanding these distinctions is vital for the correct diagnosis and staging of thyroid malignancies
questions.learning: Papillary thyroid cancer is derived from the follicular cells of the thyroid, not the parafollicular C-cells. Parafollicular C-cells give rise to medullary thyroid cancer, which secretes calcitonin.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A chest X-ray is obtained for a 6-year-old child with poor feeding, digital clubbing, and cyanosis. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease beyond infancy. It is characterized by cyanosis, digital clubbing, poor feeding/failure to thrive, and hypercyanotic (“Tet”) spells due to right ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

Classic chest X-ray finding:

• Boot-shaped heart (Coeur en sabot) due to right ventricular hypertrophy
• Decreased pulmonary vascular markings (pulmonary oligemia)

Key differentiating features:

• Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA):

• Severe cyanosis immediately after birth
• Egg-on-a-string appearance on chest X-ray

• Hyaline Membrane Disease:

• Respiratory distress in preterm neonates
• Ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male patient presents with ptosis which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. He also complains of excessive fatiguability towards the end of the day which improves with rest. Placing an ice pack over his eyes significantly decreases the ptosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myasthenia gravis

From the given clinical picture, myasthenia gravis is the most likely diagnosis. This patient has symptoms of ptosis, progressive weakness, and excessive fatiguability which improves with rest.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness.

Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age.

Clinical features of myasthenia gravis:

* Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or during late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical

* Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis

* Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling

* Weakness in chewing

* Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of palate and tongue

* Difficulty in swallowing

* Deep tendon reflexes are intact

* Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse.

Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Grave's disease, neuromyelitis optics, systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.

Diagnosis:

* Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increases transmission)

* Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies

* Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response.

* Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission.

Treatment:

* Anticholinesterase drugs - Pyridostigmine.

* Thymectomy.

* Immunosuppression therapy with glucocorticoids, azathioprine, tacrolimus, rituximab, etc.

* Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Following image denote which side of placenta?
questions.explanation: The image depicts the fetal surface of the placenta, also known as the chorionic plate. This side is characterized by its smooth, shiny, and bluish-white appearance, covered by the transparent amnion. Critically, the umbilical cord is seen attaching directly to this surface, and large fetal vessels are visible radiating from the cord insertion. In contrast, the maternal surface (Options B and D), also known as the basal plate, is rough, dull, and dark red, divided into 15–20 cotyledons by septa. The decidual surface (Option C) refers specifically to the maternal tissue (decidua basalis) that remains attached to the maternal side of the placenta after delivery. Therefore, the presence of the umbilical cord and the smooth chorionic membrane makes it clear that this is the fetal side

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the colon specimen image shown below from a 14-year-old boy, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The gross specimen shows a colon covered in "hundreds of small adenomatous polyps," which is the classic appearance of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP). FAP is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a mutation in the APC gene. In a 14-year-old boy, the discovery of extensive polyposis is pathognomonic. While FAP inevitably leads to "Colon cancer" (Option B) by age 40 if untreated, the primary diagnosis of the specimen itself is the polyposis syndrome. Juvenile polyps (Option C) are usually solitary and hamartomatous rather than numerous and adenomatous. Ulcerative colitis (Option D) presents with diffuse mucosal inflammation and ulcers, not hundreds of discrete polyps (though inflammatory pseudopolyps can occur, they look different). Total proctocolectomy is the mandatory treatment for FAP because the risk of malignancy is 100%. Screening of first-degree relatives via colonoscopy is also essential

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient of sickle cell anemia developed aplastic crisis after a viral infection. The agent causing it is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Parvovirus B19

Parvovirus B19 causes aplastic crisis in patients with hemolytic anemias (e.g., sickle cell disease) by selectively infecting and destroying erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow.

• Virus type: single-stranded DNA virus (only ssDNA virus)
• Target cells: erythroid progenitors via P antigen (globoside receptor)
• Pathogenesis:

o    Temporary cessation of erythropoiesis

o    Leads to severe anemia (aplastic crisis) in patients with high RBC turnover

• Clinical features:

o    Sudden drop in hemoglobin

o    Reticulocytopenia

o    Fatigue, pallor

• Other manifestations:

o    Erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek rash) in children

o    Hydrops fetalis in pregnant women

Why not others:

• CMV, EBV, HBV: do not specifically target erythroid precursors to cause aplastic crisis

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient with a history of chronic ear infection presents with fever, headache, vomiting, irritability, and confusion. His CT brain is shown in the image below. What is the possible diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Temporal lobe abscess

The clinical vignette depicting features of CNS infection (fever, headache, vomiting, and confusion) in a patient with a chronic ear infection and the CT image showing a ring-enhancing lesion point to a diagnosis of a temporal lobe abscess.

Temporal lobe abscess is an intracranial complication that can arise from chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM).

Brain abscess typically progresses through four stages. The first stage is the stage of invasion (initial encephalitis), which often goes unnoticed. Symptoms such as headache, malaise, low-grade fever, and drowsiness may be present.

The second stage is the stage of localization (latent abscess), during which a capsule forms around the abscess, effectively localizing the pus.

The third stage is the stage of enlargement (manifest abscess). The abscess enlarges, leading to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) and the development of edema surrounding the abscess. As a result, symptoms worsen.

The final stage is the stage of termination (rupture of abscess). At this point, the abscess expands and eventually ruptures into the ventricle or subarachnoid space, which can result in potentially fatal meningitis.

Signs of raised ICP may include headache, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, drowsiness, confusion, papilledema, and coma.

Characteristic findings associated with temporal lobe abscess include nominal aphasia, homonymous hemianopia, seizures, contralateral motor paralysis, pupillary changes, and oculomotor palsy.

The preferred diagnostic imaging modality for temporal lobe abscess is a CT scan of the brain. This imaging study reveals a ring-enhancing lesion indicative of a brain abscess.

Medical treatment involves initiating intravenous antibiotics, typically metronidazole. Raised ICP can be addressed using dexamethasone or mannitol.

Surgical intervention is the definitive management and involves drainage of the abscess followed by radical mastoidectomy to address the underlying CSOM.

Other options:

Option B: Cerebellar abscess is a form of brain abscess and is usually associated with an otogenic source of infection. It can occur as a direct extension through Trautmann's triangle or via retrograde thrombophlebitis.

An MRI image showing cerebellar abscess is given below:

Option C: Subdural abscess refers to the focal collection of purulent material between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.

An MRI image showing subdural abscess is given below:

Option D: Meningitis is the inflammation of the leptomeninges which includes the arachnoid mater and pia mater. It can be due to an infectious or noninfectious etiology. It presents with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, and signs of meningeal irritation. Ring enhancing lesion on neuroimaging is not a feature of meningitis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What stage of embryonic development is shown in the following image?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates a blastocyst, which typically forms around Day 5 of embryonic development. It is identifiable by its unique structure: an outer layer of cells called the trophoblast (which forms the placenta), a cluster of cells inside called the inner cell mass (which becomes the embryo), and a central fluid-filled cavity known as the blastocoel. A morula (Option A) is an earlier stage (Day 4) consisting of a solid ball of 16–32 cells without a cavity. An ovum (Option B) is the single-cell unfertilized egg. A gastrula (Option D) is a later stage (Day 14+) where the embryo differentiates into three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). Implantation into the endometrial wall begins as the blastocyst stage is reached. Understanding these distinct morphological stages is fundamental for studying embryogenesis

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ions in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is responsible for the resorption of divalent ions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. K+

Potassium (K+) in the thick ascending limb of loop of Henle is responsible for the resorption of divalent ions such as, calcium, magnesium, etc.

This resorption is driven by the lumen-positive potential difference across the cells of the thick ascending limb, created by the potassium leak into the lumen.

Mechanism of resorption in thick ascending limb:

• The luminal membrane contains a Na+-K+-2Cl- cotransporter.
• There is net resorption of Na+, K+ and Cl- in the thick ascending limb as follows:
• All three ions are transported into the cell on the cotransporter.
• Na+ is extruded from the cell by the Na+-K+ ATPase in the basolateral membrane.
• K+ and Cl- diffuse through channels in the basolateral membrane, down their respective electrochemical gradients.
• Most of the K+ leaves the cell across the basolateral membrane; the remaining portion of K+ however diffuses back into the lumen.
• This K+ leak into the lumen generates a positive electrochemical potential difference in the lumen.
• This lumen-positive potential difference drives the resorption of ions such as sodium(Na+), magnesium (Mg2+), calcium (Ca+),etc.,

questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: An 18-year-old woman presents with a rapidly progressive purpuric rash over both lower limbs. Two days earlier, she developed mild pain in her knees and ankles. The lesions initially appeared around one knee and subsequently spread symmetrically over both legs. She has no fever, constitutional symptoms, gastrointestinal complaints, or recent sore throat. Laboratory investigations show: • Hemoglobin: 14 g/dL • Platelet count: 260,000/mm³ • Leukocyte count: 9,000/mm³ Which of the following histopathologic findings is most likely in a biopsy of the skin lesion?
options: Extensive intravascular fibrin deposition without inflammatory infiltrate
Obliterative endarteritis with lymphocytes and plasma cells
Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils around vessels
Small-vessel wall damage with perivascular neutrophilic infiltration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Small-vessel wall damage with perivascular neutrophilic infiltration

This patient most likely has cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, presenting with:

• Palpable purpura over dependent areas, especially the lower limbs
• Arthralgia
• Normal platelet count
• Absence of systemic toxicity

The characteristic histology is small-vessel vasculitis with neutrophilic infiltration, vessel-wall necrosis, and fragmented neutrophil nuclei known as leukocytoclasia.

Typical biopsy findings include:

• Perivascular neutrophils
• Fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels
• Nuclear debris from fragmented neutrophils
• Extravasation of red blood cells

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Extensive intravascular fibrin deposition without inflammatory infiltrate: More consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation.
• B. Obliterative endarteritis with lymphocytes and plasma cells: Classically seen in syphilis.
• C. Necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils around vessels: Suggests eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, usually associated with asthma and eosinophilia.

High-yield pearl:

• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis = palpable purpura + normal platelets + neutrophilic small-vessel inflammation.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following beta blockers has a short duration of action?
questions.explanation: Esmolol (Option C) is an ultra-short-acting cardioselective beta-1 antagonist with a half-life of only 9 minutes. It is rapidly hydrolyzed by red blood cell esterases, which allows for very precise titration when given intravenously. This makes it the drug of choice for managing acute perioperative hypertension or tachycardia. Nadolol (Option A) is a long-acting beta-blocker with a half-life of 20–24 hours, requiring only once-daily dosing. Propranolol (Option B) is a non-selective agent with an intermediate duration of 3–6 hours. Atenolol (Option D) is also an intermediate-to-long-acting cardioselective agent. Because Esmolol's effects are almost immediately reversible by stopping the infusion, it provides a unique safety advantage in unstable patients. Therefore, Esmolol is the definitive answer for the shortest-acting beta-blocker

questions.text: Which of the following is not included in the SAFE strategy for trachoma?
questions.explanation: The WHO-recommended "SAFE" strategy is a comprehensive approach to eliminate trachoma, the world's leading infectious cause of blindness. Each letter represents a specific intervention: S Surgery for individuals with trichiasis (in-turned eyelashes) to prevent corneal scarring. A Antibiotics (typically oral azithromycin) to treat active Chlamydia trachomatis infection in the community. F Facial cleanliness to reduce the transmission of the bacteria via fingers and flies. E Environmental improvements, such as increased access to water and improved sanitation, to eliminate breeding sites for flies. While "Evaluation of the control program" (Option D) is an essential administrative task for any public health initiative, it is not one of the four technical pillars that constitute the "SAFE" acronym. The strategy addresses both the immediate clinical needs of patients and the underlying socio-environmental factors that allow the disease to persist in endemic regions

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The usage of the given device in the picture is?
options: Measure the length of the uterus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Menstrual regulation/aspiration

The instrument given in the image is Karman’s cannula which is used for menstrual regulation or aspiration.

Menstrual regulation or aspiration is the aspiration of the endometrial cavity 1-3 weeks after a missed period in a woman with a previous normal cycle and a positive urine pregnancy test. It is performed using Karman's cannula.

Procedure -

* Under aseptic precautions, the cervix may be gently dilated using 4-5 mm size dilators.

* Then 5-6mm Karman’s cannula is inserted and attached to a 50ml syringe for suction.

* The cannula is rotated, and pushed in and out with gentle strokes.

This procedure is contraindicated in advanced pregnancy and in the presence of local pelvic inflammation.

The drawback of the procedure - an implanted zygote , and an ectopic pregnancy can be missed.

Other options:

Option A:  Hysterosalpingography is done using a Rubins cannula.

Option B:  The length of the uterus is measured using Simpson's uterine sound.

Option C: Retraction is done using Doyen's retractor

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old male patient presents with a pelvic fracture following blunt abdominal trauma. No blood is seen at the meatus. Catheterization does not produce significant urine output. The radiological image is given below. What is the next step in management?
options: Pelvic packing along with B/L percutaneous nephrostomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Laparotomy

The given clinical scenario of blunt abdominal trauma, minimal urine output on catheterization, and the pattern of contrast extravasation in the given image indicate intraperitoneal bladder rupture. The absence of blood at the meatus rules out urethral injury. The preferred next step of management, in this case, is laparotomy.

Bladder rupture may be extraperitoneal or intraperitoneal.

• The bladder is related to the peritoneum only on its superior surface. Therefore, if the bladder rupture is towards the superior surface, the urine leaks into the peritoneal cavity, i.e. urine extravasation will be intraperitoneal.
• Whereas, bladder rupture due to injury to the anterior or lateral surfaces does not rupture the peritoneum. In such cases, the urine leaks into the perivesical space but does not enter the peritoneum, i.e. urine extravasation will be extraperitoneal.

Intraperitoneal bladder rupture is caused by a blow or fall on the distended bladder. Intraperitoneal bladder rupture manifests as sudden severe pain in the hypogastrium and syncope. There will be an associated increase in BUN and creatinine due to systemic absorption of the extravasated urine and it may also lead to chemical peritonitis.

Investigations :

• CT scan can be done to diagnose bladder rupture.
• A plain erect X-ray may show a ground-glass appearance.
• Intravenous urography (IVU) may confirm a leak.
• Retrograde cystography will confirm the diagnosis.

Intraperitoneal bladder rupture leads to extravasation of the contrast material into the peritoneal cavity, around the bowel loops and paracolic gutters. Hence, an outline of bowel loops can be seen. The image below shows intraperitoneal bladder rupture, with arrows showing contrast material in the peritoneal cavity:

Extraperitoneal bladder rupture leads to extravasation of the contrast material into the perivesical space and the fascia planes anterior to the peritoneum. The image below shows extraperitoneal bladder rupture, with contrast material in the retro-pubic space (no contrast can be seen within the peritoneal cavity).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young man is brought to the hospital with high-grade fever and altered consciousness. On examination, the patient had neck rigidity and pain when bending the neck. A lumbar puncture was performed and it showed a WBC count of 1500 cells/μL, majority being neutrophils, elevated pressure with protein of 120 mg/dL, and a glucose level of 70 mg/dL (blood glucose level - 300 mg/dL). How will you manage the index case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vancomycin+ ceftriaxone

The given clinical scenario with high fever, altered consciousness, neck rigidity, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showing neutrophilic pleocytosis with low sugar point toward a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis. The initial treatment involves the administration of 3rd-generation cephalosporin like ceftriaxone along with vancomycin for 10–14 days.

Hyperglycemia due to the pathological stress from the infection can mask the reduced CSF glucose. It can be correctly inferred from CSF/blood glucose ratio. A ratio <0.4 is highly significant for bacterial meningitis.

The most common cause of meningitis in adults over 20 years of age is Streptococcus pneumoniae.

The classic clinical triad of meningitis includes fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. Other common symptoms include decreased consciousness, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and seizures. Cutaneous signs such as petechiae, purpura, or an erythematous macular rash may be present.

Kernig's sign and Brudzinski's sign can indicate meningeal irritation. Kernig's sign is positive when there is resistance and pain in extending the knee with the hip flexed at 90 degrees. Brudzinski's sign is positive when there is involuntary flexion of the hips and knees in response to passive neck flexion. However, these signs may not be reliable in certain patient groups, such as infants, elderly individuals, or those with altered mental status.

When bacterial meningitis is suspected, blood cultures should be obtained, and empirical antimicrobial therapy should be initiated without delay. The diagnosis is confirmed by examining cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). CSF analysis shows increased polymorphonuclear leukocytes, decreased glucose concentration, increased protein concentration, and increased opening pressure. CSF bacterial cultures and Gram stain are used to identify the causative organism.

Prompt initiation of empirical antimicrobial therapy is crucial in suspected cases of bacterial meningitis. Commonly used antibiotics include third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins (such as ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or cefepime) that cover Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae and Vancomycin if there is a high suspicion of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection. Ampicillin with metronidazole is added when Listeria monocytogenes is suspected, particularly in neonates, pregnant women, individuals over 50 years, and immunocompromised individuals.
questions.learning: Vancomycin+ ceftriaxone — The given clinical scenario with high fever, altered consciousness, neck rigidity, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showing neutrophilic pleocytosis with low sugar point toward a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true about skeletal muscle contraction?

1. Extracellular Ca2+ is not important for contraction
2. Ca2+ is released from mitochondria
3. Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
4. Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels on sarcolemma have no role in EC coupling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 only

During the contraction of the skeletal muscle, the Ca2+ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Only statement 3 is correct.

Excitation contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fibre (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle.

The steps of excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle are as follows:

• Motor-neuron discharge causes the release of acetylcholine at the motor endplate, which binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
• This causes increased Na+ and K+ conductance in the endplate membrane, leading to the generation of end-plate potential, which is a local potential.
• When the local endplate potential reaches a threshold for the muscle fibre, and an action potential is generated.
• The generated action potential passes inward through the T tubules, leading to the spread of depolarisation.
• The depolarization of the muscle fibre causes the release of Ca2+ from terminal cisterns of sarcoplasmic reticulum and diffusion to thick and thin filaments.
• The calcium released, binds to troponin C, uncovering myosin-binding sites on actin.
• The formation of cross-linkages between actin and myosin and sliding of thin on thick filaments causes contraction of the skeletal muscle.

Steps in relaxation:

• The cytoplasmic calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, by the action of SERCA (sarcoplasmic endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase).
• Once the calcium concentration is lowered, the interaction between actin and myosin ceases, and the muscle relaxes.

Other options:

Statement 1: Incorrect - Extracellular calcium levels play an important role in muscle contraction. When there is a decrease in extracellular calcium as in hypocalcemia, the voltage-gated sodium channels are activated, which causes sodium influx. The increased intracellular sodium concentration causes sustained depolarization, which may lead to tetany.

Statement 2: Incorrect - Ca2+ is not released from mitochondria. It is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Statement 4: Voltage-gated calcium channels on T-tubules (part of sarcolemma) are activated by a depolarizing stimulus, which causes the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increased calcium concentration will eventually lead to muscle contraction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding for two months. What is the next line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Endometrial sampling

The next line of management in a 50-year-old woman with abnormal uterine bleeding is endometrial sampling.

Indications for endometrial sampling:

• Any female > 45 years with abnormal uterine bleeding
• A female of age < 45 years having exposure to excessive estrogen such as in PCOD, severe obesity, tamoxifen treatment
• Women with failed medical management and persistent bleeding
• Transvaginal ultrasound findings >12 mm in premenopausal women and > 4 mm in postmenopausal women.

Endometrial sampling may be done by either curettage or aspiration biopsy by pipelle or vibra aspirator.

Note: Transvaginal ultrasound is a better first-line investigation to assess AUB. Since TVS is not included in the options, endometrial sampling is the next best answer. Assessing the reason for AUB and ruling out malignancy in the postmenopausal age group are the initial steps before prescribing any treatment.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient complains that he feels like the room is spinning when he gets up from lying down or turning his head. He has no history of loss of consciousness. Which of the following could be the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

The given clinical scenario, with complaints of dizziness associated with postural change and no history of loss of consciousness is suggestive of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

BPPV is one of the common causes of recurrent vertigo, and the episodes are brief (<1min) and are always provoked by changes in head position. The attacks are caused by free-floating calcium carbonate crystals usually dislodged from the posterior canal.

A positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver confirms the diagnosis of BPPV. In this maneuver, the patient begins sitting up with their head turned 45 degrees toward the ear to be tested. Then the patient is made to lie down quickly with their head past the end of the bed. Then, the patient's neck is extended 20 degrees below the horizontal. The clinician then watches the patient's eyes for torsional and up-beating nystagmus, which should persist for no more than one minute. This would indicate a positive test.

Epley's maneuver is performed to reposition the crystals into the macula from the semicircular canals. This is only a temporary cure and there is a high rate of recurrence.
questions.learning: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — The given clinical scenario, with complaints of dizziness associated with postural change and no history of loss of consciousness is suggestive of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the options below does not serve as an indication for performing a cesarean section?
questions.explanation: Previous history of macrosomia. A Cesarean section is indicated when a vaginal delivery would pose a significant risk to the mother or infant. Absolute cephalopelvic disproportion (Option A) means the fetal head cannot physically pass through the maternal pelvis, necessitating surgery. Central placenta previa (Option C) is a life-threatening condition where the placenta completely covers the internal os, making vaginal birth impossible due to hemorrhage risk. Advanced carcinoma of the cervix (Option D) is an indication because the tumor tissue is friable and obstructive, making vaginal delivery dangerous. A previous history of macrosomia (delivering a large baby, Option B) is NOT a direct indication for a C-section in a current pregnancy. Each pregnancy is assessed independently; unless the current fetus is suspected of being macrosomic in a way that suggests disproportion, a trial of labor is usually encouraged. Therefore, a past history of macrosomia alone does not mandate surgical delivery.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The commonest indication for liver transplantation in children is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Biliary atresia

Biliary atresia is the most common indication for liver transplantation in children.

Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA) is defined as a partial or total absence of permeable bile duct between the porta hepatis and the duodenum. It is due to inflammatory fibrosis of the biliary tree. It leads to obstruction to bile flow thereby causing the leaking of conjugated bilirubin into the circulation.

Infants have symptoms of jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine right after birth. In advanced disease, infants present with failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, and ascites due to liver cirrhosis.

HIDA scan is the investigation of choice for extrahepatic biliary atresia. An intraoperative cholangiogram is a gold standard investigation for diagnosis.

Management of extrahepatic biliary atresia

Type I

Atresia restricted to the common bile duct

Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy

Type II

Atresia of the common hepatic duct

Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)

Type III

Atresia of the right and left hepatic duct

Children with biliary atresia, who do not achieve successful drainage after hepatoportoenterostomy (Kasai's procedure), require liver transplantation within the first year of life.

questions.text: Which of the following diseases are covered under the scheme represented by the logo shown below?
questions.explanation: The logo displayed belongs to the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS). This program was launched by the Indian government to address the rising burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs). The scheme specifically focuses on four major diseases: Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases (CVD), and Stroke. Options A, B, and D are incorrect because they include Bronchial Asthma or Hypertension as primary acronym components, although those conditions may be managed under related health initiatives. The NPCDCS aims to provide health promotion, early diagnosis, and management of these four major NCDs through infrastructure development and manpower training at various levels of the healthcare system. The slogan "Health In Your Hands" emphasizes personal and community-level prevention efforts. This program is a critical component of India’s public health strategy to reduce premature mortality from chronic, lifestyle-related conditions through structured population-based screening and care
