questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following radiological image was taken to access the urinary tract, identify the investigation shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP)

The radiological image shown above is that of an Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP), also known as Intravenous Urography (IVU).

IVP is an X-ray with special contrast injected into the veins to visualize the kidneys, ureter, and bladder.

Normal Structure seen in IVP:

Renal arteries → Nephrogram (cortex > medulla) → Calyces (~1 min) → Pelvicalyceal system (~15 min with compression) → Ureters → Postmicturition KUB shows normal drainage.

Indications of IVP:

* Calculi: size, location

* Obstruction: level, effects on renal excretion

* Functional versus mechanical obstruction (post-diuretic IVU)

* Ureteric fistula or Ureteric stricture

* GU Tuberculosis

* Collecting system integrity: trauma/intervention

* Congenital anomalies

* Upper tract urothelial lesion

It is a cheaper, readily available alternative to CT in resource-limited settings

Other options:

Option A: X-ray KUB: It is used to specifically visualize KUB (kidney, Ureter, Bladder). The X-ray KUB image below shows a thimble bladder caused due to TB of the bladder.

Option C: Retrograde Pyelogram is an X-ray test in which a special contrast is inserted into the urethral orifice of the penis via a catheter to visualize more distal urinary tract abnormalities. It is used to diagnose urethral strictures, injuries, blockage, and diverticula ( it is for the urethra, not the ureter). RGP Image below shows a bulbar urethral stricture.

Option D: Micturating CystoUrethrogram, also known as a voiding cystourethrogram (VCU). In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foley's catheter, the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It helps diagnose posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve. The following image shows a voiding cystourethrogram in a patient with grade V VUR.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 30-year-old man came with choking episodes after ingestion of fish bone while eating. The fishbone got impacted at the level of T in the esophagus. Which is the most likely site of obstruction?
questions.explanation: The esophagus has four normal anatomical constrictions where foreign bodies frequently become impacted. The fishbone in this scenario is impacted at the T4 vertebral level, which specifically corresponds to where the arch of the aorta crosses the esophagus. This site is approximately 9 inches (25 cm) from the incisors. The cricopharyngeus muscle (Option C) creates the first narrowing at the C6 level, roughly 6 inches from the incisors. The left main bronchus (Option A) causes a third constriction at the T6 level, about 11 inches from the incisors. The diaphragmatic hiatus (Option D) is the final narrowing at the T10 level, approximately 15 inches (40 cm) from the incisors. Because T4 is the identified level of impaction, the pressure from the aortic arch creating an indentation in the esophageal wall is the physiological cause of the obstruction
questions.learning: The esophagus has four normal anatomical constrictions where foreign bodies frequently become impacted. The fishbone in this scenario is impacted at the T4 vertebral level, which specifically corresponds to where the arch of the aorta crosses the esophagus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In what sequence do muscles develop rigor mortis, progressing from early to late?
options: Orbicularis oculi, neck, face, thorax, upper limb
Orbicularis oculi, neck, facial muscles, upper limb, thorax
Neck, muscles of eyelid, upper limb, thorax
Neck, muscles of eyelid, facial muscles, thorax, upper limb
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Orbicularis oculi, neck, face, thorax, upper limb

Rigor mortis follows a cephalocaudal progression (Nysten’s law)—from small, active muscles to larger muscle groups.

Correct sequence (early → late):

• Orbicularis oculi (eyelids)
• Neck
• Facial muscles
• Thorax
• Upper limbs
• Abdomen
• Lower limbs

Timeline (approximate):

• Begins: 1–2 hours after death
• Fully established: 6–12 hours
• Disappears: 24–48 hours

Forensic significance:

• Helps in estimation of time since death
• Assists in determining body position after death
questions.learning: Orbicularis oculi, neck, face, thorax, upper limb Rigor mortis follows a cephalocaudal progression (Nysten’s law)—from small, active muscles to larger muscle groups.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient has a history of a flying foreign body injury to the eye. After 8 weeks, heterochromia iridis is noted. Which of the following substances is most likely involved in the deposition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iron

History of trauma from a flying object followed by subsequent heterochromia iridis is suggestive of siderosis bulbi which happens due to iron deposition.

The presence of iron deposits in the eye especially in industrial workers is called siderosis bulbi. It refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and causing atrophy.

The earliest change is the deposition of iron in the anterior capsule of the lens where oval patches are arranged in a ring corresponding with the edge of the dilated pupil. This eventually leads to the formation of cataract.

Clinical features:

* Iris: first stained greenish and later turned reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis.

* Pupil: iron deposition in the sphincter leads to mydriasis.

* Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract.

* Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium.

* Secondary open-angle glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.
questions.learning: Iron History of trauma from a flying object followed by subsequent heterochromia iridis is suggestive of siderosis bulbi which happens due to iron deposition.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In the management of celiac sprue, patients are advised to adhere strictly to a gluten-free diet to prevent symptom exacerbation and intestinal injury. Which of the following food items should be avoided by individuals with celiac disease?
questions.explanation: Celiac disease is an autoimmune-mediated enteropathy triggered by the ingestion of gluten, a protein complex found in certain grains. Wheat (Option B) is the most common source of gluten and must be strictly avoided by individuals with this condition. Other grains to avoid include barley and rye (often remembered by the acronym "BROW": Barley, Rye, Oats, Wheat). Ingestion of even small amounts of gluten leads to villous atrophy in the small intestine, resulting in malabsorption and symptoms like diarrhea and weight loss. Rice (Option A), Dhal (Option C, lentils), and Ragi (Option D, finger millet) are naturally gluten-free and are safe, recommended alternatives for a celiac-friendly diet. Patients must be educated about hidden sources of gluten in processed foods and medications. Adhering to a lifelong gluten-free diet is the only effective treatment to prevent long-term complications such as osteoporosis and intestinal lymphoma
questions.learning: Celiac disease is an autoimmune-mediated enteropathy triggered by the ingestion of gluten, a protein complex found in certain grains. Wheat (Option B) is the most common source of gluten and must be strictly avoided by individuals with this condition.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old female with nephritic range proteinuria is found to have low serum complement levels. Which of the following can be the likely etiology? 1. Systemic lupus erythematosus 2. Post-infectious glomerulonephritis 3. Infective endocarditis 4. Mesangio-capillary glomerulonephritis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Low serum complement (C3 and/or C4) in a patient with nephritic syndrome suggests immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis, where complement is consumed during activation of the classical or alternative pathway. It helps narrow the differential diagnosis of glomerulonephritis.

• Glomerulonephritis associated with low complement:

• Systemic lupus erythematosus (Lupus nephritis)
• Post-infectious glomerulonephritis (PIGN)
• Infective endocarditis-associated GN
• Membranoproliferative (Mesangiocapillary) glomerulonephritis (MPGN)

• Glomerulonephritis with normal complement:

• IgA nephropathy
• Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)
• Minimal change disease
• Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
• Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome)
• ANCA-associated vasculitis
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 and 4 Low serum complement (C3 and/or C4) in a patient with nephritic syndrome suggests immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis, where complement is consumed during activation of the classical or alternative pathway.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presents with easy fatiguability and was diagnosed as iron deficiency anemia. She was advised to take oral iron supplements. Foods containing which of the following should not be taken along with her iron supplements?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tea

Absorption of iron is decreased by tannates found in tea.

Tea contains compounds called tannins, which are polyphenolic compounds. These tannins have been shown to inhibit the absorption of non-heme iron from plant-based foods. Non-heme iron is the type of iron found in plant foods and is not as easily absorbed by the body as heme iron, which is found in animal-based foods.

Tannins bind to iron in the gastrointestinal tract, forming complexes that are poorly absorbed by the body. This can lead to decreased absorption of dietary iron, potentially contributing to iron deficiency if tea is consumed in large quantities, particularly with meals. The inhibitory effect of tea on iron absorption is more pronounced when consumed during meals rather than between meals.

In contrast, substances like ascorbic acid (found in fruits like amla) can enhance the absorption of non-heme iron, while certain foods like lime juice and sprouts don't significantly affect iron absorption.

Iron absorption:

Increased by ascorbic acid, citric acid, amino acids and sugars in the diet.
Decreased by phosphates, carbonates, oxalates, and tannates.
questions.learning: Tea Absorption of iron is decreased by tannates found in tea. Tea contains compounds called tannins, which are polyphenolic compounds.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following features is not included in the American Association for the Surgery of Trauma (AAST) classification system for grading splenic injuries?
questions.explanation: The AAST splenic injury scale is used to categorize the severity of trauma to the spleen based on specific anatomical and radiological findings. Its primary components include the depth and extent of parenchymal destruction or laceration (Option A), the presence and size of a subcapsular or intraparenchymal hematoma (Option D), and the degree of vascular involvement (Option B), such as active hemorrhage or hilar devascularization. While adjacent organ involvement (Option C) is a critical factor in the overall management of a trauma patient and determines the comprehensive injury severity score, it is NOT a specific component used to grade the injury to the spleen itself within the AAST organ-specific classification. The AAST system focuses strictly on the intrinsic damage to the splenic tissue and its immediate blood supply. Understanding this distinction is important for surgeons to accurately stage injuries and decide between non-operative management and surgical intervention like splenectomy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old factory worker presents to the emergency department with headache, vomiting, and blurred vision after consuming locally prepared alcohol. What is the treatment of choice for methanol poisoning?
questions.explanation: Methanol poisoning is a medical emergency that occurs after ingesting tainted illicit alcohol. The toxicity is not caused by methanol itself but by its metabolite, formic acid, which causes severe metabolic acidosis and irreversible damage to the optic nerve (blurred vision). The treatment of choice (antidote) is Fomepizole. Fomepizole is a potent competitive inhibitor of the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase; it prevents the conversion of methanol into its toxic metabolites, allowing the parent methanol to be safely excreted. If fomepizole is unavailable, intravenous ethanol can be used as an alternative. Flumazenil (Option B) is the antidote for benzodiazepines. N-acetyl cysteine (Option C) is for acetaminophen overdose. Naloxone (Option D) is for opioid toxicity. Along with the antidote, patients often require aggressive administration of sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis and urgent hemodialysis to rapidly remove methanol and formic acid from the blood. Rapid intervention is essential to prevent permanent blindness and death

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During a dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR), which of the following bones are typically removed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lacrimal

During a dacryocystorhinostomy, a portion of the lacrimal bone is typically removed to create a passage for tear drainage.

The lacrimal bone is indeed a key bone involved in dacryocystorhinostomy. In this procedure, a portion of the lacrimal bone is often removed to create a passage for tear drainage.

Other options:

Frontal (a): The frontal bone is not typically removed during a dacryocystorhinostomy. DCR primarily involves the lacrimal bone and sometimes parts of the nasal bone.

Ethmoidal (b): The ethmoidal bone is not typically removed during a standard DCR. The primary bone involved is the lacrimal bone.

Maxillary (c): The maxillary bone is not typically removed during a dacryocystorhinostomy. The main focus is on the lacrimal bone.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A middle-aged, obese P3L3 woman presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and is diagnosed with an endometrial polyp with a single feeding vessel, as shown on hysteroscopy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hysteroscopic polypectomy

Hysteroscopic polypectomy is the treatment of choice for symptomatic endometrial polyps. It allows direct visualization and complete removal of the polyp along with its stalk (feeding vessel), reducing recurrence and providing tissue for histopathological examination to exclude malignancy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Dilatation and curettage (D&C): Blind procedure with a high chance of missing focal lesions or incomplete removal.
• B. LNG-IUS: May reduce abnormal uterine bleeding but does not remove the polyp.
• C. Hysterectomy: Not first-line for a benign endometrial polyp; reserved for selected cases with coexisting pathology or confirmed malignancy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with paresthesia of the hands and feet, generalized weakness, easy fatigability, pallor, and ataxia. Which vitamin deficiency best explains this combination of symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation combines hematological and neurological symptoms. Pallor and fatigue suggest anemia, while tingling (paresthesia), weakness, and ataxia (loss of coordination) indicate subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. This specific combination is the classic manifestation of Vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 is essential for both red blood cell production and the maintenance of the myelin sheath in the nervous system. Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency (Option A) causes beriberi, which involves peripheral neuropathy or heart failure but typically not ataxia and pallor together. Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency (Option C) presents with cheilosis and glossitis. Vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency (Option D) causes pellagra, characterized by dermatitis and diarrhea. Because B12 deficiency is unique in causing both macrocytic anemia and progressive dorsal column neurological deficits, it is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation combines hematological and neurological symptoms. Pallor and fatigue suggest anemia, while tingling (paresthesia), weakness, and ataxia (loss of coordination) indicate subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male presents with a one-hour history of sudden-onset chest pain. His ECG shows ST- segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. In a multispecialty hospital setting, what is the most appropriate treatment for this case of inferior wall myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with an acute Inferior Wall ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI). In a multi-specialty hospital (which implies the presence of a cardiac catheterization lab), the best (gold-standard) treatment is Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) or Primary Angioplasty. Primary angioplasty is superior to thrombolysis (Option A and B) because it achieves higher reperfusion rates and lower rates of re-occlusion and intracranial hemorrhage. Thrombolytic agents like Alteplase or Streptokinase are only preferred if PCI cannot be performed within 90-120 minutes of first medical contact. Dabigatran (Option D) is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor used for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation, not for the acute management of a myocardial infarction. Inferior wall MIs are usually due to Right Coronary Artery occlusion. Immediate mechanical reperfusion is the most effective way to salvage the myocardium and improve patient outcomes

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 13-year-old boy visits a fish farming area and accidentally ingests a white, odorless substance. Soon afterward, he develops an exaggerated adverse reaction to a medication he is taking. Which compound is most likely responsible for enhancing the toxic effects of the drug?
questions.explanation: Rotenone is a naturally occurring, white, odorless compound derived from the roots of several tropical plants and is commonly used as a broad-spectrum insecticide and piscicide (fish poison) in fish farming areas. Mechanistically, rotenone is a potent and specific inhibitor of Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. By blocking the transfer of electrons from iron-sulfur centers to ubiquinone, it halts ATP production and generates reactive oxygen species, leading to severe cellular oxidative stress and potentially enhancing the toxicity of other medications metabolized through similar pathways. Antimycin A (Option C) is a piscicide that inhibits Complex III, but it is less commonly described in this clinical accidental ingestion context. BAL (Option B) is a heavy metal chelator. Alkyl guanidines (Option A) can also inhibit Complex I but are not standard environmental toxins found in fish farms. Rotenone exposure is also a significant concern in neurological research as it is used to induce parkinsonian-like symptoms in animal models due to its high toxicity to dopaminergic neurons
questions.learning: Rotenone is a naturally occurring, white, odorless compound derived from the roots of several tropical plants and is commonly used as a broad-spectrum insecticide and piscicide (fish poison) in fish farming areas.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 37-year-old woman from Bihar presents with fever and unexplained weight loss over the past 6 months. Examination reveals massive splenomegaly and blood investigations show anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia. What is the vector of the organism causing this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phlebotomus species

From the given clinical features, the most likely disease is visceral leishmaniasis or Kala azar caused by Leishmania donovani, and the vector is a female Phlebotomus sandfly. A patient from Bihar presenting with fever, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly with a smear examination showing anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypergammaglobulinemia point towards the diagnosis.

Leishmaniasis is transmitted by the bite of an infected female Phlebotomus sandfly. In India, it is endemic to Bihar, West Bengal, Jharkhand, and Uttar Pradesh. Patients present with high fever, hepatosplenomegaly, weight loss, and emaciation. The skin becomes dry, rough, and darkly pigmented. There is anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia.

The parasite exists in 2 forms:

• Amstigote form (also called LD bodies)- It is seen within macrophages and contains a kinetoplast.
• Promastigote form- It is the infective form in the sandfly. The kinetoplast is seen at the anterior end.

Kinetoplast are non-nuclear DNA present in addition to nucleus. They consist of blepharoplast and parabasal body. Flagellum originates near the kinetoplast.

Diagnosis of kala-azar is mainly by demonstration of amastigotes within macrophages in tissue aspirates such as blood smears, bone marrow, splenic, or lymph node aspirate. It is the gold standard for diagnosis.

The image below shows amastigotes located intracellularly within macrophages.

Treatment is with a pentavalent antimonial compound. In Bihar, there is resistance to antimony so amphotericin-B-deoxycholate or miltefosine is preferred.

In human beings, different species of Leishmania can cause the following diseases:

• Visceral leishmaniasis, or kala-azar,
• Cutaneous leishmaniasis,
• Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, and
• Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis.

The life cycle of Lesihmania is shown below.

Other options:

Option B: The Aedes mosquito is the vector for diseases such as dengue, chikungunya, and Zika virus, none of which fit the clinical profile of visceral leishmaniasis.

Option C: Mites are vectors for diseases such as scrub typhus, which typically presents with fever and an eschar, but it does not explain the massive splenomegaly or hematologic findings seen in this case.

Option D: Ixodid ticks are vectors for tick-borne diseases such as Lyme disease and babesiosis. These conditions do not present with the clinical features observed in this patient.
questions.learning: Phlebotomus species From the given clinical features, the most likely disease is visceral leishmaniasis or Kala azar caused by Leishmania donovani, and the vector is a female Phlebotomus sandfly.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study initiated in 2012 at Delhi University with 5000–6000 individuals aimed to evaluate the role of physical activity and its impact on cardiovascular diseases was to be assessed in 2024. What type of study does this represent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prospective Cohort Study

The preferred study type is a prospective cohort study, as participants were grouped based on their exposure to a risk factor—physical activity and then observed over time to determine whether the outcome, namely the impact on cardiovascular diseases, occurred or not.

A prospective cohort study is a study in which the outcome has not yet occurred at the time that the investigations begin. They begin in the present and continue in the future. The design of a prospective cohort is shown below.

A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as a forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study. It can be divided into:

* Prospective cohort studies: The outcome has not occurred at the time of the beginning of the investigation.

* Retrospective cohort studies (Option C): The outcome has occurred before the beginning of the investigation.

* Combination cohort studies: Both retrospective and prospective elements are combined.

A cohort is a group of individuals who share a common experience or characteristic within a defined time. The cohort groups are selected before the appearance of the disease under investigation. They are divided into study and control cohorts. The study cohorts are exposed to a particular factor thought to be related to the disease occurrence whereas the control cohorts are not exposed to this particular factor.

Studying the effects of exposure to uranium in causing lung cancer is an example of a cohort study. Uranium miners are taken as the study cohort and other individuals who are not exposed to uranium mining are taken as the control cohort.

Other options:

Option A: In a case-control study, the study begins with the outcome and goes retrospectively to find out the exposure among the cases and controls.For example, to find the exposure to smoking associated with already diagnosed lung cancer patients.

Option D: An ecological study is any kind of study in which data is collected about a population and is analyzed at that level. Unlike the case with cohort studies, in these studies, no data is available or analyzed about individuals.

Pearl PF2100: Cohort Study

* A cohort study progresses from cause (exposure) to effect (disease).

* It is also known as forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study.

* Design of a cohort study:

* Types of cohort study:

* Prospective (concurrent) cohort studies

* Retrospective (historical) cohort studies

* Combination cohort studies

* Steps of cohort study:

* Selection of study subjects

* Obtaining data on exposure

* Selection of comparison groups

* Follow-up

* Analysis in terms of incidence rates and estimation of risk

* Advantages of cohort study:

* Incidence can be calculated

* Several possible outcomes related to exposure can be studied at the same time

* Provides direct estimate of relative risk

* Calculation of dose-response ratio

* Minimization of certain biases

* Disadvantages of cohort study:

* Cannot use for uncommon diseases

* Expensive, requires a large population and longer time

* Many common administrative and ethical problems

* High attrition and selection of subjects is difficult

* Dynamism of diagnostics is difficult to incorporate

* Tends to alter the behaviour of subjects known as Hawthorne effect.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are true about Late Dumping Syndrome, except? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diarrhea

Late dumping syndrome is a consequence of peptic ulcer surgery characterized by reactive hypoglycemia occurring typically 1-3 hours after meals. It develops when carbohydrate-rich food causes a rapid rise in blood glucose, triggering an excessive insulin response that leads to subsequent hypoglycemia. Diarrhea is typical of early dumping.
questions.learning: Diarrhea Late dumping syndrome is a consequence of peptic ulcer surgery characterized by reactive hypoglycemia occurring typically 1-3 hours after meals.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is related to Navjat Shishu Suraksha karyakram?
questions.explanation: The Navjat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (NSSK) is a national program in India specifically designed to improve the survival rates of the Newborn population. The program focuses on providing essential newborn care and basic resuscitation training to healthcare providers who attend births at all levels of the healthcare system. The primary interventions include the prevention of hypothermia, prevention of infection, initiation of early breastfeeding, and basic newborn resuscitation using a bag and mask. While the health of the Mother (Option A) and Pregnant woman (Option D) is closely linked to neonatal outcomes, they are the focus of separate programs like Janani Suraksha Yojana. The term Children (Option B) usually refers to an older age group handled under programs like the IMNCI. NSSK specifically targets the first few minutes and hours of life, which are the most critical for reducing the high neonatal mortality rate. Ensuring that every birth is attended by a trained provider who can deliver these essential services is the program's ultimate goal
questions.learning: The Navjat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (NSSK) is a national program in India specifically designed to improve the survival rates of the Newborn population.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following pathogens is correctly matched with its intrinsic drug resistance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Candida krusei - Fluconazole

Among the given options, Candida krusei shows an intrinsic resistance to fluconazole.
The primary or intrinsic resistance of C. krusei to azoles (fluconazole and itraconazole) is mediated through reduced susceptibility of the target enzyme (lanosterol 14α-demethylase) to inhibition by these drugs. However, improved susceptibility is seen with newer generation azoles such as voriconazole.

Life-threatening systemic infections caused by Candida and Aspergillus species are usually seen in severely ill and immunocompromised patients such as HIV, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia, and transplant recipients on immunosuppressants. C. albicans and C. dubliniensis are most susceptible to currently available azoles, C. glabrata is less susceptible, whereas C. krusei is intrinsically resistant to fluconazole. Resistance occurs due to overexpression or point mutation in the gene encoding the target enzyme lanosterol 14α-demethylase. Voriconazole is the preferred therapy for multi-drug resistant infection with C. krusei.

C. albicans and C. glabrata (Option C) showing resistance to Amphotericin B has been increasingly reported over the past several years. But this is a secondary resistance due to alteration or a decrease in the amount of ergosterol in the cell membrane. Amphotericin B is indicated to treat C. glabrata that has developed resistance to azoles.

Aspergillus fumigatus, the most common species to cause Aspergillus infection worldwide, also shows an intrinsic resistance to fluconazole. It is susceptible to echinocandins like micafungin, which acts by inhibiting beta-(1,3)-D-glucan synthase, an enzyme necessary for the synthesis of the cell wall.

Other options
Option A : Aspergillus niger is a common cause of otomycosis and is susceptible to azoles like voriconazole, amphotericin B, and echinocandins.
Option D : The drug of choice for treatment of sporotrichosis is itraconazole.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Streptococci

questions.text: Which phase of the menstrual cycle features vacuolation as a histological feature?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Secretory phase

Subnuclear vacuolation is a histological feature of the secretory phase of the menstrual cycle.

The histological features as per the respective phases are:

Proliferative/oestrogenic phase:

* The glands of the functional layer are simple tubules with regular epithelium

* The endometrium is thick, stoma compact, and short straight glands are present.

* Arteries become more coiled and spiralled

Secretory phase :

* The secretory phase of the endometrium begins on the 15th day and persists until the onset of menstruation.

* Subnuclear vacuolation (presumptive evidence of progesterone activity)

* Corkscrew-shaped glands

Menstrual Phase:

* Glands shrink with prominent vessels and haemorrhagic spots.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A clinical assessment video shows a 7-year-old girl with continuous, slow, writhing involuntary movements involving the hands and fingers. What is the correct semiological term?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Athetosis

Athetosis is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by continuous, slow, sinuous, writhing involuntary movements, predominantly affecting the distal limbs (hands and fingers). These movements often worsen during voluntary activity and disappear during sleep.

The video description of continuous, slow, writhing movements of the hands and fingers is classic for athetosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Hemiballismus: Characterized by violent, flinging, large-amplitude movements of one side of the body, usually due to a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.
• C. Chorea: Consists of rapid, irregular, jerky, dance-like movements that flow randomly from one body part to another.
• D. Myoclonus: Characterized by sudden, brief, shock-like muscle jerks, not slow writhing movements.
questions.learning: Athetosis Athetosis is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by continuous, slow, sinuous, writhing involuntary movements, predominantly affecting the distal limbs (hands and fingers).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
Identify the imaging modality given below.

USG- Ultrasonography
MRI- Magnetic resonance imaging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. USG

The image shown in the question is the USG of the neck.

Sonographic examination of the neck shows the thyroid gland, muscles, blood vessels, bony structures or cartilages, and nerves. The thyroid of a healthy patient appears homogeneously echogenic with a uniform echotexture on USG. Lateral to the thyroid, the large blood vessels (the common carotid artery and more laterally, the internal jugular vein) can be identified. In the above image, hypoechoic areas are suggestive of the lumen of vessels seen in the neck i.e common carotid artery and internal jugular vein.

Neck ultrasonography is the preferred modality for routine radiographic evaluation of the thyroid gland, as it offers the most accurate visualization of thyroid nodular disease. It also allows for the concomitant performance of percutaneous fine-needle aspiration biopsy of thyroid lesions.

Neck ultrasound can also be used to localize parathyroid disease.

Other options:

Option B: Fluoroscopy is an imaging modality that allows real-time X-ray viewing of a patient with high resolution. During this procedure, radiologists usually use contrast material (dye) to highlight the area being examined.

Below image shows the fluoroscopy of neck.

Option C: The below image shows the X-ray appearance of neck in AP view.

Option D: Relative to the neck musculature, the thyroid is hyperintense on MRI images.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden onset of hematemesis. He has been taking aspirin for his arthritis and drinks alcohol occasionally. He gives a history of occasional abdominal pain. On examination, there is no abdominal mass or tenderness. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Peptic ulcer

This patient with a history of aspirin use, now presenting with abdominal pain and a sudden onset of hematemesis most likely has a bleeding peptic ulcer.

Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) accounts for around 2/3rd of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The major causative factors are Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs. Prostaglandins protect gastric and duodenal mucosa from acid and pepsin. They increase mucin and bicarbonate secretion and increase mucosal blood flow. They also promote epithelial cell proliferation. NSAIDs like aspirin disrupt these naturally protective mechanisms and increase the risk of peptic ulcer formation in the stomach and the duodenum.

They present with abdominal pain, bleeding, or signs of peritonitis due to perforation. Significant hemorrhage occurs when duodenal or gastric ulcers penetrate branches of the gastroduodenal or left gastric arteries, respectively.

Other options:

Option A: Mallory-Weiss tears are partial-thickness tears of the mucosa and submucosa occurring near the gastroesophageal junction. They occur in patients with a history of repeated emesis and are classical in alcoholic patients after a period of intense retching and vomiting following binge drinking.

Option B: Esophagitis commonly occurs due to repeated exposure of mucosa to the acidic gastric secretions in gastroesophageal reflux disease. It results in chronic blood loss and commonly presents as anemia or guaiac-positive stools. Ulcerations of superficial mucosa due to esophagitis generally do not bleed acutely.

Option D: Esophageal varices commonly occur due to portal hypertension in patients with cirrhosis. A history of liver disease or the stigmata of portal hypertension and cirrhosis would suggest variceal bleeding.
questions.learning: Peptic ulcer — This patient with a history of aspirin use, now presenting with abdominal pain and a sudden onset of hematemesis most likely has a bleeding peptic ulcer.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Question 198.Which of the following findings is usually not seen in patients who have received a massive blood transfusion?
questions.explanation: Massive blood transfusion is defined as replacing the patient's entire blood volume within 24 hours. The electrolyte imbalance that is characteristically absent is hypercalcemia; instead, patients frequently develop hypocalcemia (Option C). This occurs because the citrate used as an anticoagulant in stored blood binds to the patient's ionized calcium. Other options are common complications: DIC (Option A) can occur due to the underlying trauma and coagulopathy; febrile transfusion reactions (Option B) are common due to leukocytes in the blood; and dilutional thrombocytopenia (Option D) is a hallmark of massive transfusion as stored blood is deficient in functional platelets . Therefore, because citrate causes a reduction in serum calcium, hypercalcemia is not expected. Clinicians must often supplement calcium during massive protocols to prevent cardiac arrhythmias and further coagulation defects. Thus, "Hypercalcemia" is the correct "absent" finding for this clinical scenario
questions.learning: Massive blood transfusion is defined as replacing the patient's entire blood volume within 24 hours. The electrolyte imbalance that is characteristically absent is hypercalcemia; instead, patients frequently develop hypocalcemia (Option C).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with ptosis, diplopia, and generalized muscle weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest. She also has difficulty chewing and swallowing, especially in the evening. A Tensilon test is positive. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of fluctuating weakness, ptosis, diplopia, and a positive Tensilon (edrophonium) test are classic for Myasthenia Gravis (MG). While the Tensilon test is a useful bedside screening tool, the Anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody test is the most specific laboratory investigation to confirm the diagnosis. Approximately 85% of patients with generalized MG will have detectable AChR antibodies. Single-fiber electromyography (SFEMG) (Option B) is the most sensitive test for MG, showing increased jitter, but it is not as specific as antibody testing. A CT scan of the chest (Option A) is performed after diagnosis to screen for an associated thymoma but is not a confirmatory test for MG itself. MRI of the brain (Option D) is done to rule out other causes of cranial nerve palsies but would be normal in MG. Early diagnosis is vital because MG is highly treatable with anticholinesterase inhibitors, immunosuppressants, and occasionally thymectomy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A male patient who is suffering from a psychotic disorder is on antipsychotic, antidepressant and antihypertensive treatment. He suddenly developed tachycardia and chest tightness. On evaluation he had metabolic acidosis. ECG showed widened QRS complex and prolonged QT interval. Which of the following drugs is responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amitriptyline

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of torsades de pointes. Only amitriptyline causes this condition, among the above drugs.

Torsades de pointes (French: twisting of points) is a life-threatening form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with rapid asynchronous complexes and an undulating baseline on ECG.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient with a history of a fall presents to the emergency department and undergoes a CT scan of the brain (shown below). What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The CT scan shows a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection along the cerebral convexity, consistent with a subdural hematoma (SDH), typically caused by rupture of bridging veins following trauma. In this case, the most appropriate treatment depends on the underlying cause and severity. Here, the question implies conservative management, likely in a patient with coagulopathy (e.g., on anticoagulants). Therefore, Vitamin K is administered to reverse anticoagulation and promote clotting, helping to control further bleeding. Key concept: 1. Small or stable SDH → conservative management 2. Correct coagulopathy → Vitamin K (if warfarin-related) Why other options are incorrect: (A) Alteplase & (B) Reteplase: Thrombolytic drugs; would worsen intracranial bleeding (D) Surgery: Indicated only in large hematoma or significant mass effect, not in stable cases Thus, in a stable SDH with bleeding tendency, Vitamin K is the appropriate treatment

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following receives venous drainage from the left atrium and both ventricles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Great cardiac vein

The great cardiac vein receives venous drainage from the left atrium and both ventricles.

The great cardiac vein begins at the apex of the heart. It ascends in the anterior interventricular sulcus. At the coronary sulcus, the great cardiac vein turns to the left and lies at the base of the heart. Here, it is associated with the circumflex branch of the left coronary artery. In the coronary sulcus, the great cardiac vein enlarges to form the coronary sinus.

The middle cardiac vein begins near the apex of the heart and ascends in the posterior interventricular sulcus. It is associated with the posterior interventricular branch of the right or the left coronary artery.

The small cardiac vein begins in the anterior section of the coronary sulcus between the right atrium and the right ventricle. It continues in this groove onto the base of the heart and then enters the coronary sinus. It accompanies the right coronary artery in its course and may receive the right marginal vein.

The posterior cardiac vein lies on the posterior surface of the left ventricle just to the left of the middle cardiac vein. Anterior veins of the right ventricle drain the anterior portion of the right ventricle and enter the right atrium directly.

Venae cordis minimae, or veins of Thebasius, drain directly into the cardiac chambers and are mainly associated with the right atrium and right ventricle.
questions.learning: Great cardiac vein — The great cardiac vein receives venous drainage from the left atrium and both ventricles. The great cardiac vein begins at the apex of the heart.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is/are criteria for anaphylaxis? a. Persistent abdominal cramps and vomiting b. Hypertension c. Urticaria and swollen lips d. Respiratory distress
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. a, c & d

Allergen exposure

↓

IgE on mast cells cross-links

↓

Mast cell degranulation

↓

Histamine, leukotrienes release

↓

Vasodilation + bronchospasm + edema

↓

Anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis is an acute, systemic hypersensitivity reaction involving skin, mucosa, respiratory, and gastrointestinal systems.

Diagnostic criteria include urticaria with angioedema, respiratory compromise, and persistent gastrointestinal symptoms like cramps and vomiting.

| System | Features

| ------ | --------

| Skin | Urticaria, angioedema

| Respiratory | Dyspnea, wheeze, stridor

| Cardiovascular | Hypotension

| GI | Vomiting, cramps

Hypotension, not hypertension, is the cardiovascular manifestation of anaphylaxis.

Hence, options a, c, and d fulfil criteria for anaphylaxis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme acts as the primary glucose sensor in pancreatic β-cells and plays a key role in regulating insulin secretion?
questions.explanation: Insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells is triggered by rising blood glucose levels. The critical first step in this process is the phosphorylation of glucose, which is catalyzed by hexokinase IV, also known as glucokinase. Unlike Hexokinases I, II, and III (Options A, B, and C), which have a high affinity for glucose and are inhibited by their product (glucose-6-phosphate), hexokinase IV has a low affinity and is not inhibited by its product. This low affinity allows the enzyme to act as a "glucose sensor," ensuring that its activity increases linearly as blood glucose levels rise above normal fasting ranges. This metabolic rate-limiting step determines the rate of ATP production, which ultimately leads to the closing of K+ channels and the release of insulin. Therefore, hexokinase IV is the specific enzyme uniquely suited for glucose sensing and the regulation of insulin secretion
questions.learning: Insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells is triggered by rising blood glucose levels. The critical first step in this process is the phosphorylation of glucose, which is catalyzed by hexokinase IV, also known as glucokinase.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 12 week old child presented with fever, cyanosis and fatigue. His chest X ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation

The given X-ray shows figure of 8 or snowman appearance characteristic of total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (TAPVC).

TAPVC refers to a condition in which pulmonary veins instead of draining into the left atrium drain into the right atrium directly or indirectly. This results in anomalous drainage of pulmonary venous blood flow into the systemic venous circulation. It is a cyanotic heart disease with features of congestive heart failure. The patients are irritable and have failure to thrive.

The following types are seen:

• Supracardiac (most common): Common pulmonary vein drains into superior vena cava or the left innominate vein
• Cardiac: Pulmonary veins drain into the right atrium or coronary sinus.
• Infracardiac (always obstructive and most dangerous): Pulmonary veins drain into portal vein or inferior vena cava.

Snowman appearance is classically seen in supracardiac variant of TAPVC. The dilated vertical vein on the left, brachiocephalic vein on top, and the superior vena cava on the right form the head of the snowman; the body of the snowman is formed by the enlarged right atrium. It is shown in the image below.

Other options:

Option B: Tetrology of Fallot comprises pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding of the aorta over the ventricular septum, and right ventricular hypertrophy. On chest X-Ray, the cardiac silhouette appears like a boot ("coeur en sabot”).

Option C: In the transposition of great arteries, the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left ventricle. The X-ray shows cardiomegaly with cardiac contours which appear like an egg on a string.

Option D: Pericardial effusions occur when excessive fluid gets collected in the pericardial space. The X-ray shows globular enlargement of the cardiac shadow giving a water bottle configuration.
questions.learning: Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation — The given X-ray shows figure of 8 or snowman appearance characteristic of total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (TAPVC).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In POPQ classification for uterovaginal prolapse, the only measurement done after reducing the prolapse is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Total vaginal length

The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system is the standardized and internationally accepted method for assessing pelvic organ prolapse. It uses nine specific measurements relative to the hymenal ring. Among these, Total Vaginal Length (TVL) is the only measurement recorded after completely reducing the prolapse.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Genital hiatus (GH): Measured with the prolapse present, from the external urethral meatus to the posterior hymen.
• B. Point C: Represents the leading edge of the cervix (or vaginal cuff after hysterectomy) and is measured during maximal straining, not after reduction.
• C. Point D: Represents the posterior fornix (only if the uterus is present) and is also measured with the prolapse present.
questions.learning: Total vaginal length — The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system is the standardized and internationally accepted method for assessing pelvic organ prolapse.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with tingling in the lateral three fingers and loss of sensation at the base of the thumb on the dorsal hand. Which nerve is involved?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms of tingling in the lateral digits and loss of sensation at the dorsal base of the thumb point to the superficial branch of the radial nerve. This nerve provides cutaneous sensation to the dorsum of the hand, particularly the first web space and the dorsal aspect of the lateral three-and-a-half fingers, excluding the nail beds. The ulnar nerve (Option B) supplies the medial one-and-a-half digits and is not involved here. While the median nerve (Option C) supplies the lateral three-and-a-half digits, its distribution is primarily palmar and includes only the distal dorsal phalanges (fingertips); it does not supply the dorsal root of the thumb. The Anterior Interosseous Nerve (Option D) is a purely motor branch of the median nerve and has no cutaneous sensory distribution. Therefore, the specific loss of sensation on the dorsal aspect of the thumb base confirms radial nerve involvement
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms of tingling in the lateral digits and loss of sensation at the dorsal base of the thumb point to the superficial branch of the radial nerve.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a study to see the effect of a new antihypertensive drug, two groups were made, one group was given the new drug, and the other group was given a different drug. Their mean BP was compared later. Which kind of statistical study is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Unpaired T test

The test of choice to measure the difference in means between two groups in a study, with one group being a control is Unpaired T test.

In this scenario, two groups are being compared hence, Student's t test/ Unpaired t test will be used. If 2 groups are being tested, then T tests are used. In that, if the same group is tested before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used.

Other options:

Option A: The chi-square test is used to compare qualitative data between 2 groups with independent measures.

Option B: The analysis of variance test (ANOVA) is used to test the difference between two or usually more than two groups (means) and here the inferences are made by analyzing the variances.

Option D: Paired t-test compares paired data or pre-intervention and post-intervention data of the same group. This doesn't apply here as the groups are not paired.

Pearl PF0591: Tests of Significance

How to choose which test to use?

* See the variable. Are the variables quantitative or qualitative?

* If the variables are qualitative (nominal), then Chi square test is used.

* If the variables are quantitative, then see whether 2 groups are being tested, or more than 2 groups.

* If 2 groups are being tested, then T tests are used. In that, if the same group is tested before and after, paired T test is used. Otherwise, unpaired T test is used.

* If more than 2 groups are being tested, then use ANOVA.

The tests:

1. T Tests

* Unpaired t tests

* Also known as the student’s t test, independent t test, two-samples t test.

* It's the most commonly used t test and it tests the difference between two groups (the means of 2 groups) independent of each other and indicates how significant the differences are.

* Paired t tests

* "Pairs before marriage are not the same after!"

* So remember paired test is mainly used in comparison of a before and after scenario

* Also known as correlated t test, dependent samples t test.

* It is mainly used on dependent samples For example, the cholesterol level of a person before and after using a specific drug.

* It can also be used when you put the same condition under test using different items or things. For example, same crash safety tests for different cars.

* T scores

* The t score is referred to as the ratio of the difference between two groups and the difference within the groups.

* The smaller the t score, the more similarity there is between two groups and vice versa.

2. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

* The analysis of variance test (ANOVA) is used to test the difference between two or usually more than two groups (means) and here the inferences are made by analyzing the variances.

3. Chi-Square Test

* The Chi-Square test (χ2) is a non-parametric(non-numeric) test and it is used to test hypotheses in relation to nominal scale data or categorical data.

* It is a test of proportions and associations.

* A Chi-square distribution is usually positively skewed but it approaches a normal distribution as its degrees of freedom increases.

* If the frequency of any of the cells of the categorical table is <5, then Fisher’s exact test is used.
questions.learning: Unpaired T test — The test of choice to measure the difference in means between two groups in a study, with one group being a control is Unpaired T test.

questions.text: Blood spill in the operation theatre is cleaned with _____.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: 57-year-old unconscious man is brought to the emergency department by his wife. Thirty minutes prior, the patient developed severe chest pain and asked to be taken to the hospital. On the way, he became unresponsive. In the emergency department, the patient has no spontaneous respirations or circulation and is pronounced dead. An autopsy examination is performed, and a cross-section of the mid-right coronary artery is shown in the exhibit. Which of the following is the most likely immediate cause of death in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ventricular fibrillation

This patient had sudden collapse and death within minutes of severe chest pain, consistent with an acute myocardial infarction. The most common immediate cause of death in the first hour of MI is a lethal ventricular arrhythmia, especially ventricular fibrillation, due to acute ischemia–induced electrical instability.

A. Atrial fibrillation – Rarely causes sudden cardiac death.

B. Cardiac free wall rupture – Occurs 3–7 days post-MI, not within minutes.

D. Ventricular septal rupture – Also a late complication (3–7 days) causing acute heart failure, not instant death.
questions.learning: Ventricular fibrillation — This patient had sudden collapse and death within minutes of severe chest pain, consistent with an acute myocardial infarction.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the largest fund for population and reproduction-related programs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. UNFPA

United Nations Population Fund or formerly known as United Nations Fund for Population Activities(UNFPA), is the largest fund for sexual and reproductive health activities.

The goals of UNFPA are:

* To support reproductive health care for the women and the youth

* To help pregnant women, especially the ones who face maternal complications

* Provide access for all to modern contraceptives.

* Provide training for health workers to ensure childbirths are supervised by skilled attendants

* Prevention of gender-based violence and female genital mutilation

* Prevention of teen pregnancies and ending child marriage

* Delivery of safe birth supplies, dignity kits, and other materials to survivors of conflict and natural disaster

* Collection of data, census and analyze them for development and planning.

The Resources and Funding are divided into core resources and non-core resources.

Core resources are used to effectively provide essential sexual and reproductive health services to those in need and in crisis.

Non-core resources include thematic funds such as UNFPA Supplies, the Maternal and New-born Health Thematic Fund, the Humanitarian Action Thematic Fund, Population Data Thematic Fund, and other funds which are goal-based. Some of the others include regional, issue-based or multi-country programs and initiatives.
questions.learning: UNFPA United Nations Population Fund or formerly known as United Nations Fund for Population Activities(UNFPA), is the largest fund for sexual and reproductive health activities.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 48-year-old male presents to the ER with confusion and shaking of the entire body. He has a history of excessive alcohol consumption. What is the cause of delirium tremens in an alcoholic?
options: Small doses of regular consumption of alcohol
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute infection

Among the given options, acute infection can be a cause of delirium tremens in an alcoholic patient.

Physical illness e.g., hepatitis or pancreatitis predisposes to the syndrome; a person in good physical health rarely has delirium tremens during alcohol withdrawal.

The syndrome usually develops on the third day of admission. A patient admitted for an unrelated condition may unexpectedly have an episode of delirium, which is the first sign of a previously undiagnosed alcohol-related disorder.

Episodes of delirium tremens usually begin at the age of 30-40 years, after 5 to 15 years of heavy drinking, and are typical after a binge. Gradual withdrawal of alcohol does not cause delirium tremens. However, sudden withdrawal can cause it.

Treatment of alcohol withdrawal:

• For patients showing withdrawal symptoms, chlordiazepoxide 25-50 mg every 2-4 hours can be administered orally.
• For patients with delirium tremens, 50-100 mg of chlordiazepoxide should be administered every 4 hours.
• If oral administration of drugs is not possible, intravenous lorazepam can be tried.
questions.learning: Acute infection Among the given options, acute infection can be a cause of delirium tremens in an alcoholic patient. Physical illness e.g., hepatitis or pancreatitis predisposes to the syndrome; a person in good physical health rarely has delirium tremens…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the underlying defect in the congenital malformation shown below?
questions.explanation: The image shows a fetus with caudal regression (sirenomelia/mermaid-like deformity) characterized by fusion of lower limbs and absent or malformed lower body structures. This type of congenital anomaly arises due to a defect in mesoderm formation, particularly in the caudal region of the embryo. During gastrulation (3rd week), the primitive streak forms, and cells migrate to create the three germ layers—ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The mesoderm is responsible for forming muscles, bones, blood vessels, and lower limb structures. If there is defective migration or formation of mesoderm (especially caudal mesoderm), it leads to severe malformations like sirenomelia or caudal regression syndrome. Why other options are wrong: (A) Morulation : Early cell division stage; no organ or limb formation involved (B) Neurulation : Affects neural tube → causes spina bifida/anencephaly, not limb fusion (D) Lateral folding : Causes body wall defects (e.g., omphalocele), not caudal limb anomalies
questions.learning: The image shows a fetus with caudal regression (sirenomelia/mermaid-like deformity) characterized by fusion of lower limbs and absent or malformed lower body structures.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which among the following is pressure epiphysis
questions.explanation: A pressure epiphysis is the articular end of a long bone that participates in joint formation and is responsible for transmitting the weight of the body. The head of the humerus is a classic example, as it forms the shoulder joint and bears mechanical load during arm movement. Other examples include the head of the femur and the lower end of the radius. Regarding the distractors, terms like the "elbow joint" (Option B) and "wrist joint" (Option C) refer to the entire articulation rather than a specific epiphysis. The sternum (Option D) is a flat bone and does not possess epiphyses in the same manner as long bones. Additionally, there are traction epiphyses (like the humeral tubercles) which serve as attachment points for muscles but do not transmit weight. Therefore, the head of the humerus specifically fits the functional definition of a pressure epiphysis
questions.learning: A pressure epiphysis is the articular end of a long bone that participates in joint formation and is responsible for transmitting the weight of the body.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Regarding cold ischemia time (CIT) during organ preservation, which statement is most accurate?
options: Heart can safely tolerate >24 hours of cold ischemia
Kidney typically tolerates the longest CIT among solid organs
Liver tolerates longer CIT than kidney
CIT has no effect on graft survival if UW solution is used
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kidney typically tolerates the longest CIT among solid organs

Cold ischemia time (CIT) is the duration an organ remains preserved at low temperature between procurement and transplantation.

Clinical importance

• Longer CIT → increased risk of delayed graft function

• Higher acute rejection rates

• Reduced long-term graft survival

• Even with preservation solutions (e.g., UW solution), prolonged CIT worsens outcomes.

Organ tolerance to cold ischemia (approximate safe limits)

• Kidney: 24–36 hours (longest tolerance)

• Liver: 8–12 hours

• Pancreas: 12–18 hours

• Heart: 4–6 hours (least tolerant)

• Lung: 6–8 hours
questions.learning: Kidney typically tolerates the longest CIT among solid organs Cold ischemia time (CIT) is the duration an organ remains preserved at low temperature between procurement and transplantation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 40 year old P2L2 presents to your office with foul smelling bloody discharge per vaginum. She has been diagnosed with Carcinoma of the cervix Stage III B as per FIGO classification. What is the primary treatment option for this case?
options: Radical Hysterectomy + Pelvic lymph node dissection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chemoradiation

The treatment option for Stage III B Ca Cervix ,as per FIGO 2018 guidelines is Chemoradiation.

Chemoradiation can improve survival rates. It allows for remission in certain cases or reduction in morbidity.

Pelvic exenteration may be considered in cases where a fistula is present.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male patient presented with a sudden onset of scrotal pain and discharge. Based on the image below, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fournier's gangrene

The given scenario of an elderly male patient with sudden-onset scrotal pain and discharge, with the image showing a blackish discoloration of the scrotum, is likely to be Fournier's gangrene.

Fournier's gangrene is an uncommon polymicrobial infection involving the perineal soft tissue, external genitalia, and perianal region. There is subcutaneous tissue inflammation leading to obliterative arteritis and gangrene. It typically follows minor injuries or procedures in the perineal area, urethral dilatation, and injection for hemorrhoids are some of the etiological factors.

Clinically, sudden scrotal pain with associated prostration, pallor, and pyrexia can be seen. Other features such as crepitus and foul-smelling exudate can be present.

Emergency surgical debridement is needed after initial measures like fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics are undertaken. Urinary diversion and other supportive measures are useful in the management of the condition.

Other options:

Option A: Torsion of testis is a surgical emergency typically seen in the age group of 10-25 years. It is characterized by sudden groin and lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Examination findings reveal a swollen, tender scrotum and testis with a twisted tender cord above it and loss of cremasteric reflex.

Option B: Acute epididymo-orchitis is an infection of the epididymis and testis. It is seen in sexually-active young men. In older men, it is seen following a urinary tract infection, secondary to an indwelling catheter. The features include groin ache, fever, swollen and painful epididymis and testis.

Option C: Scrotal carcinoma is a rare carcinoma that is seen in workers exposed to oil, coal products, and aromatic hydrocarbons. It starts as a wart or ulcer in the scrotum and can extend to the testis.
questions.learning: Fournier's gangrene — The given scenario of an elderly male patient with sudden-onset scrotal pain and discharge, with the image showing a blackish discoloration of the scrotum, is likely to be Fournier's gangrene.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate next step in management for an elderly man who has been on prolonged bed rest and now presents with acute breathlessness and chest pain?
questions.explanation: The patient's history of "prolonged bed rest" (a major risk factor for Deep Vein Thrombosis) followed by "sudden onset breathlessness and chest pain" is the classic clinical presentation of a Pulmonary Embolism (PE). In a hemodynamically stable patient with a high clinical suspicion of PE, the most appropriate next action and the definitive gold standard for diagnosis is a CT Pulmonary Angiogram (CTPA) (Option A). While an ECG (Option B) should be done to rule out myocardial infarction, it often shows non-specific findings in PE. A plain CT thorax (Option C) without intravenous contrast would not be able to visualize the intravascular clots. Echocardiography (Option D) is useful for identifying right ventricular strain in severe cases but is not a primary diagnostic tool for the embolus itself. Therefore, CTPA should be prioritized to confirm the presence of emboli in the pulmonary arteries and initiate immediate anticoagulation therapy
questions.learning: The patient's history of "prolonged bed rest" (a major risk factor for Deep Vein Thrombosis) followed by "sudden onset breathlessness and chest pain" is the classic clinical presentation of a Pulmonary Embolism (PE).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which region of the digestive tract produces and secretes the enzyme enteropeptidase?
questions.explanation: Enteropeptidase, also known as enterokinase, is a crucial enzyme for protein digestion. It is secreted by the brush border cells (enterocytes) of the duodenum. The primary role of enteropeptidase is to catalyze the conversion of the inactive pancreatic proenzyme trypsinogen into its active form, trypsin. Once trypsin is formed, it triggers a cascade of activation for other pancreatic proteases like chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase. The stomach (Option A) secretes pepsinogen, which is activated by hydrochloric acid. The jejunum (Option C) and ileum (Option D) are primarily involved in the absorption of nutrients rather than the initiation of this specific proteolytic cascade. A deficiency in enteropeptidase can lead to severe protein malabsorption and failure to thrive. Thus, the duodenum is the critical anatomical site for the secretion of this "master switch" enzyme of protein digestion
questions.learning: Enteropeptidase, also known as enterokinase, is a crucial enzyme for protein digestion. It is secreted by the brush border cells (enterocytes) of the duodenum.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with fever, and his viral serology shows HBsAg positive and IgM anti-HBc antibody positive. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these results?
questions.explanation: The combination of HBsAg positive and IgM anti-HBc positive is diagnostic for Acute Hepatitis B infection. HBsAg indicates the presence of the virus, while the IgM class of antibodies against the core antigen (anti-HBc) is a definitive marker for a primary, recent infection within the last six months. In Chronic Hepatitis B (Option B) or persistent infection (Option D), HBsAg remains positive for more than six months, but the core antibody shifts from the IgM to the IgG class. The Window Period (Option C) occurs when HBsAg has disappeared but the anti-HBs antibody has not yet appeared; during this specific time, IgM anti-HBc might be the only detectable marker of a recent infection. Clinically, acute hepatitis B presents with fever, jaundice, and significantly elevated transaminases. Most adults clear the virus spontaneously. Monitoring markers is essential to differentiate acute from chronic states, as chronic infection carries risks of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
questions.learning: The combination of HBsAg positive and IgM anti-HBc positive is diagnostic for Acute Hepatitis B infection. HBsAg indicates the presence of the virus, while the IgM class of antibodies against the core antigen (anti-HBc) is a definitive marker for a…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Sudden painful loss of vision in one eye is due to the lesion at?
questions.explanation: Sudden, painful loss of vision in one eye is the classic clinical presentation of Optic Neuritis, an inflammatory lesion of the optic nerve. This is most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis. The pain is typically retro-orbital and is significantly worsened by eye movements. Lesions at the Optic chiasma (Option B) typically result in bitemporal hemianopia—a painless, bilateral visual field defect. Lesions of the Optic tract (Option C) or the Visual cortex (Option D) cause homonymous hemianopia affecting the field of vision in both eyes, and these are almost always painless. Other causes of sudden vision loss, like Central Retinal Artery Occlusion or Retinal Detachment, are characteristically painless. Therefore, the combination of sudden onset, lateralization to one eye, and localized pain points specifically to an optic nerve pathology. Immediate ophthalmological and neurological evaluation is required, often involving MRI of the brain and orbits to assess for demyelinating disease
questions.learning: Sudden, painful loss of vision in one eye is the classic clinical presentation of Optic Neuritis, an inflammatory lesion of the optic nerve. This is most commonly associated with multiple sclerosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Arrange the stages of wound healing in the correct sequence?
questions.explanation: Wound healing is a dynamic, overlapping process that follows a strictly programmed sequence to restore tissue integrity. 1. Hemostasis: Immediate vasoconstriction and platelet plug formation to stop bleeding. 2. Inflammation: Begins within minutes; neutrophils and macrophages arrive to clear debris and pathogens. 3. Proliferation: Fibroblasts migrate to the site, depositing collagen and creating granulation tissue, while new blood vessels form (angiogenesis). 4. Remodeling (Maturation): The final, longest phase where the temporary Type III collagen is replaced by stronger Type I collagen and the scar matures. Options A, B, and D provide incorrect chronological orders. Understanding this sequence is vital for wound management; for example, excessive inflammation can lead to chronic non-healing wounds, while a failure in the remodeling phase can result in hypertrophic scars or keloids. Clinicians must ensure that each phase progresses normally to achieve optimal functional and aesthetic outcomes
questions.learning: Wound healing is a dynamic, overlapping process that follows a strictly programmed sequence to restore tissue integrity. Hemostasis: Immediate vasoconstriction and platelet plug formation to stop bleeding.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How is water collected for bacteriological examination during a disease outbreak?
options: Collect water from already leaking taps
Before collecting, let water flow for at least 1 minute
Water sample container is kept close to the tap avoid spillage
Collect from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Collect from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing

During a disease outbreak, for collection of a water sample for bacteriological examination from a tap in regular use, water is collected from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing.

If water samples are to be collected from a tap that is not regularly used, they should be first sterilized by heating. Then, the tap is cooled and opened fully and the initial water stream is let out to flow before the sample is collected.

The sample bottle must be held near the base with a hand and the stopper and paper cover over it are removed together and held in the fingers.

Other options:

Option A (Collect water from already leaking taps): Collecting water from leaking taps is not recommended as it increases the risk of contamination and may not provide an accurate representation of water quality.

Option B (Before collecting, let water flow for at least 1 minute): This option is close to the correct answer but falls short, as it is recommended to let the water flow for at least two minutes to flush out stagnant water in the pipe.

Option C (Water sample container is kept close to the tap to avoid spillage): While keeping the sample container close to the tap is a good practice to avoid spillage, it is not the main concern during the collection of water samples for bacteriological examination.
questions.learning: Collect from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing During a disease outbreak, for collection of a water sample for bacteriological examination from a tap in regular use, water is collected from a gentle stream of water to avoid splashing.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 5 year old boy fell on his outstretched hand. X-ray is shown below. Which of the following vessel is most commonly affected?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brachial artery

The given X-ray shows a supracondylar fracture of the humerus and injury to the brachial artery is the most common vascular complication.

The fracture most commonly caused by a fall on an outstretched hand in a child is the supracondylar fracture of the humerus. As the hand strikes the ground, the elbow is forced into hyperextension resulting in a fracture of the humerus above the condyles.

• The brachial artery is usually injured by the sharp edge of the proximal fragment.
• Sometimes flexor muscles of the forearm - flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus (medial-half) may suffer ischemic damage leading to Volkmann's ischemia leading to compartment syndrome.

While injury to the brachial artery is the commonest vascular complication, however, malunion is the most common complication of supracondylar fracture of the humerus.

Other delayed complications:

• Malunion - Cubitus varus / Gunstock deformity
• Volkmann’s ischaemic contracture
• Myositis ossificans
questions.learning: Brachial artery — The given X-ray shows a supracondylar fracture of the humerus and injury to the brachial artery is the most common vascular complication.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 73-year-old patient presents with painless rectal bleeding. Which of the below-mentioned investigations are done for this patient?

1. Colonoscopy
2. CECT
3. CEA
4. CA 19-9
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Colonoscopy, CECT and CEA (Carcinoembryonic antigen) can be done in an old patient presenting with painless rectal bleeding. Serum CA 19-9 is a pancreatic cancer biomarker and has no role in this case.

Rectal bleeding occurs due to pathology of the lower gastrointestinal tract below the ligament of Treitz. The differentials that can be considered in a case of rectal bleeding are:

• Colon cancer
• Inflammatory bowel disease
• Diverticular diseases
• Hemorrhoids
• Angiodysplasia

Colonoscopy with biopsy has a key role in the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease, distinguishing between ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s colitis and monitoring the response to treatment. Colonoscopy is also the investigation of choice if colorectal cancer is suspected, especially in old patients. Angiodysplasia is suspected in patients above the age of 50 and can be identified by a colonoscopy.

Computed tomography (CT) colonography is sensitive in picking up polyps and has the advantage of being less invasive than colonoscopy. Spiral CT can aid in the diagnosis of complicated diverticular disease.

Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is a non-specific serum biomarker that is elevated in colorectal cancer and hence may be done in this case.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Colonoscopy, CECT and CEA (Carcinoembryonic antigen) can be done in an old patient presenting with painless rectal bleeding. Serum CA 19-9 is a pancreatic cancer biomarker and has no role in this case.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents in OPD with a history of fever and cough for 5 days. On auscultation, crepts were heard on right side. Chest X-ray is given below. Mark the correct finding in this case?
options: Apical segment of Right lower lobe consolidation
Posterior segment of right lower lobe consolidation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right middle lobe consolidation

Right middle lobe consolidation is suggested by the obscuration of the right heart border and the specific location of opacity on the chest X-ray, aligned with the patient's clinical presentation of respiratory symptoms.

Key Radiological Sign → Silhouette Sign ⭐

Right heart border is obscured

This is the giveaway because-

• Right middle lobe lies adjacent to right heart border
• When it consolidates → the border disappears

| Lost Border | Diagnosis

| ----------- | ---------

| Right heart border | Right middle lobe ⭐

| Left heart border | Lingula
