questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a causality triage scenario, following a road traffic accident, whom would you treat first?
options: 60-year-old conscious patient with pants covered in blood
40-year-old female who is unconscious with laboured breathing
20-year-old female who is agitated with anxiety and increased breathing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 40-year-old female who is unconscious with laboured breathing

In triage, priority is given based on immediacy of life-threatening conditions, following the ABCDE (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) principle.

An unconscious patient with laboured breathing has a compromised airway and respiration, which are immediately life-threatening and require urgent intervention.

Patients who are conscious, crying, anxious, or bleeding but stable can be managed after stabilization of airway and breathing–threatened cases.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A body fluid sample is being studied and has Na: 10 mEq/L, K: 140 mEq/L, CI: 4 mEq/L. Identify the compartment from which the sample has been obtained.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intracellular fluid

The sample obtained is from the intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment. The ICF contains large quantities of potassium (K+) ions - 140 mEq/L . The ICF also has lesser amounts of sodium (Na+) and Chloride (Cl-) ions.

The extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment includes interstitial fluids and plasma. In contrast to the ICF, the ECF has an abundance of sodium, chloride, calcium and bicarbonate ions, and lesser amounts of potassium, phosphate and magnesium ions.

The image below depicts the proportion of the important anions and cations present in the intracellular and extracellular fluids.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of increased urinary frequency. On cystoscopic examination, a pale ureteric orifice is observed. A KUB X-ray has been provided for evaluation. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with increased urinary frequency and a pale ureteric orifice on cystoscopy, which is a classic feature of genitourinary tuberculosis (GU TB). In bladder tuberculosis, chronic inflammation leads to fibrosis, reduced vascularity, and scarring, giving the ureteric orifice a pale, gaping (“golf hole”) appearance. The provided KUB X-ray supports this diagnosis by suggesting calcifications or irregularities in the urinary tract, which are commonly seen in chronic TB infection. Over time, TB can lead to a contracted bladder (“thimble bladder”), ureteric strictures, and renal involvement. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Bladder carcinoma → Typically shows irregular mass, hematuria; not pale ureteric orifice (B) Schistosomiasis → Causes calcified bladder wall (“sandy patches”), but cystoscopy differs (D) Papilloma → Benign tumor with papillary projections, not associated with pale orifice

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A Tzanck smear prepared from a vesicle sample revealed multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)

Tzanck cells or multinucleated giant cells are indicative of Herpes Simplex virus.

In genital herpes, clusters of vesicles are seen on an erythematous base along with painful and pruritic lymphadenopathy and Tzanck cells or multinucleated giant cells are seen in this condition.

The Tzanck smear is a rapid, sensitive, and inexpensive diagnostic method.  Smears are prepared from the lesions, from the base of vesicles, and stained with a 1% aqueous solution of O-toluidine blue for 15 seconds. Multinucleated giant cells with faceted nuclei and homogeneously stained ground glass chromatin -  Tzanck cells are seen.

The typical herpes lesions are thin-walled, umbilicated vesicles, the roof of which breaks down, leaving tiny superficial ulcers. They heal without scarring. The most common site of cutaneous lesions in the face - on the cheeks, chin, around the mouth, or on the forehead.

Other Options:

Option B: Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) causes structural changes in the epithelial cells of the skin. These abnormal epithelial cells are called koilocytes, and their presence is characteristic of HPV infection. The koilocytes have large hyperchromatic nuclei and a perinuclear halo, as shown below. But it doesn't show any multinucleated giant cell.

Option C: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)  doesn't show any multinucleated giant cell, But it can cause infectious mononucleosis and peripheral smear finding shows Downey cells or ballerina skirt cells. They are atypical lymphocytes with abundant basophilic cytoplasm containing clear vacuolations and prominent nucleoli. They become large as a result of antigen stimulation.

Option D: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) on the other hand doesnt show any characteristic cell or multinucleated giant cell on peripheral smear. Although CD4 T cell count goes on decreasing.
